World.title: Lebanon parliament votes to abolish death penalty
World.content:
Lebanon's parliament has voted to abolish the death penalty, a move that would make it the first country in the Middle East to formally end capital punishment.

A majority of MPs in the 128-seat parliament backed the measure on Tuesday, while Hezbollah's parliamentary bloc voted against it.

The legislation will now go to the cabinet before being passed to President Joseph Aoun for signing. The government has already expressed its support for the measure.

Lebanon has not carried out an execution since January 2004, although courts have continued to hand down death sentences. Rights groups estimate that more than 78 people remain on death row.

Under the new legislation, capital punishment will be replaced with life imprisonment with hard labour. However, the legislation does not yet set out in detail how the new sentence would be enforced.

Hard labour is already written into Lebanese law but has rarely been implemented in recent years. The country's financial crisis and overcrowded prisons have limited the authorities' resources and capacity.

The latest legislation follows years of campaigning by civil society groups and lawyers for the removal of capital punishment from Lebanese law.

"We cannot solve a crime with a crime or end violence with violence," Oragit Younan told the BBC.

As co-founder of the Lebanese Association for Civil Rights, she led a nearly three-decade campaign to abolish the death penalty in Lebanon.

"We are in a war, and people [have been] killed every day, so even in this situation, we can fight, we can struggle for human rights, and we can win. We can be a model for others," she said.

Tuesday's vote in parliament follows more than two decades of a de facto moratorium on executions. An execution required a decree signed by the president, prime minister and justice minister - but no such decree has been signed since 2004.

Under Lebanese law, the death penalty could previously be imposed for some of the country's most serious offences, including aggravated murder, certain terrorism-related crimes resulting in death, treason, espionage and offences against state security.

Previous attempts to abolish the death penalty have failed, including legislation introduced in parliament in 2004 and a proposal from the justice ministry in 2008.

Lebanon's move comes as the use of the death penalty remains contested elsewhere in the Middle East.

Jordan resumed executions in June, carrying out its first since 2017.

In Israel, its parliament has approved legislation that allows for the expansion of the circumstances in which capital punishment can be imposed.

Israeli MPs passed a new law in May to impose the death penalty and conduct public trials for those involved in the Hamas-led attacks and mass hostage-taking in Israel in October 2023.

Elsewhere, the UN human rights chief has said he is alarmed by the rise in executions in Iran, with capital punishment continuing to be used "to instil fear among the population and suppress dissent".

In Iran, at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests, UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk said earlier this month.

World.title: Bondi Beach shooting hero's assault charges dropped by police
World.content:
A man who was hailed a hero for disarming one of the Bondi Beach shooters in December has had assault charges against him dropped by police.

Ahmed al Ahmed was charged in June with domestic violence common assault, as well as stalking and intimidation, after an alleged incident with his father in March at a home in southwest Sydney. Ahmed denied both charges.

On Wednesday, in a local Sydney court, prosecutors withdrew the charges after it was agreed that Ahmed would abide by an apprehended domestic violence order for 12 months, limiting his contact with his father.

Outside the court, Ahmed, 44, welcomed the development, telling reporters that he was a "free man" and that he hoped for "peace".

Defence lawyer Mohamed Sakr said in court that the order prohibiting Ahmed from assaulting, threatening, stalking or intimidating his father had been accepted without admissions, according to national broadcaster ABC.

Ahmed made global headlines last year after footage emerged of him tackling one of two gunmen who had opened fire during a Jewish event at Sydney's Bondi Beach, killing 15 people.

World.title: ANALYSIS: OsunDecides2026: Ex-governors, their remarkable feats, low moments
World.content:
Osun State was created from the old Oyo State in August 1991 by the military government of General Ibrahim Babangida. Since then, the state has been ruled by appointed military administrators and elected civilian governors, each leaving a distinct imprint on its political and developmental trajectory.

The state’s first administrator was Leo Ajiborisha, a colonel, who oversaw the establishment of some of the institutions required to run the newly created state before handing over to its first elected governor, late Isiaka Adeleke, in January 1992.

The return to civilian rule in 1999 ushered in a succession of elected administrations led by Bisi Akande, Olagunsoye Oyinlola, Rauf Aregbesola and Gboyega Oyetola. The incumbent governor, Ademola Adeleke, was elected in 2022 amidst several political controversies.

Over the past three decades, these administrations have pursued different approaches to governance. Some have been celebrated for fiscal discipline, social welfare programmes, institutional development, and infrastructure, while others have been criticised for debt accumulation, labour disputes, political infighting, electoral controversies, and allegations of financial impropriety.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

This analysis examines the major achievements and low moments associated with each administration and what they reveal about the evolution of governance in Osun State, as the state prepares for another gubernatorial election on Saturday.

Leo Ajiborisha: Building the foundation

Leo Ajiborisha, a military officer, was appointed the first administrator of Osun State upon its creation in 1991.

His administration largely focused on establishing the basic institutional framework of the new state and preparing it for the transition to civilian rule.

Among the notable steps taken during his tenure was the establishment of the Osun State Civil Service Commission in September 1991. His administration also established the Osun State Broadcasting Corporation, with its radio station in Ile-Ife, which commenced operations in November 1991.

Mr Ajiborisha handed over power to Isiaka Adeleke in January 1992, marking the beginning of elected civilian administration in the new state.

Mr Ajiborisha’s tenure was brief, reflecting the transitional nature of the military administration.

He later held senior military positions, including Director of Operations at the Defence Headquarters and Principal Staff Officer to former Head of State Abdulsalami Abubakar.

Isiaka Adeleke: The first civilian governor

Isiaka Adeleke became Osun State’s first elected governor in January 1992 under the defunct Social Democratic Party (SDP).

As the pioneer civilian governor, he faced the task of consolidating the institutional structures established during the state’s formative period.

One of the notable initiatives of his administration was the establishment of the Osun State Polytechnic, Iree, which is now part of the state’s tertiary education infrastructure.

Mr Adeleke’s administration was abruptly terminated following the military takeover of November 1993, which aborted Nigeria’s Third Republic.

His tenure, therefore, lasted only about two years and did not provide sufficient time for many of his administration’s programmes to mature and manifest.

He eventually served as a two-term senator, representing Osun West from 2007 to 2011 as a PDP member. He was later reelected under the APC in 2015 but died in April 2017.

Anthony Udofia and Anthony Obi: The return to military rule

Following the 1993 military takeover, Nigeria and Osun returned to military administration.

Anthony Udofia became the second military administrator of the state under the regime of Sani Abacha, Nigeria’s late head of state. His administration focused largely on maintaining government operations and pursuing social and developmental programmes.

Mr Udofia was replaced by Anthony Obi, who served as military administrator from August 1996 to August 1998. Mr Obi’s tenure coincided with one of the most politically uncertain periods in Nigeria’s history.

Mr Obi was later redeployed to Abia State, where he remained until the return to civilian rule in May 1999.

Theophilus Bamgboye: Preparing for civilian rule

Theophilus Bamgboye became the fourth military administrator of Osun State under General Abdulsalami Abubakar’s transitional government.

His administration operated during the final phase of military rule and was primarily concerned with maintaining government institutions while preparing the state for the return to democratic governance in 1999.

Mr Bamgboye, an indigene of Omu-Aran in Kwara State, handed over to Bisi Akande, the first elected governor of Osun State under the Fourth Republic.

Bisi Akande: Fiscal discipline and difficult reforms

Mr Akande, who was elected on the platform of the Alliance for Democracy, governed the state from 1999 to 2003.

His administration was strongly associated with fiscal discipline, institutional reforms and an emphasis on reducing government waste.

Mr Akande’s government also pursued free education and healthcare initiatives, reflecting the social-democratic orientation of the Alliance for Democracy administrations that controlled all the South-west states at the time.

His administration’s attempt to rationalise and downsize the state civil service generated significant opposition from organised labour.

The reforms, which were presented as necessary, were opposed by workers and contributed to the political difficulties the governor faced in the 2003 election.

Mr Akande eventually lost the governorship to Olagunsoye Oyinlola, thus spending only one term of four years in office. He had served as the secretary to the defunct Oyo State Government and later deputy governor of the state under late Governor Bola Ige.

Olagunsoye Oyinlola: Expanding infrastructure and education

Olagunsoye Oyinlola, a retired brigadier-general and former military administrator of Lagos State, governed Osun State from 2003 to 2010 on the platform of the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP.

His administration placed considerable emphasis on infrastructure, agriculture, education, healthcare, water supply, transportation, security and job creation.

One of his most significant legacies was the establishment of Osun State University, which was designed as a multi-campus institution to expand access to university education across the state.

His administration also implemented various welfare and development programmes, particularly in rural communities.

The low moments

Mr Oyinlola became embroiled in a prolonged legal and political dispute over the 2007 governorship election.

The dispute culminated in the Court of Appeal nullifying his election victory in 2010, resulting in his removal from office and the emergence of Rauf Aregbesola.

The episode became one of the defining political controversies of his administration and further demonstrated the growing influence of electoral litigation in Nigeria’s political system. His sack by the court led to off-cycle governorship elections in Osun.

Rauf Aregbesola: Ambitious reforms amid financial crisis

Rauf Aregbesola governed Osun State from 2010 to 2018, becoming the state’s longest-serving elected governor so far.

His administration was marked by ambitious infrastructure projects, aggressive social welfare programmes and major reforms in education.

Mr Aregbesola’s supporters often point to his administration’s expansive approach to public works and social intervention as among its most enduring legacies.

Major achievements

The administration established the Osun Youth Empowerment Scheme, popularly known as O-YES, which provided employment opportunities for thousands of young people.

In education, his government introduced the “Opon Imo”(Tablet of Knowledge) digital learning initiative, which provided students with electronic educational materials. It also constructed mega schools as part of a broader attempt to transform public education infrastructure.

Another major initiative was the O-MEALS school feeding programme, which provided meals to pupils in public primary schools.

Infrastructure was also a major feature of the administration. Mr Aregbesola’s government undertook extensive road construction and rehabilitation across urban and rural communities.

His administration also promoted cultural identity, including the adoption of the title “Ogbeni” and the designation of Isese Day as a public holiday.

The low moments

The most controversial aspect of Mr Aregbesola’s tenure was the state’s worsening financial situation and the resulting impact on workers and pensioners.

Amid declining federal allocations and the state’s debt obligations, the government introduced a “modulated” salary structure under which some workers received only part of their monthly salaries. The policy generated intense opposition from labour unions and created hardship for thousands of workers.

His education reforms also generated significant controversy. The restructuring and reclassification of schools, including the merger of some historically single-sex schools, triggered protests and religious tensions, particularly over the issue of school uniforms and the use of the hijab.

The administration’s borrowing and debt accumulation also became a major political issue. Critics argued that the loans used to finance infrastructure projects created a substantial financial burden for subsequent governments.

Mr Aregbesola’s political relationship with his successor, Gboyega Oyetola, later deteriorated, contributing to divisions within the Osun chapter of the APC.

Gboyega Oyetola: Fiscal consolidation and political turbulence

Gboyega Oyetola succeeded Mr Aregbesola in 2018 after a controversial election and governed until 2022.

Political tension in Osun State peaked during the fiercely contested September 2018 poll, which was eventually declared inconclusive. This led to a controversial supplementary rerun, which escalated allegations of voter intimidation and high-stakes manoeuvring between the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) and the opposition Peoples Democratic Party (PDP)

During the 22 September 2018 election, early tallies showed Mr Adeleke was leading Mr Oyetola by a narrow margin of 353 votes, but INEC declared the election inconclusive because the total number of cancelled votes (over 1,000) exceeded that margin.

The PDP, Mr Adeleke’s party, and various observers criticised the inconclusive status, describing it as a “manoeuvre” by federal authorities to favour the ruling party. This prompted INEC to schedule a rerun for 27 September 2018, in seven polling units across four local government areas. The political tension between the APC and PDP became apparent, as the PDP deployed almost all its forces, including both current and former governors at the time, as well as the then Senate President, Bukola Saraki; all in an effort to influence the election outcome in their favour.

Third-place Social Democratic Party (SDP) candidate Iyiola Omisore eventually aligned with the APC ahead of the rerun, despite several attempts by the PDP to gain his support.

The rerun took place under unprecedented security deployment. PDP leaders and local monitors reported widespread harassment, heavy clampdowns, and restrictions preventing their supporters and accredited journalists/observers from accessing polling units

Mr Oyetola of the APC was ultimately declared the winner after the supplementary election, cementing a highly polarised political atmosphere that left lasting friction across the state.

The Oyetola administration inherited significant financial obligations, including salary and pension arrears, while also facing the challenge of sustaining government services amid fiscal constraints.

One of his central priorities was financial management. His administration stopped the payment of modulated salaries and restored full monthly salaries to workers.

The government also began addressing inherited pension obligations and invested in healthcare infrastructure.

Major achievements

The Oyetola administration renovated and upgraded primary healthcare centres across the state and invested in the State Specialist Hospital in Asubiaro, Osogbo.

It also constructed the Olaiya Flyover in the state capital, one of the most visible infrastructure projects of his administration.

In education, his government reversed some of the controversial reforms introduced by the Aregbesola administration, including changes to school names, uniforms, and school structures.

The administration also sought to reduce the state’s reliance on new borrowing.

The low moments

Mr Oyetola’s tenure was overshadowed by intense political rivalry within the APC, particularly his deteriorating relationship with Mr Aregbesola.

The internal division weakened the party ahead of the 2022 governorship election, which Mr Oyetola narrowly lost to Mr Adeleke of the PDP.

His convoy was also attacked during the EndSARS protests in October 2020, highlighting the volatile security environment of the period.

After leaving office, the Oyetola administration faced allegations from the succeeding government concerning the management of state resources and certain projects. Mr Oyetola, who is currently the Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, and his associates rejected such allegations, describing them as politically motivated.

Ademola Adeleke: Infrastructure, welfare and political battles

Ademola Adeleke became governor in November 2022 after defeating Mr Oyetola in the governorship election.

His administration has emphasised infrastructure, workers’ welfare, healthcare and education.

The Adeleke administration has highlighted the construction and rehabilitation of roads, as well as the development of major infrastructure projects, including flyovers in Osogbo.

Workers’ welfare has also featured prominently. The government says it has cleared substantial portions of inherited salary and pension arrears while improving welfare for pensioners.

In healthcare, the administration has undertaken the rehabilitation and upgrading of primary healthcare centres, including efforts to improve power supply at health facilities.

The administration has also supported the development of the University of Ilesa and promoted initiatives to expand the state’s digital economy.

The low moments

Despite these initiatives, Governor Adeleke’s administration has faced significant political and legal controversies.

One of the biggest disputes has centred on the control of local governments following legal battles over the status of elected local government chairpersons. The controversy generated tension between the state government and opposition politicians and raised questions about compliance with court decisions.

The government also faced criticism following its decision to terminate the appointments of some workers recruited by the previous administration, particularly teachers and health workers.

Its handling of the state’s finances has similarly attracted scrutiny, with opposition politicians questioning some expenditures and projects. The administration has rejected allegations of financial impropriety and defended its spending as part of its development agenda.

Mr Adeleke’s public persona has also remained a source of political debate. His frequent public dancing, which supporters see as a sign of his accessibility and connection with ordinary citizens, has been used by critics to question the seriousness of his leadership.

The Overview

Political analysts have argued that the history of governance in Osun State reflects many of the broader challenges confronting Nigeria’s subnational governments.

The state’s early military administrators focused primarily on establishing institutions and maintaining stability. The return to democracy brought a stronger emphasis on education, healthcare, infrastructure and social welfare.

Yet the experience of successive administrations also reveals a recurring tension between ambitious development programmes and the state’s financial capacity.

Mr Akande’s fiscal reforms generated labour resistance. Mr Oyinlola’s administration was defined in part by electoral litigation, while Mr Aregbesola’s ambitious infrastructure and welfare programmes were accompanied by a severe salary crisis and concerns about debt.

Mr Oyetola attempted fiscal consolidation but struggled with internal party divisions. Mr Adeleke, the dancing governor, has pursued infrastructure and welfare programmes while facing legal disputes and political opposition. This political crisis and party fragmentation have lingered, prompting Mr Adeleke to defect to the Accord Party, where he will seek re-election on Saturday.

The political crisis/tension pattern unravelling in the state suggests that the central challenge for Osun is not merely the ability to initiate projects but the capacity to sustain them without imposing unsustainable financial obligations on future administrations.

As the state approaches another political cycle, the competing legacies of its former governors will remain important to the debate over what constitutes effective governance: infrastructure, social welfare, fiscal discipline, institutional stability or political inclusiveness.

World.title: 2027 Elections: Police, experts to address emerging security threats at Owerri conference
World.content:
Lenders Consult International says it will deepen its partnership with the Nigeria Police Force as the country prepares for the 2027 general elections, backing a strategic conference aimed at improving the management of electoral security.

The company’s Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Shina Philips, made this known on Tuesday at a press conference at the Force Headquarters, Abuja, ahead of the sixth Conference and Retreat for Senior Police Officers (CARSPO).

The three-day conference, scheduled for 21 to 23 September in Owerri, Imo State, will focus on “Developing a Nigerian Police Roadmap for Effective Management of Security During Elections.”

The Nigeria Police Force is organising the event in conjunction with Lenders Consult International.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Philips said the partnership, which began in 2019, was aimed at supporting the police as the lead internal security agency, particularly as preparations for the 2027 elections gather momentum.

“As a private organisation, Lenders Consult International is committed to strengthening our strategic partnership with the Nigeria Police as they prepare to provide adequate security during the 2027 General Elections across the country.”

He said the company’s position aligned with that of the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, on the Force’s importance to the electoral process.

Mr Philips quoted the police chief as saying, “Stability of the electoral process largely depends on the Police as the lead agency in internal democracy.”

Police to devise 2027 election security plan

According to a statement by the Force Public Relations Officer, Ani Iniedu, the conference will bring together senior police officers, policing experts and other relevant stakeholders to examine emerging electoral security challenges.

The discussions will cover intelligence-led policing, police-community partnerships, digital technologies and artificial intelligence, among other contemporary approaches to policing.

The conference will primarily involve officers of the rank of Commissioner of Police and above, with deliberations expected to produce practical measures to strengthen the Force’s capacity before, during, and after the 2027 elections.

The Police said the proposed strategies would focus on protecting voters, electoral personnel, candidates, electoral materials and the wider public.

Lenders Consult seeks broader support for the Police

Mr Philips said his organisation had secured sponsorship for every edition of the conference since it received approval to organise the event, describing the initiative as part of its contribution to supporting the police.

“Since inception, when we first got approval to organise the Conference and Retreat for Senior Police Officers, we have worked to secure sponsorship for every single edition. We consider this our contribution to support the selfless and patriotic work of the Nigeria Police. While commending the government’s efforts, we emphasise that Nigerians need to support the police in fulfilling their constitutional mandate to secure our society and maintain public order.”

He said the conference had evolved beyond a domestic gathering, with international participants now attending, and pledged to maintain its focus on contemporary policing approaches.

“Our vision for the Conference and Retreat has emerged as the Conference and Retreat continues to attract international participants. As the giant of Africa, Nigeria is leading the drive to adopt modern policing methods. We will continue to partner with the Nigerian Police authorities to ensure the event remains focused on delivering cutting-edge policing solutions.”

The Imo State Government will host the 2026 edition. Mr Philips expressed appreciation to Governor Hope Uzodimma for agreeing to host the conference for the third time.

“We also express our appreciation to the Governor of Imo State, His Excellency, Senator Hope Uzodimma CON, for agreeing to host this important event for the third time.”

The opening ceremony is scheduled for 10 a.m. on 21 September in Owerri.

The Police said the conference is part of efforts to strengthen strategic leadership, professionalism and operational preparedness ahead of the 2027 general elections.

World.title: Africa’s tech boom starts at home, By Sally Wentworth
World.content:
The continent is on the move: there are more than 70 Internet exchange points across Africa; Internet penetration across the continent has grown from less than 10 per cent in 2010 to over 38 per cent today; and Africa hosts some of the world’s best technical leadership, within a thriving ecosystem rooted in civil society.

21 years’ ago, if someone in Lagos wanted to send an email to someone in Abuja – a distance of about seven hundred and sixty kilometres – that email would first travel thousands of kilometres to Europe or North America before returning to Nigeria. African Internet traffic was taking a detour around the world to reach its neighbours.

This detour was expensive and slow – burdening local businesses with high transit costs and leaving African Internet users with sluggish and unreliable connections.

In response to that challenge, the African Peering and Interconnection Forum was born in 2010. The goal was simple: to solve this fundamental connectivity problem. Together, network operators, technical experts and policymakers have successfully created much of the infrastructure to keep local Internet traffic local.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Driven in no small part by Nigerian commitment, collaboration and energy, a significant amount of African Internet traffic now stays in Africa.

The continent is on the move: there are more than 70 Internet exchange points across Africa; Internet penetration across the continent has grown from less than 10 per cent in 2010 to over 38 per cent today; and Africa hosts some of the world’s best technical leadership, within a thriving ecosystem rooted in civil society.

…we must continue to build a strong, united African technical community. This is why the Forum in Kigali matters: It brings together everyone who powers our digital ecosystem – from data centre operators and fibre providers to hardware builders. We need to fortify these connections and develop this precious community, both within African countries and across borders.

Last year, the African Peering and Interconnection Forum met in Lagos to promote the development of national and cross-border interconnection. Next week, the momentum generated in Nigeria carries over directly to East-Central Africa, where the Forum convenes again in Kigali.

It comes at a crucial time. Africa is poised to harness the advantages of the global digital economy. But to realise this opportunity, three things are crucial.

First, we must continue to build a strong, united African technical community. This is why the Forum in Kigali matters: It brings together everyone who powers our digital ecosystem – from data centre operators and fibre providers to hardware builders. We need to fortify these connections and develop this precious community, both within African countries and across borders. Ultimately, this group of people is laying the groundwork for Africa’s future economic success.

Second, we must all stay true to the goal of ensuring that people everywhere have access to affordable, reliable, and resilient Internet. About a third of the world, including many people in Africa, still do not have access to the Internet. It does no good to create the infrastructure if people cannot afford to pay for the connectivity. According to the International Telecommunication Union, a smartphone can cost up to 40 per cent of the average monthly income in some countries. And mobile Internet is 14 times more expensive in Africa than in Europe. We must do what it takes to bring down these costs.

We must vigorously defend the Internet, leveraging the great power of the ecosystem that helped build the Internet in the first place – the nonprofits, researchers, standards bodies, civil society groups, and public-interest institutions who believe the network should work for everyone.

Finally, people everywhere must have an Internet experience that is safe, secure, and protects them online. We see threats show up in numerous ways – in phishing scams that steal identities, empty accounts, and compromise organisations with a single click. And, at another extreme, we see some governments use technology to target people beyond their borders through surveillance, intimidation, and physical threats.

In February, our Nigeria Chapter delivered one of its largest national campaigns to date, equipping over 2,500 Nigerians with vital skills in cybersecurity, online scam identification, and social media safety.

We must vigorously defend the Internet, leveraging the great power of the ecosystem that helped build the Internet in the first place – the nonprofits, researchers, standards bodies, civil society groups, and public-interest institutions who believe the network should work for everyone.

This unseen ‘global army for good’ draws much of its strength and inspiration from the work done by its network in Africa.

Africa’s 1.5 billion people deserve the full benefits of a truly connected continent. Powered by a young, dynamic population ready to lead the next wave of global innovation, Africa holds its digital future firmly in its own hands.

Sally Wentworth is the President and CEO of the Internet Society.

World.title: Airport operations will continue amid aviation unions’ strike – FAAN
World.content:
The Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN) has assured passengers that airport operations will continue despite the ongoing industrial action by aviation unions.

FAAN, in a statement issued on Tuesday, said it was working with aviation agencies, airlines, security agencies and other stakeholders to minimise the impact of the industrial action and ensure that airport operations were not disrupted.

The authority said it was closely monitoring developments and remained committed to maintaining safe, secure and orderly operations at Nigeria’s airports.

The assurance comes after the industrial action disrupted flight operations earlier on Tuesday, with some airlines suspending or rescheduling services following restrictions on access to airport terminals in Lagos and Abuja.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Air Peace, Enugu Air, and United Nigeria Airlines announced operational disruptions, affecting some passengers with flights suspended or rescheduled.

The action followed grievances by aviation unions over the alleged restriction of workers’ freedom to unionise and the alleged non-remittance of the five per cent Ticket Sales Charge (TSC) collected from passengers.

The unions include the National Union of Air Transport Employees, Air Transport Services Senior Staff Association of Nigeria, and the National Association of Aircraft Pilots and Engineers, with the Nigeria Labour Congress and the Trade Union Congress backing the action.

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) Director-General, Chris Najomo, urged the unions to suspend the industrial action pending the return of the Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, who the regulator said was working to resolve the dispute.

The NCAA appealed to all parties to embrace dialogue and cooperation, expressing confidence that the matter would be resolved and that normal flight operations would be restored as soon as practicable. The regulator also assured passengers that flight safety had not been compromised and that it continued to discharge its statutory safety oversight responsibilities.

FAAN moves to minimise disruption

FAAN said it recognised the legitimate role of organised labour and supported efforts by Mr Keyamo and other stakeholders towards an amicable resolution of the dispute.

“In the interim, FAAN is working closely with the relevant aviation agencies, airlines, security agencies and other stakeholders to minimise the impact of the industrial action and ensure that airport operations are not disrupted,” the authority said.

The authority also said earlier operational challenges affecting the movement of some flights within the airside environment had been addressed through ongoing inter-agency coordination.

It said measures were being sustained to support the orderly continuation of flight operations.

“FAAN remains committed to ensuring that Nigeria’s airports remain safe, secure, functional and accessible to passengers and other airport users,” it said.

FAAN advised passengers to remain calm and maintain contact with their respective airlines for real-time information about their flights.

The authority said it remained confident that ongoing engagements under the minister’s leadership would lead to a speedy and mutually acceptable resolution of the dispute.

It also appreciated passengers for their understanding and patience amid the disruption.

The latest assurance comes as airlines continue to adjust their operations in response to the industrial action, with passengers advised to confirm their flight status with their respective airlines before travelling to the airport.

FAAN said its priority remained maintaining safe, secure and functional airports while efforts to resolve the dispute between the unions, airlines and government continue.

World.title: Afrilition: Why the African diaspora matters for attaining a future of excellence, By Adéwálé Àjàdí
World.content:
It is absolutely critical that the opportunity to build synergies and leverage capacity across the African world is forged towards as a future alternative to the exploitation, colonialism and brutal hegemony that is currently the global approach. The wider diaspora, coordinated with a continental focus of 54 countries, can become the engine for a future that is inclusive and interdependent. The next two generations of Africans need this systemic change, and Afrlition lays it out starkly and hopefully with clarity.

The African expression of identity and character in the 21st century has to be transcontinental. It has forever been so: in the DNA of human beings, both the mitochondrial and Y chromosomes go back to African origins. Afrilition, thankfully, offers Africanness based on self-identification, not genetic or even official origins. As a book or manifesto, the focus is the engagement of the willing or remnants, as there are many born on the continent who are white supremacist in orientation and mental model. This is nothing shocking, since their formal socialisation offers Africa as a foil to perceived European or Western excellence. Afrilition targets those who choose African identity worldwide.

Across the Americas, there are many remnants – especially in the Caribbean, South America, and North America — as there are in Europe and increasingly in Asia. Africans across the globe, whose understanding and experience vary but whose commitment is unwavering towards an authentic and disciplined Afrocentric tomorrow. Often we forget to highlight the newer African world that existed, even when the world formally ended the Trans-Atlantic enslavement and trade in African people — including the return of formerly enslaved people who fought on the side of the British against the US colonialists.

Many of these people ended up in Nova Scotia, Canada; especially in Halifax. They were joined by the Maroons, who had fought the British to a standstill in Jamaica, and some of them were then sent to Sierra Leone as part of an unprepared return effort, and possibly as a colonial prototype. There was the return or exile from Bahia of those alleged champions and participants of the Imale uprising to the West Coast of Africa in their multitudes and interspersed with returned formerly enslaved Cubans.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The stories of the African American support for Abyssinia in the First World War, including helping to form the Air Force then. Some fighting aside, for raising money to support the defence of Abyssinia. Many Caribbean people came out of enslavement only to be sent to West African outposts to replace failed European missionaries, many of whom were just left to survive and sometimes die without support. All these, as Edward Wilmot Blyden was crafting his pioneering work on the African Character as the first Pan-African ideal. He was from St Thomas in the Caribbean, but got educated in Freetown, Sierra Leone, the centre of African schooling. The critical input of the African Diaspora has continued for generations, in the face of popular scepticism on the relevance, importance, or even alleged complicity of Africans in the enslavement decimation of its population.

In the past few weeks, the African Union and the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) signed a Memorandum of Understanding to integrate Caribbean economies into the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), laying the foundation to engage a 1.4 billion strong African market predicted to be soon over three billion! The African Union has formally recognised the Caribbean as the ‘Seventh Region’ of Africa, with a consultative seat in the AU.

One of the interesting stories that the Diaspora holds is that of literacy and how much the African world has engaged with the narrative that literacy, as defined in the Western education system, is critical to transformation. Two of the countries that are at the top of world literacy are the creations of the brutal trans-Atlantic enslavement of Africans — Cuba and Barbados — which both have 100 per cent literacy. The example of Barbados is quite distinct, as it is a majority African descendant country. At full emancipation in 1838, literacy was estimated to be below 10 per cent.

The brutality of the enslavement of Afro-Barbadians was quite notorious in a very diabolical system, as its exceptionally brutal approach was imported into the Southern United States of America to destroy the spirit of rebellion. The vast majority of the emancipated population were field labourers who were denied formal education to the point of death. Even at emancipation, the white plantation owners strongly and widely resisted widespread literacy. Today their descendants are number one in the world, along with others.

The African descendants of the US faced even more ongoing resistance from the first Reconstruction, and in the face of a more recalcitrant government and people, they built over 100 private universities and thousands of schools, fighting daily stereotypes that, in paradox, suggested they did not desire education and were somehow of less intelligence or capacity. These were all allegations that are not borne out by objective data or analysis. In later articles and exploration of Afrilition, we will look at this foundation and the often ignored incredible transformation of Nigerian literacy.

Afrilition offers the African world a route that will inspire our better angels and coordinate the pursuit of our dreams. It most certainly offers us the clarity of purpose to avoid the constant triggers that are distracting our productive energies and leverage our varied capabilities.

In the past few weeks, the African Union and the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) signed a Memorandum of Understanding to integrate Caribbean economies into the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), laying the foundation to engage a 1.4 billion strong African market predicted to be soon over three billion! The African Union has formally recognised the Caribbean as the ‘Seventh Region’ of Africa, with a consultative seat in the AU. The African Diaspora, which includes everyone who affirms the African identity, is across the world.

It is absolutely critical that the opportunity to build synergies and leverage capacity across the African world is forged towards as a future alternative to the exploitation, colonialism and brutal hegemony that is currently the global approach. The wider diaspora, coordinated with a continental focus of 54 countries, can become the engine for a future that is inclusive and interdependent. The next two generations of Africans need this systemic change, and Afrlition lays it out starkly and hopefully with clarity.

Afrilition offers the African world a route that will inspire our better angels and coordinate the pursuit of our dreams. It most certainly offers us the clarity of purpose to avoid the constant triggers that are distracting our productive energies and leverage our varied capabilities. What the willing African Diaspora shows us in their rise from enslavement and progress towards a world-class presence, is that they are key partners in Afrilition’s promise of African excellence.

Adéwálé Àjàdí, a lawyer, creative consultant and leadership expert, is author of the newly released Afrilition: 21st Century African Manifesto, and Omoluwabi 2.0: A Code of Transformation in 21st Century Nigeria.

World.title: Army rescues nine more kidnap victims in Kogi
World.content:
Troops of the Nigerian Army have rescued nine more people kidnapped along the Ajaokuta-Itobe road in Ofu Local Government Area of Kogi State.

The Nigerian Army said in a post on its official social media handle that the victims were rescued after troops from Patrol Base Itobe pursued the kidnappers to the outskirts of Adumu in Dekina Local Government Area and engaged them in a gun battle.

The incident occurred after the kidnappers ambushed commuters along the route, taking several passengers into the surrounding bush.

When the troops arrived at the scene, they found an abandoned Toyota Hiace bus and Toyota Sienna vehicle, with the passengers missing.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The soldiers subsequently followed the route taken by the fleeing kidnappers and made contact with them near Adumu.

During the ensuing gun battle, the troops overpowered the criminals, forcing them to abandon the captives and flee into the bush with suspected gunshot wounds.

The nine rescued victims comprised two elderly men, two elderly women, four other adult males and an infant.

They were evacuated to safety and handed over to the police, Itobe Area Command, for further necessary action and reunification with their families.

The army said troops were continuing to search the area for other possible victims and to apprehend the fleeing kidnappers.

The latest rescue is the second major rescue operation reported in the Ofu-Dekina axis within two days.

On Monday, the army said a joint team of soldiers, naval personnel, police officers, local vigilantes and hunters rescued 16 people abducted from the Ojuwo-Ajengo-Memarebo and Ojiwo-Itobe roads in Ofu Local Government Area.

The army said the 16 victims, comprising six adult males, six adult females and four children, were abandoned by their abductors after security forces engaged the criminals in a gun battle near Adumu.

One hunter was killed during that operation, while a police officer sustained injuries.

The latest incident occurred along the same general corridor where security agencies have intensified operations following repeated attacks on commuters.

On 9 August, the Kogi Police Command also reported that its operatives had rescued 15 kidnap victims after a gun battle with their abductors along the Itobe-Anyigba Highway in Ofu Local Government Area.

The police said the incident occurred around 4 p.m. between Ojuwo Ajengo and Mamerebo, which it identified as a kidnapping flashpoint.

The reports have highlighted the security challenge along the road network linking Ofu, Dekina and other parts of Kogi, where suspected kidnappers have repeatedly used surrounding forests to abduct travellers and evade security forces.

The army urged residents to continue providing credible information to security agencies to support operations against criminal groups in the area.

World.title: Trump secretly switched planes in Turkey over Iranian threat – Report
World.content:
US President Donald Trump’s trip from Turkey last month involved an elaborate ruse to evade a potential Iranian assassination threat.

Mr Trump, on his trip from Turkey, secretly swapped planes, switching from Air Force One, which the White House said he was aboard, to an alternate military aircraft.

The Washington Post reports that the US president was secretly transferred to a military aircraft with a catering truck after he boarded Air Force One.

PREMIUM TIMES reported the NATO summit in July, where he lashed out at Spain for declining the request to allow the US to use the joint military bases on its territory for operations against Iran.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

This clandestine manoeuvre to change aircraft was attributed to the potential threat of an Iranian attack on the US leader.

Mr Trump’s trip from Ankara also came a day after the US began its 13-day military strikes on Iran.

He had earlier said he was Iran’s “number one target” during the summit in Ankara.

This paper reports that Iran’s supreme leader has also previously vowed revenge for the elimination of his father and predecessor, Ali Khamenei, who was killed by a US-Israeli joint strike in February.

Mr Trump had arrived in Turkey in a Boeing 747-8 jumbo jet donated by Qatar last year.

Hours before his departure on 8 July, Mr Trump announced he would leave Ankara aboard the old Air Force One rather than the new jet he had taken to the NATO summit.

Mr Trump said he was switching planes “for old time’s sake,” and that American forces stationed at a UK refuelling stop would be able to check out the new plane.

Footage captured by the press showed the president walking into the old Air Force One. CBS News reported that the footage also showed a catering truck visible on the other side of the jet.

Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth also boarded the smaller military aircraft using external stairs to make the trip appear normal.

However, several minutes later, the truck pulled away and drove off to another US government plane, which the Washington Post reported was an Air Force C-32A.

The Post reported that Mr Trump then flew from Ankara to a refuelling stop in the United Kingdom on that military aircraft, unbeknownst to the journalists and White House officials who were travelling with him and were aboard Air Force One.

The BBC reports that the officials and press members believed they were on board the same aircraft as the president.

The New York Times and CBS News previously reported that intelligence officials flagged a specific threat of an attack on the president or his jet, which triggered additional precautions.

The journalists and some White House staff aboard Air Force One were told to keep their window shades shut. It was an unusual request.

Meanwhile, the security of the Qatar-provided aircraft has been called into question.

The US spent months retrofitting the $400 million Boeing 747-8 to prepare it for the president, according to the BBC.

In a statement to CBS News, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said, “The new Air Force One is perfectly safe for the president’s travels, but will receive additional upgrades and enhancements in the fall, which will take approximately one month to complete.”

World.title: Jos bishop disowns ex-employee implicated in alleged plot to kidnap his wife, another
World.content:
A former worker of the Anglican Diocese of Jos and two security operatives (names withheld) are helping the police over an alleged plot to kidnap the wives of the incumbent and immediate-past bishops, the diocese has revealed in a statement.

The diocese announced that security agencies had intervened before the suspects executed the plot.

It rejected reports portraying the principal suspect as a serving clergyman under the current Bishop of Jos, Ephraim Gongden.

The church said the suspect worked with the diocese but had been dismissed in 2022 by the former bishop and had never been reinstated by Mr Gongden.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The clarification was contained in a statement issued on Tuesday by the Registrar of the Anglican Diocese of Jos, Harrison Ugwuala.

The statement followed the circulation of reports and photographs on social media, which, according to the church, linked the suspect to the current diocesan administration and portrayed Mr Gongden as being connected to the alleged crime.

Suspect no longer with the Anglican Diocese

According to the diocese, the principal suspect presents himself as a clergyman and had previously worked within the diocese.

“He was NOT reinstated by the present Bishop of the Anglican Diocese of Jos,” the statement said.

“The individual is NOT a clergyman in the employment, authority, or jurisdiction of the Anglican Diocese of Jos,” it said.

“The Anglican Diocese of Jos has no working relationship whatsoever with this individual.”

Reports of the alleged kidnapping plot had identified the suspect as a clergyman, creating the impression that he was still affiliated with the Anglican Church.

The diocese said that the description was inaccurate and could wrongly associate the current church leadership with the alleged criminal activity.

Two bishops’ wives allegedly targeted

The alleged plot involved the wives of both bishops.

The diocese did not disclose how the alleged plot was uncovered or how the suspects were arrested.

It confirmed the kidnap attempt and commended the security agencies for their intervention.

The diocese also did not comment on the alleged roles of the two security operatives or disclose whether they were serving members of any particular security agency.

The matter is expected to be clarified as investigations by the security agencies progress.

Complaint over alleged cyber-bullying

The diocese said it had reported what it described as misinformation and cyber-bullying arising from the incident to relevant security and legal authorities.

It urged members of the church and the wider public to remain calm while investigations continue.

“Evil will not have the last word,” the church said.

The police have yet to disclose the names of the suspects.

World.title: Osun election: Adeyanju writes US, UK to sanction Fadaunsi over alleged threat
World.content:
Human rights lawyer, Deji Adeyanju, has urged the United States, United Kingdom and Canada to impose sanctions on Senator Francis Fadaunsi over his alleged threat against members of the Accord Party ahead of the Osun State governorship election.

Adeyanju said he had petitioned the three countries over the alleged remarks, asking them to consider visa restrictions and other sanctions against the senator.

He also called on all leading candidates in the election to condemn any threat or call for violence against political opponents.

Adeyanju spoke on Arise TV’s Prime Time programme while reacting to the ongoing political activities ahead of the Osun governorship election.

He said Fadaunsi’s alleged remarks were particularly concerning, arguing that they amounted to an attempt to encourage violence against members of the Accord Party.

“Again, that takes me to the unfortunate remarks that we’ve just heard of Senator Fadaunsi, very regrettably threatening that members of the Accord Party be killed,” Adeyanju said.

He added that it was “very clear” to him that the senator was allegedly engineering attacks against members of the party.

According to Adeyanju, the United States has consistently expressed interest in promoting democracy in Nigeria and has warned against political violence.

He said the petition was intended to draw the attention of the three countries to the alleged threat and seek appropriate action.

Adeyanju said the level of violence and tension surrounding the forthcoming election was worrying.

“For a very long time, we’ve not witnessed this level of violence preceding an election,” he said.

Speaking further on the Arise Town Hall session on the Osun governorship election, Adeyanju said he was unimpressed by the candidate of the African Democratic Congress, whom he accused of making broad campaign promises without providing clear implementation plans.

He, however, praised the combative approach of the All Progressives Congress candidate, saying the opposition candidate appropriately challenged the incumbent governor and questioned the management of state resources.

Adeyanju said Governor Ademola Adeleke impressed him the most during the town hall session because he attempted to account for some of the projects carried out by his administration.

He rated the town hall performance “60/40” in favour of Adeleke over the APC candidate.

Adeyanju also said Adeleke raised allegations of infractions by the APC, some of which he said had been discussed by social media users, particularly allegations that the party was interfering with the democratic process.

World.title: Ronaldo marries long-time partner Georgina Rodriguez in Portugal
World.content:
Portugal and football superstar Cristiano Ronaldo has married his long-time partner, Georgina Rodriguez, in a private civil ceremony in Portugal.

Ronaldo, 41, and Rodriguez, who have been together since 2016 after meeting in Madrid, confirmed the

marriage by sharing a photograph on Instagram showing off their wedding rings.

The ceremony was held in Cascais, a coastal resort town located about 20 miles west of Lisbon, and was attended by the couple’s five children.

The wedding comes just four days before Ronaldo’s club, Al Nassr, begin their 2026-27 Saudi Pro League campaign.

Ronaldo and Rodriguez have been in a long-term relationship for nearly a decade, with the pair frequently sharing glimpses of their family life on social media.

The Portuguese forward remains one of football’s most prolific goalscorers, having scored nearly 1,000 goals during a career that has taken him through Sporting, Manchester United, Real Madrid, Juventus, Al Nassr and the Portugal national team.

The wedding also comes after Ronaldo recently featured in his sixth FIFA World Cup, matching Argentina captain Lionel Messi’s record for the most appearances at the men’s tournament.

Ronaldo previously confirmed that the 2026 World Cup was his final appearance at the tournament, although he stopped short of deciding whether he would retire from international football altogether.

“I’m sad to be leaving the World Cup like this,” he said. “I gave it my all. I did my best. It was my last World Cup, yes, but I’ll now have time to reflect and be with my family. I won’t be making any rash decisions.

“I don’t decide anything in the heat of the moment. Now is not important whether I will continue.

“I played 23 years in the national team and won three titles. Before Cristiano, Portugal had not won anything. The Euros was the most important. For me, 2016 has the same dimension as a World Cup, honestly.”

World.title: A fight to the finish in Osun, by Rotimi Fasan
World.content:
In concluding my piece here two weeks ago on the Osun State governorship election that is scheduled to hold on Saturday this week, I had suggested that Governor Ademola Nurudeen Jackson Adeleke had successfully skirted around the political landmine represented by the federal might that could have been deployed against him to threaten his chances in the election by President Bola Tinubu. I was not being prematurely sanguine in reaching that conclusion about the attitude of President Bola Tinubu to the Osun State election. My conclusion was based on the pragmatism of Governor Ademola Adeleke’s decision to support the re-election bid of President Bola Tinubu against the backdrop of his thwarted attempt to decamp from the Peoples Democratic Party to the All Progressives Congress, from where he had decamped to the PDP in 2017.

President Bola Tinubu had up to the last couple of weeks assumed what would seem a neutral position in who becomes the next governor of the State of the Living Spring between the two leading contenders, the incumbent Ademola Adeleke, and the APC candidate, Asiwaju Munirudeen Bola Oyebamiji, aka AMBO, the former finance commissioner in the administration of Governor Gboyega Oyetola, the former chief of staff in the Rauf Aregbesola administration that I had in my earlier intervention on this subject erroneously referred to as a former deputy governor. While Abuja had since February 2025 seized Osun State local governments’ allocation following the disputed control of the local governments between the Oyetola-led APC and its successor PDP government at the LGA level, the decision had been portrayed as a local issue that would be determined on entirely legal principle between the APC and the PDP in Osun State. This was the case even if the fund seizure was at the behest of the Bola Tinubu-led federal government through the office of the Attorney-General and Minister of Justice, Chief Lateef Fagbemi.

President Tinubu had during this time maintained a respectable distance from the dispute and had warmly received both the governor and his older sibling, Dr. Deji Adeleke, in audience. It was as if whatever might be going on in Osun State concerning local political disputes was between the governor, his party and his opponents in the APC. But the state branch of the APC under the leadership of Governor Adeleke’s old rival, Gboyega Oyetola, had always taken an aggressively uncompromising, even hostile, attitude to Governor Ademola Adeleke, his government and the policies of the government. It was in that mood that they blocked the governor’s attempt to join the APC when, due to internal wrangling, the PDP came apart at the seams and became a sinking ship from which every politician was desperate to bail out. Had Adeleke been allowed in, he would have become the leader of the APC in Osun and automatically picked the ticket as the APC candidate in this week’s election.

The APC in Osun would have nothing to do with that arrangement and they rejected it offhand. They have since behaved with the full assurance of a challenger confident of victory. As the election comes close, so has their belligerence grown apace. The Accord Party that has accommodated Governor Adeleke after the APC rebuff has not been sitting on its hands either. Its confidence that it would win the Saturday election has neither waned nor wavered. It has taken up the challenge thrown at it by the APC despite being but a newcomer to the mainstream of politics in Osun State. But the sudden entry of Governor Adeleke into the party with the full weight of incumbency power has not only given fillip to the Accord Party, it has galvanised it into the forefront of Osun politics.

The contest between Governor Ademola Adeleke and his old APC rivals has become more contentious and chaotic in the few days leading to the election. The violence that has characterised politics in the state and which goes back to the end of late 2024 to the beginning of 2025 has increased exponentially in the last seven days with accusations and counteraccusations of violence and the resort to self-help in canvassing and countering opposing views. At the centre of this all is the perception that Abuja has given up its neutral stand as the display and actual deployment of federal might has been alleged. This is where President Bola Tinubu is perceived to have swung behind his party’s candidate, jettisoning whatever gentlemanly agreement there might have been between him and Adeleke. The gloves are being taken off and the APC, at both the local and federal levels, suddenly seems determined to make Osun the 32nd state under their direct control.

While the Accord Party influence is limited to what Governor Adeleke and his family have to mobilise, including the star power of the governor’s nephew, Davido, a leading afrobeats musician who occasionally puts his foot in his mouth, the APC has brought the full weight of the party’s leadership machinery across the country to bear on the election with incumbent and former governors and leaders of the party trooping into Osogbo to give their support to their candidate. Not even former governor Kayode Fayemi, who has kept a sullen distance away from the APC while appearing to be fraternising with APC opponents in both the NDC and ADC, wants to be left out. They are all making their way to Osogbo. This could be intimidating to anyone not courageous enough to take the heat, much less a governor who many had thought the election was his to lose until a few weeks ago.

He is not giving up, though, despite apparent acts of intimidation including the arrest in the last one week of key members of his team, including the secretary to the state government, Teslim Igbalaye, and the commissioner for the environment and sanitation, Mayowa Adejoorin. It all culminated with the freezing of an account of the state government by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission. It took the intervention of President Bola Tinubu in what would seem an attempt at seizing a political moment to grab the headlines for that decision to be rescinded following national outcry. The balance of terror seems even and neither side appears ready to blink. Whereas in 2018 Adeleke was carefree enough to let his victory go beneath the quicksand of ‘government magic’, that is INEC’s and the courts’ manipulative antics, then the election was declared inconclusive. Now he has tasted power, he knows it is sweet and he is not likely to give it up without a fight. And whatever the outcome of the election, whoever emerges the winner will be grateful for making it through the crucible of this fraught campaign and emerging from it alive.

World.title: Infrastructure terrorism: How scavengers wreak havoc on public facilities
World.content:
Residents call for urgent intervention

By Olasunkanmi Akoni

It happened within 90 seconds and six sets of gutter guards were gone. The gutter guards covered the drainage directly in front of the twin-duplex and also served as a bridge to aid entrance. Without the CCTV, the property owners would have been left wondering how it happened.

The recording time was 2:25 a.m. Two scavengers were on the prowl. They surveyed the area briefly and swung into action. No one is sure whether they had conducted reconnaissance earlier in the day. Moreover, the swiftness and dexterity with which they removed the guards and loaded them into their carts was stunning. It happened in an upscale estate in the Alimosho area of Lagos State. Nnamdi Alozie, one of the occupants, set out for his office around 5:30 that morning, only to ram his Hyundai Sonata straight into the gutter.

“I couldn’t have imagined that someone would remove the gutter guards in front of a house. The gate engine slides the gate to a corner so I didn’t observe that the guards were gone. It was when we checked the CCTV that we saw the two scavengers,” Alozie lamented. He said he spent over half a million naira to repair his car. That was a private property. This happened in January, 2024.

Present day infrastructure terrorism

Last weekend, a cocktail of emotions ran through the spines of Lagosians (and indeed Nigerians) as they saw video clips of the vandalisation of the Alakija-Festac link bridge in Lagos. Residents first raised the alarm about scavengers removing iron reinforcements from the structure’s pillars, fearing imminent collapse and a possible threat to lives and property.

Vandalism at its vilest

To properly appreciate the matter, visualize this: The main pillars carrying the entire weight of the link-bridge, made of concrete reinforced with iron rods, were the objects of the attack. Imagine using metal tools to scrape the cement covering, thereby exposing the iron rods. Once the scavengers locate the rods in the concrete pillars, they cut them off. That is just one aspect.

Another aspect is digging out the laterite piling that forms the ascending part of the bridge. The scavengers dug into the laterite piling to create a hollow space under the bridge as a place of abode with a tarpaulin covering for doors. To dig out the laterite and sand piling, they scraped off the concrete plaster. The asinine thinking that could effectuate such criminal sabotage of public infrastructure is better left to the imagination.

Scavengers also have stripped the sides of the bridge concrete exposing the iron rods.

Hard questions

Why would anyone do that to an infrastructure that serves all – including the criminal scavengers? Is it about ignorance of the consequences of such an act? Is it about the quest to make a living? Or is it just sheer wickedness?

The video that saved the day

Meanwhile, Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu, in a swift response, inspected the site for an on-the-spot assessment of damage and necessary immediate intervention, declaring a manhunt for criminal suspects of public infrastructure vandalism in the State.

The viral video which circulated on social media at the weekend showed a resident drawing the attention of authorities to the damaged bridge, accusing scavengers of breaking the concrete on the bridge pillars and extracting the iron rods inside, thereby compromising its structural integrity and ultimately the safety of the motoring public and all citizens.

“This is the bridge that was constructed all the way from Alakija to link inside Festac. These scavengers have started removing iron from the pillars that support the bridge. They break the concrete and started removing the iron. See how they have dug into the reinforcement of the bridge. It is very disturbing. They used billions of naira to construct this and see what scavengers have done. And this is what we are doing on a daily basis to make sure that this does not happen in Lagos,” the concerned male resident who did not identify himself said in the video.

The Mile 12 discovery

Meanwhile, a fresh concern emerged again following another bridge in Lagos, somewhere at Mile-12, showing a vandalized part of the concrete side of the overhead bridge with a suspect caught in the act by vigilant residents who lamented the spate of bridge vandalism in the State.

Residents who reacted to the criminal act, however charged relevant authorities to intervene immediately to prevent further damage and protect public safety across the metropolis. The residents also called for increased security and surveillance around public infrastructure to curb the activities of scavengers and vandals.

A state under siege

In most parts of Lagos, scavengers are wreaking havoc at an alarming rate. Last month, the Lagos State Police Command ordered a raid on a scavengers’ enclave along LASU/Iba expressway where drugs and dangerous weapons were discovered. Arrests were also made.

However, many people were shocked to learn that some of the scavengers arrested for the vandalisation of the Alakija-Festac link bridge were sentenced to very lenient prison terms of two to three months. But under Section 337 of the Criminal Law of Lagos State, 2015, willfully and unlawfully damaging property is punishable by up to three years’ imprisonment. For some estates in Lagos, the cart pushers who are referred to as ‘Baban bola’ have been barred from entering their estates. But the Lagos State government has begun a crackdown.
