World.title: Merz’s deal with the Taliban alarms Afghan dissidents in Germany
World.content:
Under pressure from the rising far right, Germany is letting Taliban officials staff Afghan missions in exchange for more deportations. Afghan activists say the arrangement puts them at risk.

Zarmina Paryani and her four sisters fear they may soon have to again face the persecutors they fled from in Afghanistan — and this time inside Germany.

Paryani and her sisters were imprisoned twice in Kabul for protesting against the Taliban after the Afghan militants retook the capital in 2021, the 27-year-old said. After going into hiding for several months, the family eventually made their way to Germany in search of safe haven.

But now, Berlin has struck a Faustian bargain that allows the Taliban to deepen its diplomatic foothold in Germany in return for cooperation on deporting Afghan migrants back to Afghanistan. For Paryani and other Afghan activists who resisted the Taliban at home, the arrangement is giving their former persecutors new leverage over their lives in exile.





“It’s hard to accept that my fate and my affairs are being discussed with the very same representatives whose oppression, prisons, whippings and violence I fled from,” Paryani, who worked as a midwife in Kabul and now lives in western Germany, told POLITICO.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government first struck a deal with the Afghan government announced last October that gives Taliban officials control of diplomatic missions in Berlin and Bonn in exchange for permission to return Afghan migrants directly to Afghanistan. That cooperation was deepened early this summer with a deal that allows more Taliban officials to work in Germany in return for cooperation on additional deportation flights — now up to three per month.

Under the new deal, Germany has expanded deportations to include not only Afghan men convicted of crimes, but also, more broadly, Afghan men with no protected status or legal right to remain in Germany.

The agreement with the Taliban makes Germany an outlier in Europe, making it the first EU country to allow Taliban-appointed officials to work in diplomatic missions inside the country. Before the agreement, Western-oriented Afghan officials representing the former government in Afghanistan had remained in charge.

The arrangement comes as Merz’s government grapples with rock-bottom approval ratings and the rise of the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, now the country’s most popular political force, according to polls. The AfD’s surge comes ahead of two elections in the former East Germany, where the far-right party is ahead in polls by wide margins. In one of those states, Saxony-Anhalt, the party may take real governing power for the first time since it was founded in 2013, a result that would serve as a great humiliation for the conservative Merz, who was elected chancellor last year partly on a promise to crack down on migration.





The AfD’s rise is piling pressure on the chancellor to deliver on his election pledge to deport more migrants — even as he insists that working with the Taliban does not legitimize a regime notorious for its human rights abuses. Overall, Afghans are the third-largest group of refugees or people who have fled war to come to Germany, behind Ukrainians and Syrians.

“We are not extending a hand to this Taliban regime,” Merz said in the German parliament in June. “Rather, we are seeking cooperation at the necessary technical level, which is in our country’s national interest.”

‘Nightmares’ and ‘psychological distress’

For Afghan rights activists in Germany, one of the worst consequences of Berlin’s deal with the Taliban is that it may particularly put at risk some 35,000 Afghans who came to Germany under special humanitarian programs for people deemed especially vulnerable to the Taliban. They include Paryani and her sisters in addition to thousands of human rights activists and Afghans who worked with the German military during its nearly two-decade presence in the country.

Paryani and others fear they will have to face the Taliban when attempting to renew their Afghan passports — which they need to extend their humanitarian visas — at Afghan diplomatic missions. Another 321,000 Afghans live in Germany as refugees or with other forms of protected status. They do not necessarily need Afghan passports, unless they want to apply for a permanent residence status.

More generally, activists and refugees also fear the Taliban, with their growing presence in Germany, could gain access to personal information held in databases in German missions, including details about their families, making them susceptible to blackmail and extortion.

Afghan activists speak at a protest camp at Berlin’s Alexanderplatz on August 15, 2025, the fourth anniversary of the Taliban takeover. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images

“Given my personal history and my stance on extremism, I am concerned for my safety and that of my family,” one former teacher from Afghanistan granted anonymity due to his fear of retribution from the Taliban told POLITICO.

The former teacher, who lives in Germany with a humanitarian visa, said German immigration officials have asked him to renew his expired Afghan passport, a request that he fears will force him to deal directly with his persecutors.

“This situation continues to cause me significant psychological distress,” he said. “Sometimes I wake up at night because of nightmares related to the Taliban and this situation.”

‘Vulnerable to blackmail’

With its handling of the Taliban, Merz’s government is setting a precedent that will be closely watched by other EU countries. Government officials in Austria and Belgium have said they’re watching Germany’s cooperation with the Taliban closely. Taliban officials also held talks focused on deportations with the EU Commission in June in Brussels.

But Hamid Nangialay Kabiri, the former head of the Afghan consulate in Bonn, who quit last September in protest over the initial deal allowing Taliban officials to serve in diplomatic missions in Germany, warned that the German government’s decision to cooperate with the Afghan regime would come back to haunt it — and that the Taliban would use their new leverage over Germany to advance their interests in Europe, including by building networks that intimidate dissidents.

“They are destroying my country, and now they are coming here,” he said. “They are not thinking of diplomacy. They have a lot of plans in their mind.”





It’s a sentiment politicians inside the left-leaning opposition also share.

“The German government has made itself vulnerable to blackmail,” Schahina Gambir, a lawmaker for the Greens who was born in Kabul, told POLITICO. “We’re seeing recognition through the back door. The Taliban are being granted access to embassies, they’re being granted immunity, they’re given channels for dialogue — and at the same time, the situation for women and girls in Afghanistan is getting worse and worse.”

There are already signs that the Taliban are exercising their newfound leverage.

Last May, Kabul unexpectedly halted a deportation flight at the last minute, seemingly seeking to extract additional concessions from the German government. A couple of weeks later, Berlin announced the terms of the latest agreement allowing additional Taliban-appointed officials to work at diplomatic missions in Germany.

Officials in Berlin depicted the new deal as a victory and a practical necessity, allowing for more deportations.





“To increase the number of repatriations, more passports must be issued, more identities must be verified, and so on,” Martin Giese, a spokesperson for Germany’s foreign ministry, said at the time. “To this end, it will also be necessary for more consular officials to be involved.”

But Paryani, the Afghan midwife who fled to Germany with her four sisters, said the Taliban would use their new power to torment them in the country they had sought safety in.

“A Taliban member once wrote to me: ‘Just wait until our embassy in Germany reopens. Then we’ll find you there,'” she said of a comment that had surfaced under one of her social media posts about two years ago. She then deemed it irrelevant because it seemed so unrealistic.

“Today, I feel as though that threat has become a reality,” she said.

World.title: Zelenskyy’s Balkan fumble
World.content:
Since Zelenskyy’s visit, Vučić threatened to physically redirect the Iber River that runs from Serbia to Kosovo in retaliation for Kosovo demolishing Serb-owned houses along the reservoir’s shore. Doing so would move that would drain the reservoir supplying much of Kosovo’s water and crucial cooling capacity to its largest power plant.

In addition, Serbian Foreign Minister Marko Djurić and Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama exchanged barbs on X, with the latter accusing Serbia of being in “a political bubble” and being in denial over the fact that “Serbia lost Kosova” long ago.

Kosovo was an Albanian-majority southern province of Serbia for most of the 20th century. Its people held broad political rights under socialist Yugoslavia until a decade-long Serb crackdown on dissent led to the armed conflict of 1998-99. A three-month NATO bombing campaign drove Serbian forces out and made the province a U.N. protectorate.

Kosovo declared independence in 2008 and, to date, it is recognized by over 100 nations, including the U.S., U.K. and 22 of the 27 EU member countries. It is also a potential EU candidate country, submitting its application in December 2022.

The country’s status has long been a favorite talking point for Russian President Vladimir Putin, who has used it to justify invading Georgia in 2008 and annexing Crimea in 2014. Kosovo’s Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca said he took note of Zelenskyy’s views “with regret” and that such rhetoric echoes “Russia’s attempts to invoke Kosova as a precedent.”

As for why Ukraine’s leader would wade into the intractable Balkan issue at all, it likely comes down to weaponry.

World.title: Farage vs. Binface: Inside the Clacton by-election circus
World.content:
The feeling that the town has been made to look daft was apparent even among those preparing to vote once again to return the Reform UK leader to parliament. And it’s not the rival candidate wearing a trash can on his head that they’re holding responsible for the “farce.”

Thursday may not be the end of the matter, either. A parliamentary investigation into Farage’s alleged failure to declare millions of pounds of donations in the run-up to his 2024 election could mean yet another by-election — and a tougher battle for the right-wing populist next time around.

Bid for absolution

This self-inflicted campaign is taking place because of Farage’s decision to resign his parliamentary seat and put his fate in the hands of Clacton’s residents.

Ordinary punters, he argued, should be the ones to have their say as he faced mounting questions over undeclared donations. The gamble was that such a vote would absolve him of wrongdoing in the eyes of the public, regardless of the findings in two parliamentary probes — one over a £5 million donation from a crypto-entrepreneur, and the other into support from a convicted fraudster. Farage has denied wrongdoing in both instances, arguing that help was given in a personal capacity.

Reform UK Party Leader Nigel Farage gestures as he speaks during a press conference on a plan to deport foreign prisoners on August 10, 2026 at Royal Horseguards Hotel in London. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images

But Britain’s main political parties took one look at this ploy and opted out. That’s how Count Binface, one of the most enthusiastic inheritors of a rich British tradition of standing as a satirical candidate in elections, ended up as Farage’s most high-profile rival.

Others risking their £500 deposit to get their names on the 90-cm-long ballot paper include rival jokesters with names ranging from Howling Laud Hope, Nick the Incredible Flying Brick and Baron Von Thunderclap. Broadcast rules mean the 34-strong candidate list needs to be read in full at every mention of Farage’s by-election on TV.

World.title: Breakfast looks a lot more expensive under EU pesticide plans
World.content:
Even under more plausible scenarios envisioned by the researchers, in which external growers get on board to varying degrees, consumer prices would rise and EU agricultural imports decline. Though that would in turn boost domestic production, with exact numbers depending on producers' willingness to adapt.

The findings lay out an unpalatable political choice for Brussels: Keep angry farmers' tractors off the streets, or hit consumers' wallets as they fulfill basic needs at the grocery store.

The proposed residue ban, which is part of the food and feed safety simplification package, is popular with European farmers seeking a level playing field with foreign growers — after all, it was partly designed to appease their ire over the EU's trade deal with the Mercosur bloc of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay. In order to avoid leaving any residue on fruits and vegetables, producers would essentially have to stop using the substance in question.

However, critics say it clashes with global trade rules, as it essentially imposes EU rules on foreign producers, which is known as a mirror clause.

A wide range of international producer groups argue that the proposed ban goes beyond existing health protections in order to push a one-size-fits-all approach, ignoring the reality that growers around the world face different pests, climates and farming conditions.

“The choice is between berries that are available all year round — healthy, safe and at a fair price — or limited production at a high price,” said Amine Bennani, president of the Moroccan Association of Red Fruit Producers.

World.title: Swarming jellyfish overrun French nuclear plant on same date two years in a row
World.content:
Three fishing vessels are now “constantly patrolling off the coast of the plant" to conduct "preventive fishing operations [...] 24/7,” the company added.

Tuesday’s jellyfish invasion comes a the latest in a series of climate change-driven incidents that have affected French nuclear energy during a particularly infernal summer.

Nuclear power plants are typically built by rivers or on coastlines so they can use nearby water sources to cool their reactors. But a record number in France this summer have been forced to temporarily shut down due to heatwaves and droughts affecting their water supply.

Rising sea temperatures have made jellyfish swarms more common along the French coast in recent years, and those swarms can affect a plant’s ability to bring in seawater — which is what happened at Gravelines. Following last year’s incident at the plant along the North Sea, EDF installed cameras and deployed fishing boats to monitor the situation.

While the vessels “prevented a massive influx of jellyfish” on Saturday and Sunday, they were eventually overwhelmed as the swarm grew from “about 100 kilograms” to “several dozen tons,” the French state-owned utility giant said.

Opponents of nuclear energy were quick to jump on the incident.

“This only highlights that nuclear power plants are ill-equipped to deal with the consequences of climate change,” the French branch of Greenpeace said in statement.

World.title: 'You want it darker?' The ideal total solar eclipse playlist is here
World.content:
The moon is due to pass directly between the Earth and the sun this evening, leaving millions of mainland Europeans experiencing the first full solar eclipse in two decades.

 

Considering the next total solar eclipse is not due to occur until 2081 for France, 2090 for the UK and not until the next century for Germany (Spain, on the other hand, get to see one next year), it's worth getting it just right.

We're of the opinion that everybody needs the perfect soundtrack for a celestial event of this magnitude, so to here are our handpicked eclipse (and eclipse-adjacent) songs to accompany you through the sunlight block – in chronological listening order for maximum effect.

Len - 'Steal My Sunshine'

This 90s song by one-hit-wonder Canadian alt-rock band Len was initially released on the soundtrack to the 1999 crime comedy film Go, and became an instant summer hit. Not hard to hear why, as it’s a sun-kissed tune about not plunging anyone into depression by stealing their happiness. Yes, it sounds like an outdated 90s throwback; sure, it’s twee; and granted, good taste dictates that it should only be played at pool parties. But you try resisting that sugary sweet chorus... This should open your eclipse playlist before the great concealing, before things get a bit more ominous... DM

Bill Withers - 'Ain't No Sunshine'

I know, I know, I know, I know that Bill Withers' 'Ain't No Sunshine' is the perfect addition to any total solar eclipse playlist. Inspired by the 1962 film Days of Wine and Roses, Withers penned the soulful masterpiece while working at a toilet seat factory, aged 31. When the song went gold, the record company awarded the singer with a golden toilet seat, marking the start of his new career. The song has since been covered by the likes of Paul McCartney, Tom Jones and Prince, but we can all agree that Wither’s rendition remains unmatched. TF

Bonnie Tyler - 'Total Eclipse Of The Heart'

We sadly lost Bonnie this year, and what better way to honour her musical legacy than by playing her biggest hit? As you “turn around” to look at the sun being obscured by the moon, there’s nothing more appropriate to listen to than her 1983 ballad ‘Total Eclipse of the Heart’. It was written by the late Jim Steinman, a composer with a flair for the theatrical (his other hits include Meat Loaf's ‘I'd Do Anything for Love (But I Won't Do That)’ and Celine Dion's ‘It’s All Coming Back to Me Now’). Whether or not the solar event mirrors your own internal torment, we can surely all agree that belting “forever’s gonna start tonight” will add a sense of cinematic drama to the event. AB

Max Richter - 'On The Nature Of Daylight'

Arguably one of the most famous compositions from neo-classical artist Max Richter, this song off his 2004 album ‘The Blue Notebooks’ (Euronews Culture's top pick for the Best European Albums of the 21st Century) was originally conceived as a response to the Iraq War. Since then, it has been used in countless films and TV shows, from Shutter Island to Hamnet, via Jiro Dreams of Sushi, The Handmaid's Tale and The Last of Us. Granted, it may now have become an overplayed shortcut to punish your tear ducts, but listen to it during the eclipse, and you'll hopefully be reminded of how beautiful, poignant and powerfully cathartic it remains. DM

Soundgarden - 'Black Hole Sun'

From a stellar 80s power ballad to a 90s grunge anthem... Widely recognised as Soundgarden’s signature track, this was arguably Chris Cornell’s shining moment of glory (if you don’t count his often-undervalued work in the supergroup Audioslave). It came out mid-1994, when the world was still under the shock of Kurt Cobain’s death, and it’s the ideal dark anthem to listen to while you’re luxuriating in darkness, appreciating the contradictory beauty of both the eclipse and this song about concealed darkness in humanity. DM

Pink Floyd - 'Eclipse'

If you're not enjoying this playlist, there's a case to be made for just listening to the entirety of Pink Floyd's 'The Dark Side of the Moon' prior to, during and following the eclipse. But if you're sticking with us and our somewhat protracted curation, we suggest you choose the aptly titled 'Eclipse'. The album's closing track ends with the lyrics "All that is now / And all that is gone / And that's to come / And everything under the sun is in tune / But the sun is eclipsed by the moon". Perfection. DM

Leonard Cohen – 'You Want It Darker'

This year's total eclipse will pass over the Arctic, Greenland, Iceland and northern Spain. The rest of Europe will get a partial eclipse – a little more than 90%. So, why not be greedy and pick this cut from Leonard Cohen's final studio album? “You want it darker / We kill the flame." Prepare for shivers. DM

David Bowie – 'Blackstar'

While we're luxuriating in darkness (and appreciating two back-to-back tracks from artists we lost ten years ago), listen to David Bowie's title track from his final LP, 'Blackstar'. Released two days before his death, this song is tailor-made for the celestial event. And it wouldn't be a true eclipse playlist without the Starman, would it? DM

Bruce Springsteen - 'Dancing In The Dark'

Let's get a little less dour, shall we? Bruce Springsteen’s classic 1984 tune should prepare you to see the sun once more. Written about the pressures of fame and trying to force creativity, Springsteen told the BBC: “All I could do was write another song about not wanting to write another song". In the years since, it’s become a beloved anthem that always starts a fire in your belly. And how often is it that you actually get to dance in true darkness?! AB

The Beatles - 'Here Comes The Sun'

As the moon begins to move away and the sun reemerges, what better way to celebrate the return of the light than with The Beatles’ timeless classic 'Here Comes the Sun'? Written by George Harrison in early 1969 from the country house of Eric Clapton, the heartwarming song reflects the temporary respite he was experiencing from the band’s Apple Corps business affairs. As one of the standouts from the Fab Four's legendary 'Abbey Road' album, the song earned Harrison his songwriting flowers, previously reserved for Lennon and McCartney. It’s the perfect way to end your eclipse. TF

Enjoy full blackout and remember to put on special eclipse glasses. And headphones.

World.title: Solar eclipse and meteor shower: Portugal prepares for two rare celestial events
World.content:
Today the national team are not playing, the prime minister is not addressing the country, there are no COVID-19 press conferences, but the country will still stop at the same time to look at the same thing: the total eclipse of the Sun.

 

Around 19:30, in the Bragança region, the total eclipse of the Sun will occur, meaning day will turn into night as the Sun is covered by the Moon. As well as getting darker, ambient noise drops, the temperature changes and many more shadows are cast.

This will be an astronomical spectacle nobody will want to miss, not least because it is highly unusual and the last total eclipse visible from mainland Portugal took place in 1912.

But the eclipse will not be the only phenomenon to amaze this evening. From 21:30 on Wednesday, about an hour after the eclipse ends in mainland Portugal, there will also be a meteor shower. These meteors, known as the Perseids, leave a trail of light as they pass through the atmosphere.

This is an annual meteor shower, usually active from mid-July until the end of August. The peak generally occurs around 12 and 13 August.

As the Moon will be practically new, the sky will be very dark and conditions will be especially favourable for observing the phenomenon. However, for the best possible viewing experience, experts recommend finding a dark place with an unobstructed horizon.

Activity is expected to increase between midnight and 02:00, but the most favourable period to try to spot the highest number of meteors will be between 02:00 and 05:00 in the early hours of the 13th, when the Perseus constellation, the point from which the meteors appear to radiate, rises higher in the sky.

The best places to watch the phenomenon are Dark Sky Alqueva in the Alentejo, the world’s first certified dark-sky territory; in the North, the Montesinho and Bragança area in Trás-os-Montes; in the Serra da Estrela, Peneda-Gerês or any high, inland area away from settlements.

For an even more exciting experience, a few tricks also help, and it is essential to avoid looking at screens for 20 to 30 minutes beforehand so that your eyes adapt to the darkness and can focus on the meteor shower.

Back to the eclipse: Euronews has compiled everything you need to know about the phenomenon:

What is a solar eclipse?

The astronomical phenomenon known as an "eclipse" occurs when one celestial body blocks the light from another. In the case of a solar eclipse, the Moon completely or partially covers the light of the Sun, producing what is known as the "diamond ring", which lasts only a few seconds.

Where can I see the eclipse?

The eclipse will be visible across the country; however, it will not look the same in all regions. The total eclipse, which corresponds to 100%, will be visible only in the Montesinho Natural Park, in Bragança.

The deep partial eclipse, with between 92% and 99% coverage, can be observed throughout mainland Portugal.

On the islands, the Azores and Madeira, the percentage is much lower, between 74% and 77%.

It is advisable to watch the moment from a wide-open space, without many buildings in front.

Image taken from the eclipse2026.pt platform showing the eclipse obscuration map for Portugal eclipse2026.pt

What time does it happen?

The eclipse will begin at around 18:33 and end at around 20:23, lasting roughly two hours. Its maximum will be reached close to 19:30. The total eclipse phase lasts just 25 seconds.

Can I watch it without protection?

No! You must never look directly at the Sun during the phenomenon. There is only one safe way to see the eclipse: using proper eclipse viewing glasses. The phenomenon must not be watched with sunglasses, through telescopes or with the naked eye, as it can cause eye damage. Direct sunlight does not cause immediate pain, but it can burn the retina, leading to later consequences such as permanent loss of vision.

People watch the Moon partially covering the Sun during a total solar eclipse in Eagle Pass, Texas, on 8 April 2024. AP Photo

The organisations responsible also warn about the use of cameras and mobile phones, which can likewise be damaged if used without suitable filters.

In Portugal, ZEISS launched a campaign offering free eclipse glasses across the country. All you had to do was go to an optician in the Club de Visão network, after registering in advance. However, the initiative was limited to existing stock and it is no longer possible to obtain them free of charge.

You can buy eclipse glasses, but the optics community has set out some key features to check that you are purchasing the right model. The glasses must have ISO 12312-2 or ISO 12312-2:2015 certification for solar observation, as well as the CE marking printed on the frame. They must also ensure the blocking of UV, IR and intense visible light. They should be prefabricated and ready to use, with no assembly required.

You can buy the glasses in pharmacies, some supermarkets and online shops such as Astroshop, Telescopiomania, ESTUDIOPT, Aff Camera Store or Sol & Salvo, which sell these glasses for prices ranging from 2.90 to 3.25 euros per unit. These shops also offer packs for families or groups of friends.

Are there places where I can watch together with other people?

Yes. On the platform https://eclipse2026.pt (source in Portuguese) hundreds of events taking place on the day of the eclipse are listed. Some no longer accept participants, as they required prior registration. Even so, here are some of these initiatives, from north to south of the country, where you can still try to take part free of charge:

Faro and Albufeira

Promoted by the Centro Ciência Viva do Algarve, there will be guided sessions for observing the partial solar eclipse in Faro and Albufeira. In Faro, the event will take place in the Parque Ribeirinho from 18:30. Admission is free and the minimum age for participants is 12.

In Albufeira, it will be held in the parish of Paderne, at the parish castle. The event is free and will continue into the night with observation of a Perseid meteor shower.

Tavira

"Solar Eclipse and Night-time Observation of Celestial Bodies"

Organised by the Centro Ciência Viva de Tavira in partnership with Tavira municipality, it will take place in Praça da República. Admission is free and the minimum age is 3.

"During the activity, there will be a brief explanation of how solar eclipses form and discussions will be held on the importance of scientific research and observing the sky," the organisers say.

"Solar Eclipse at Praia do Arraial" and "Solar Eclipse at Praia do Barril"

Both events are organised by the Centro Ciência Viva de Tavira and are free of charge. They start at 18:30, but it is advisable to arrive a little earlier. At Praia do Arraial, the minimum age to take part is 5. At Praia do Barril, it is 3.

Oeiras The partial solar eclipse will also be visible from Santo Amaro beach in Oeiras. Here, the phenomenon is expected to reach around 95%.

The event is organised by the local authority, which has prepared a festive afternoon from 16:00, combining a summer party atmosphere with observation of the phenomenon.

As well as a DJ set, a large screen will be installed to show the eclipse live, allowing everyone to follow it without risk to their eyesight. The session will be accompanied by explanations of what is being seen.

Enxara do Bispo (Mafra)

"When the sky darkens: Understanding the Solar Eclipse and how to observe it safely" is one of the initiatives taking place in the late afternoon of the 12th. It is organised by the Associação Astronómica Horizonte Estelar, with the meeting point set for the churchyard at 17:00. The event lasts 3 hours and 30 minutes. Before the eclipse, there will be a theoretical introduction to the phenomenon and, during it, explanations will be given to participants. The minimum age to take part is 6.

Porto

"Solar Eclipse 2026 at Time Out Market Porto" is organised by the market, which invites everyone to gather in the outdoor square, with a privileged view of the Clérigos Tower. The event starts at 18:00 and runs for 3 hours.

The organisers say that "to mark the occasion, a themed cocktail called 'Eclipse' has been created. With the purchase of this cocktail, a pair of solar viewing glasses will be offered, while stocks last."

Vila do Conde

Organised by the Centro Ciência Viva de Vila do Conde, the eclipse can be observed in a group from the seafront, in front of the Farol restaurant. Admission is free and the event starts at 16:00. The recommended minimum age to observe the phenomenon is 6.

There are also private initiatives organised by groups of friends on social media pages. Check whether anything is being organised in your area.

World.title: Anxious dogs and silent birds: What happens to animals during a total solar eclipse?
World.content:
Once day seemingly and unexpectedly turns to night, many animals will likely feel confused, disorientated or stressed - thankfully, for just a few minutes.

 

Animals, both wild and domesticated, rely on important environmental cues - like light and temperature - to help them navigate their daily lives. As light fades and temperatures drop, these cues suddenly change.

Scientists who have studied animal behaviour during eclipses have a fairly clear picture of what tends to happen - even if not every animal reacts the same way.

How different species react to eclipses

People observing a total solar eclipse often notice the sudden silence. Birds that sing throughout the day frequently stop the moment darkness falls, as though evening has arrived hours early. Nocturnal animals, such as owls, can do the opposite and become active, behaving as though dusk has begun.

Many - from zoo mammals to bees and other insects - interpret the sudden darkness as nightfall. Elephants have been seen heading straight for their night-time dens, treating the eclipse as their usual lock-up signal. Others show clearer signs of stress: gorillas have charged the glass of their enclosures, while giraffes have paced and swayed.

House pets may be worried too. Dogs and cats often pace, whine or hide during totality - a response some researchers compare to how pets react to fireworks or thunderstorms.

Normality returns within minutes

Total darkness itself is brief - lasting only a few minutes. As sunlight returns, the animal behaviour reverts just as suddenly.

Birds often burst into song, reportedly singing even louder than they would at a normal dawn. Within a short time, most animals settle back into their ordinary daytime routines, as if nothing unusual had happened at all.

World.title: Worried your child is a loner? A new study says playing alone may be just fine
World.content:
The child happily doing their own thing at recess may not need rescuing from the sidelines.

 

A new study suggests some children who play alone simply prefer their own company.

Researchers at the University of Georgia in the United States found that children who often chose to play alone could still be happy with their friendships and place within a wider peer group, particularly when they felt confident that they belonged.

The study surveyed 473 students between nine and eleven years old at several elementary schools in the US state of Georgia.

Children were asked which classmates tended to play alone despite getting along well with others. They also reported how important they thought it was to belong, and how satisfied they were with their friendships and their position within their class.

Here, researchers found an important distinction between children who preferred spending time alone but still valued belonging, and those who placed little importance on fitting in.

Children in the first group were generally satisfied with both their individual friendships and their wider peer relationships. These children may accept enough invitations to remain socially connected while still feeling comfortable turning down activities when they would rather be alone.

“They prefer to be alone and do their own thing rather than playing with their peers, but they still have that other flip side of getting along well with others,” Rachael Pfanz, the study’s corresponding author and an elementary school psychologist, said in a press release.

Children who did not consider belonging important, however, were more likely to report poorer relationships with both friends and classmates.

Researchers suggest that children who regularly reject invitations may eventually receive fewer of them, leaving them increasingly isolated and dissatisfied with their social lives.

“There are things we do because we know what’s good for us,” said Michele Lease, a professor of educational psychology at the University of Georgia and co-author of the study.

“Social interaction is the same way. Turning down invitations, like avoiding exercise, leads to poorer outcomes.”

The findings also suggest adults should be cautious about assuming that children who play alone need to be pushed into large group activities.

Instead, researchers suggest introducing children to smaller groups of peers with similar interests or behaviours.

“Maybe don’t ask them to go join the big soccer game right away on the playground,” Pfanz said. “That’s a little overwhelming if they’re already preferring to play alone.”

The research team said the findings are particularly relevant for children in fourth and fifth grade, when friendship groups tend to become more established and children are increasingly able to identify which classmates are choosing solitude and which are becoming excluded.

World.title: Winding trails and coastal treks: Three of Europe’s best autumn hikes, according to Lonely Planet
World.content:
With the arrival of autumn comes a spectacular transformation of scenery and the opportunity to lace up your walking boots and to be at one with nature.

 

Hiking has become one of the most popular outdoor activities and in Europe we’re spoiled for choice when it comes to trails and routes to tackle.

In its new guide book – "Where to Go When: Hiking" – Lonely Planet has showcased more than 90 of the world's best hikes and the months to explore them in, from "micro walks and multi-day treks to pilgrimage routes and mountainous rambles".

Here we take a look at three of the featured hikes in Europe to do during the cooler autumn months, plus other popular options further afield.

Three of Europe’s best autumn hikes

Premužić Trail, Croatia (challenging)

Winding through Croatia's Northern Velebit National Park, the Premužić Trail is “one of Europe's finest examples of dry-stone engineering”, said Lonely Planet. Crafted pathways weave through rugged landscapes, passing wildflower meadows and shepherds' huts with views across the Adriatic Sea. September offers pleasant temperatures, snow-free trails and warm coastal waters, making it the “perfect time to discover this dramatic corner of Croatia”.

Coast to Coast Path, England (moderate/challenging)

Follow in the footsteps of fell-walking legend Alfred Wainwright with this west-to-east walk across England, which starts from the Cumbrian village of St Bees to Robin Hood’s Bay in Yorkshire. Going through three National Parks, this iconic route has recently been awarded National Trail status and now has clearer signage, better accessibility and is managed to a higher environmental standard. Lonely Planet recommends doing the English Coast to Coast Path in October.

Via Francigena, Swiss Alps and Northern Italy (moderate)

The Via Francigena is a pilgrimage from Bourg-Saint-Pierre in the Swiss Alps, through Italy’s Aosta Valley all the way to Rome. Hike in “historic, holy footsteps” and savour stunning panoramic mountain views, flower filled meadows and the cultural and culinary delights of Italy’s diverse regions.

Quilotoa Loop in Ecuador Photo by Jose Rueda on Unsplash

Three of the best international autumn hikes

Choquequirao – Southern Peru (challenging)

For travellers seeking an alternative to the busy Inca Trail, Choquequirao is a 15th-century Inca site that’s sometimes described as “Machu Picchu's lesser-known sister”, with a fraction of the visitors. The demanding route descends deep into the flower-filled Apurímac Canyon before climbing steeply back towards the ruins, “rewarding hikers with ceremonial platforms, temples, ritual baths and intricate llama carvings etched into its ancient terraces”. September is one of the best times to visit, with warm, clear days arriving after the peak tourist season.

Quilotoa Loop, Ecuador (easy)

Explore Ecuador's Andean highlands on a gentle and rewarding journey through traditional villages and rolling mountain landscapes before reaching the "breathtaking" Laguna Quilotoa. Nestled within the crater of an extinct volcano, the emerald-green lake is celebrated for its Indigenous culture and striking scenery. As well as crisp blue-sky mornings and lush green hillsides, November offers quieter trails and plenty of time to explore local artisan stores.

Langtang and Helambu Trek, Northern Nepal (challenging)

Journey through one of Nepal's most spectacular Himalayan regions, where dense forests, sacred lakes and centuries-old Buddhist monasteries can be found beneath snow-capped peaks. Rich in Tibetan culture, the Langtang and Helambu valleys also “tell a story of resilience”, with tourism continuing to support communities rebuilding after the 2015 earthquake. November is among the best months to trek here, bringing dry, clear days, comfortable temperatures and unbeatable mountain views.

World.title: More than 16,000 civilians detained by Russia in its invasion of Ukraine are still held, UN says
World.content:
Over 16,000 civilians captured by Russia during its conflict in Ukraine are still "deprived of their liberty," with many being held incommunicado and for reasons that violate international law, an informal UN security council meeting has been told.

 

According to Claudia Fuentes Julio, the UN assistant secretary-general for human rights. “Widespread and systematic torture and ill-treatment” of both Ukrainian civilian detainees and prisoners of war by Russia are continuing, including sexual violence.

Julio gave the estimates at the informal meeting of the Security Council called by Latvia and the United Kingdom on Monday to spotlight the plight of civilians and soldiers taken during the war that Russia launched with a full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.

The council, which counts Russia as a permanent member, heard the accounts as both Russia and Ukraine have escalated attacks in the four-year conflict.

According to Julio, since the invasion, 910 Ukrainian prisoners of war and 403 civilian detainees have been interviewed by UN human rights personnel following their release.

And more than 95% of the Ukrainian prisoners of war and 85% of the civilian detainees reported being tortured or ill-treated, often repeatedly, the U.N. official said.

They also reported sexual attacks and inhumane conditions, including food deprivation and inadequate medical services.

The Geneva-based human rights office “has documented the execution of 129 Ukrainian prisoners of war at the beginning of their captivity and the deaths of 48 Ukrainian prisoners of war in custody, resulting from torture, denial of medical care, or other inhumane conditions of detention,” Julio said.

The UN has not been permitted to visit Russian detention facilities, and its estimate of the number of people detained does not include a breakdown of adults and children.

Some former detainees shared their ordeal with the UN

The Security Council also heard emotionally wrenching accounts from some former detainees who shared their ordeal.

Crimean Tatar human rights activist Leniie Umerova, who called herself a “political prisoner” of the Russians for almost two years, and Khuan Leyva Garsiya, a Ukrainian soldier who was among the hundreds that held out for months at the Azovstal steel plant in the besieged city of Mariupol before turning themselves over to the Russians in May 2022 shared their stories.

Garsiya, who was born in Mariupol to a Ukrainian mother and Cuban father, spent 1,183 days as a POW. He said he weighed 55 kilograms (120 pounds) when he was freed, pulling out a picture of his emaciated body to show the council.

Garsiya said he was tortured, beaten harder, and humiliated more than other prisoners because the Russians suspected that he was a foreign mercenary due to his Cuban ancestry or an American spy because he went to college in the United States.

“Russians were outraged that someone with a connection to Cuba, whom they consider an ally, would fight against their occupation army,” said Garsiya, who is still in the Ukrainian military.

UN also said Russian detainees reported abuses

UN human rights experts also interviewed 816 Russians and 57 third-country national prisoners of war from over 45 countries who were members of the Russian armed forces in Ukraine, said Julio, the assistant secretary-general.

About half reported torture or ill-treatment, primarily during the initial stages of captivity and interrogation by Ukrainians, she said.

But UN monitors reported that once they arrived in Ukrainian detention facilities, “the conditions generally comply with international humanitarian law and have improved since 2022.”

Responding to the claims, Russia’s deputy UN Ambassador Maria Zabolotskaya told the council the Russian armed forces are complying with international humanitarian law, which includes the treatment of prisoners. She claimed Russian prisoners in Ukraine faced “torture and degradation and moral and physical abuse.”

She called the Security Council meeting part of “a disinformation campaign against Russia,” funded by NATO countries involved in the Ukraine conflict. The aim, she said, “is to derail efforts towards a peace settlement and to justify strikes on the territory of Russia and against civilians.”

For Ukraine's part, Volodymyr Pavlichenko, Kyiv's deputy UN ambassador, expressed his displeasure that Russia was not prepared to talk about the return of POWs, "including their POWs," and all civilian detainees, including kidnaped children.

World.title: How Christopher Columbus saves his life in Jamaica with an eclipse: astronomical ruse
World.content:
It was 1504 and Christopher Columbus was on his fourth voyage to the New World when his ships ran aground off the coast of Jamaica, which, although it had been christened in 1494 as the island of Santiago, was always known by the name given to it by the native people 'Xaymaca' or 'Yamaya', meaning "land of wood and water". The admiral and his crew were stranded, unable to put to sea, trapped on an island they could not leave.

 

A dead end in Jamaica

The chief scribe of the voyage, Diego Méndez, tried the only possible solution: to set off by canoe to La Española, in what is now the Dominican Republic, to ask for help from the governor Nicolás de Ovando. It took him five days to get there, but Ovando, who deeply distrusted Columbus, refused to send assistance and kept Méndez back for months. Meanwhile, in Jamaica, the castaways had managed to establish a trading relationship with the indigenous people, who supplied them with food in exchange for trinkets and European tools.

For months the arrangement held, but hope gradually faded. A mutiny broke out among the sailors themselves, which heightened tensions with the islanders. The inhabitants of the island, tired of the conflict and at the end of their tether, decided to stop supplying the Europeans with food. Columbus's crew were on the brink of starving to death.

Astronomical tables, Columbus's salvation

It was then that Columbus resorted to one of the most ingenious ploys in the history of exploration: his astronomical tables. The navigator was carrying the "Almanach Perpetuum", an astronomical calendar compiled by the German astronomer Johann Müller, known as 'Regiomontanus', which recorded with great accuracy the movements of celestial bodies for the years ahead, including lunar eclipses.

Columbus consulted his papers and found what he was looking for: on 29 February 1504 there would be a lunar eclipse visible from Jamaica. The Moon would turn a deep crimson red, the distinctive colour it takes on during total eclipses because of the refraction of sunlight through Earth's atmosphere, the same phenomenon that is today popularly known as the blood moon.

Three days before the eclipse, Columbus summoned the indigenous leaders and told them that his Christian God was deeply angered with them for having cut off the food supply. As a sign of his wrath, he warned them, that very night the Moon would disappear and turn blood red.

The eclipse and the Taíno surrender

When the night of 29 February came, the Jamaican sky behaved exactly as the admiral had predicted. The Moon gradually began to darken and took on the unmistakable reddish hue of a total eclipse. The native people, terrified by what they interpreted as a supernatural sign, came to beg Columbus to intercede with his God to stop the phenomenon.

The navigator, as his son Hernando recounts in the admiral's biography, pretended to withdraw to pray and consult the deity. He calculated the exact moment at which the eclipse would begin to wane and then reappeared before the islanders, telling them that his God had accepted their plea and would pardon the indigenous people if they resumed supplying food.

When the Moon returned to its normal appearance, the indigenous people were convinced. The supply of provisions resumed until a ship finally chartered by Diego Méndez arrived to pick up the castaways. Columbus landed at Sanlúcar de Barrameda in November 1504. He would die two years later, in Valladolid, in May 1506.

Science as a means of survival

Columbus's episode is one of the most famous examples in the history of science of how astronomical knowledge can become a tool for survival. He was not the only explorer to resort to this tactic; there are numerous similar stories attributed to other European adventurers in different parts of the world.

What makes the Columbus case distinctive is its documentary precision: the date of the 29 February 1504 eclipse has been verified by modern astronomers, who have confirmed that it was visible from Jamaica with the characteristics described in the historical sources.

The admiral and "discoverer of America" did not improvise: he calculated, waited for the right moment and used the scientific knowledge of his time with a cool-headed efficiency that saved his life and that of his crew.

World.title: Indonesia: Passengers rescued after Bali ferry catches fire
World.content:
Authorities said they had visually confirmed that no passengers remained on the burning ferry, but were still confirming the total number.

Indonesian authorities rescued over 130 people from a burning ferry on Wednesday near the tourist island of Bali.

The fire broke out on the Padang Bai-Lembar ferry route connecting Bali and Lombok and is also used by tourists travelling between the two popular destinations.

It is the second major ferry fire in Indonesia this month.

What Indonesian authorities said about the ferry fire

Muhammad Hariyadi, who heads the Mataram Search and Rescue Office, told Metro TV that all passengers had been rescued and there were no immediate reports of casualties.

"We have approached the ship and confirmed that all passengers are no longer on board," he said. "We visually see no passengers on the ship."

Visuals released by Indonesian authorities showed black smoke billowing from the burning ferry in Bali waters Image: BASARNAS/AP Photo/picture alliance

In a statement later, Hariyadi said the total number of passengers on board was still being verified. He had initially said the ferry was carrying 114 passengers and 17 crew members, referring to the passenger manifest data released by Padang Bai's port authority.

The ferry also had 44 vehicles and 53 motorcycles on it.

What else do we know about the fire and rescue efforts?

Fire broke out on board the Putri Yasmin Ferry at about 4:15 a.m. (1045 GMT) while it was en route from Padang Bai port in Bali to Lembar port on the adjacent island of Lombok, according to the search office in Mataram.

The agency received an emergency report nearly half an hour later and then deployed rescue vessels and personnel.

The burning ferry was in the midst of rough seas with waves as high as 4 meters (13 feet), Hariyadi said, adding that conditions had complicated rescue efforts.

A ferry in the vicinity had evacuated 30 passengers and brought them to Bali. A search and rescue vessel was on its way to Lembar port with 59 of the rescued passengers. A naval vessel picked up another 17 passengers.

Some rescued passengers were taken to a port in Bali while others were taken to the Lombok island Image: Lana Priatna/AFP

Marine safety in Indonesia

Marine accidents are a regular occurrence in Indonesia where ferries are a common mode of transport.

Last week, five people died in a ferry fire off the coast of Java Island. Last month, a ferry transporting more than 70 people sank while sailing near Seayar Island. The rescue operation had been closed after four bodies were recovered, but 14 were officially still missing.

And in July last year, a ferry sank while travelling between Java and Bali, killing nearly 20 people.

World.title: North Korea tests missile ahead of US-South Korea drills
World.content:
The suspected ballistic missile was launched towards Japan and likely fell just outside of its special economic zone, Tokyo said.

North Korea test-fired a ballistic missile off its east coast towards Japan early on Wednesday, its neighbors said, just days before US-South Korea Joint Military drills which Pyongyang views as invasion rehearsals.

This is the second such test in less than a week.

"Our military detected at around 6:00 am (2100 GMT on Tuesday) a ballistic missile launched by North Korea from the Wonsan area towards the East Sea," Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a message to reporters.

Japan's Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi called the launch a "threat to peace and security in our region," adding that Tokyo had lodged a strong protest with North Korea through diplomatic channels in Beijing.

"It's a serious problem that affects the safety of the Japanese people," he said at a press conference.

Here's what we know about North Korea's test-launch from Japan:

North Korea launched at least one ballistic missile on Wednesday morning

Details were under close joint analysis between Japan, the US and South Korea

Missile estimated to have fallen outside Japan's exclusive economic zone in the Sea of Japan

Japan's prime minister issued instructions to maintain a complete state of readiness

No reports of damage have been confirmed

North's message ahead of joint military drills

The suspected ballistic missile launch came just two days after South Korea and the US announced that they will kick off their annual joint military drills on August 17.

The upcoming drills are a regular summer feature, designed to coordinate their defense against the nuclear-armed Pyongyang.

North Korea has condemned these drills on several occasions before, often staging missile tests before and after the exercises.

"North Korea has never simply let a South Korea-US joint military exercise pass without a response," said Lim Eul-chul, a North Korea expert at Kyungnam University.

"This is a message that Pyongyang is closely watching the upcoming drills and could stage a provocation if it deems one necessary," he said.

After last year's drills began, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un claimed the exercise had grown more provocative than before and showed Seoul and Washington's "will to ignite a war." He said it had prompted North Korea to respond with “proactive and overwhelming” countermeasures.

On August 6, the US, South Korea and Japan detected the launch of a short-range ballistic missile from the North in what was its first ballistic weapons testing activity since late June.

Pyongyang, which ususally releases details of tests a day later, did not initially confirm the launch.

World.title: Drone attack hits Libya's largest oil refinery
World.content:
Fires broke out at the Zawiya oil complex after explosives-laden drones struck the site. Hours later, fresh violence in Benghazi highlighted Libya's persistent security challenges.

Libya's National Oil Corporation (NOC) said Tuesday that fires at a fuel storage facility had been quickly brought under control after a drone attack.

The Zawiya oil complex west of Tripoli is home to the country's largest refinery and has been the scene of repeated armed clashes between warring factions fighting for primacy in the country since the fall of former strongman leader Moammar Gadhafi in 2011.

What happened in the drone attack on Libya's Zawiya oil refinery?

Monday's attack by an as yet undeclared actor targeted the Zawiya Oil Refining Company with explosives-laden drones, causing a tank containing about 4.5 million liters (1.2 million gallons) of gasoline to collapse after a fire.

Owner Brega Petroleum Marketing said the fires had been brought under control far faster than expected, with engineers telling Reuters news agency that damage had been limited, though operations were interrupted.

In a statement on X, Abdulhamid Dbeibah, Libya's internationally recognized prime minister, wrote that the crime of targeting civilian infrastructure would "not go unanswered."

Libya's UN-recognized Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah condemned the drone attack on the Zawiya oil complex, saying the targeting of civilian infrastructure would "not go unanswered" [FILE: October 13, 2022] Image: Yousef Murad/AP Photo/picture alliance

"The use of drones to strike vital facilities," wrote Dbeibah, "is not a random incident, but rather an organized and dangerous act that requires a firm response to protect the state and its institutions and prevent its recurrence."

Officials from Libya's electricity provider said two further drones targeted the Zawiya power plant early Tuesday morning, with one hitting the fire-fighting system but causing no damage.

What is the security situation in divided Libya?

Libya has remained divided since the 2011 uprising that toppled Gadhafi. Dbeibah's UN-recognized government is based in Tripoli in the west, while eastern and parts of southern Libya are controlled by the Libyan National Army (LNA), a military force led by commander Khalifa Haftar.

Amid those tensions, the LNA said its head of military intelligence, Fawzi al-Mansouri, was killed in a car bombing in Benghazi on Monday night.

According to the LNA, an explosive device attached to al-Mansouri's vehicle detonated as he left a mosque. Authorities have not identified those responsible.

Khalifa Haftar commands the Libyan National Army (LNA), which controls eastern Libya and parts of the country’s south [FILE: September 5, 2024] Image: Abdullah Doma/AFP/Getty Images

Khaled Haftar, one of Khalifa Haftar's sons, said an investigation had been opened, adding that initial "indicators point to a despicable terrorist tactic," according to AFP news agency.

His office later said authorities had arrested a "terrorist cell" in Benghazi that was allegedly preparing acts of sabotage, but did not say whether it was linked to al-Mansouri's killing.

Al-Mansouri was a prominent military figure close to the Haftar family and had played a key role in fighting jihadist groups in eastern Libya.

How has Libya's political division affected oil production?

The split between dueling administrations has stunted the country's oil producing progress and kept foreign investors wary as rival sides clash over control of the oil revenues that pour into the Central Bank of Libya.

In 2024, a standoff over control of the bank slashed the country's oil exports by more than half.

Libya holds Africa's largest proven oil reserves, yet has struggled to return to pre-2011 production levels of 1.6 million barrels per day. June production hit 1.44 million barrels per day, the highest output levels since 2013, but far short of its target of 2 million barrels per day.

World.title: UNESCO: 2.4 million girls barred from school in Afghanistan
World.content:
Five years after the Taliban returned to power, millions of Afghan girls remain excluded from secondary education. UNESCO warns of lasting social and economic consequences.

Around 2.4 million girls in Afghanistan have been denied access to secondary education since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, UNESCO said Tuesday.

The figure has risen by about 200,000 since last year and could reach nearly four million by 2030 if the ban remains in place.

"Afghanistan remains the only country in the world where girls and women are formally banned from secondary and higher education," Hoda Jaberian, UNESCO’s program coordinator for education in emergencies, said.

"Five years is not a temporary interruption in a child’s education. It is clearly almost an entire secondary school cycle."

Why are Afghan girls banned from secondary schools and universities?

The Taliban seized power on August 15, 2021, as US and NATO forces withdrew after two decades of war.

They initially assured the international community that women would be allowed to continue studying.

Taliban fighters took control of Afghanistan's presidential palace in Kabul after President Ashraf Ghani fled the country [FILE: August 15, 2021] Image: Zabi Karim/AP/picture alliance

But secondary schools were closed to girls in March 2022. Women were barred from universities in December that year.

The Taliban described both measures as temporary, but they remain in force.

The authorities say they respect women's rights in line with their interpretation of Islamic law and Afghan culture. They have also insisted the issue is a domestic matter.

Restrictions extend beyond education. Women face limits on employment and movement and have been barred from public parks, gyms and beauty salons.

The UN has described the broader system of restrictions as “gender apartheid.” Russia is the only country to formally recognize the Taliban administration.

What has happened to girls' education since the Taliban takeover?

UNESCO says the restrictions have reversed two decades of progress.

Girls had very limited access to schooling in 2001. By 2021, nearly one million were enrolled in secondary education.

"Afghanistan had made really major progress in expanding girls’ access to education," Jaberian said. "But unfortunately, much of that progress now has been completely reversed."

UNESCO has called for the immediate and unconditional restoration of girls' and women's right to secondary and higher education.

The agency continues to support community-based education as well as literacy and skills programs, often held in community spaces or facilitators' homes.

How is the Taliban ban affecting Afghanistan's economy?

UNESCO estimates that excluding women from secondary and higher education could push around 600,000 women out of the workforce by 2066.

The restrictions could also cause cumulative income losses of 9.6 billion US dollars and increase the risk of early marriage.

The ban is also worsening a shortage of female teachers. UNESCO expects Afghanistan to face a deficit of more than 11,000 qualified female teachers by 2030.

"Many teachers have left the country and those who were in the system are banned from continuing teaching," Jaberian said.

She added that restrictions on women teaching boys had left some pupils with unqualified male teachers or no teachers at all.

How severe is Afghanistan's wider education crisis?

Afghanistan's education system is facing problems far beyond the ban on girls.

More than two million primary school children are already out of school for other reasons. More than 90% of 10-year-olds cannot read a simple text, while the national literacy rate stands at 37%.

Many schools are overcrowded and poorly equipped. Nearly half lack water, sanitation or heating.

Natural disasters, including earthquakes and floods, have forced around 1,000 schools to close since 2021, adding further pressure to the country's education system [FILE: November 5, 2025] Image: Sayed Hassib/REUTERS

The system is also under pressure from people returning to Afghanistan.

Three million people returned in 2025 alone, either voluntarily or forcibly. More than seven million have returned or been forced back since 2023.

Natural disasters have added to the crisis. Earthquakes, floods and other disasters have forced around 1,000 schools to close since 2021, UNESCO said.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: Ebola: Over 2,000 dead in DR Congo as virus gathers pace
World.content:
Authorities in the DRC say the Ebola virus is killing faster than any outbreak on record. Scientists have also said the outbreak may have started earlier than previously thought.

Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) said on Tuesday that an outbreak of a particularly virulent strain of the Bundibugyo Ebola virus currently raging in the east and northeast of the country has killed more than 2,000 people since the first case was confirmed.

In all, more than 4,380 infections have been recorded.

The current outbreak is the 17th ever recorded in the DRC, with Sania Nishtar of the Gavi global vaccine alliance warning it could become "the largest outbreak ever."

Until now, the worst outbreak recorded in the DRC was the one that took place from 2018 to 2020 when some 3,500 infections led to 2,300 deaths.

The pace of death is gathering momentum this time around, with the virus spreading faster and exhibiting a higher mortality rate than the 2014-2016 West African outbreak — the worst outbreak on record, which logged 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.

Congo's Ebola outbreak exceeds 4,000 cases To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The current DRC outbreak was declared on May 15, but health authorities say the first transmissions likely took place in February of earlier still.

The 1,000-death mark was not reached until nine weeks in, now — in just three-weeks' time — that figure has doubled again.

The case fatality rate of the current outbreak is 45.9% compared to 39.6% in the 2014-2016 West African outbreak.

'We haven't reached the peak yet,' says DRC health minister

Though there are vaccines against some strains of the Ebola virus, there are currently none approved for the rare Bundibugyo strain that is spreading across the DRC faster than health authorities can trace it.

Moreover, health authorities face massive logistics challenges due to the volatile security situation in the country, where bad roads and rebel violence coupled with lack of healthcare worker pay and mass strikes make it increasingly difficult to keep tabs on the illness.

"We haven't reached the peak yet," said Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba in an interview shared by the ministry on X. "Within the next three months, we expect to have already brought the spread under control and to start seeing it decline," he added.

Ebola, which is transmitted through physical contact with bodily fluids, causing a hemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past half century.

Authorities in the DRC have placed restrictions on public gatherings as well as closing the airport in Ituri Province, the epicenter of the outbreak. Still, fighting and disease have forced the displacement of masses of people in the DRC, Rwanda and South Sudan.

On Monday, the World Health Organization's (WHO) regional director told reporters that authorities are "chasing the virus… the virus is ahead of us."

WHO, DRC officials appeal to Congolese as Ebola spreads To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What's the latest on bids to treat or vaccinate this Ebola strain?

Clinical trials for two antiviral treatment methods have been ongoing since early July and on Friday the WHO recommended undertaking a full-scale human trial of the Ervebo vaccine.

Although Ervebo has proven effective against the Zaire strain of Ebola, its efficacy in fighting the Bundibugyo strain is unproven. WHO officials are hopeful that it can offer some protection against the DRC strain.

Vaccine alliance Gavi says it has made some 500,000 doses of Ervebo in its stockpiles available for the trial.

Virologists say the new Bundibugyo strain appears to have been transmitted from animals to humans and has changed from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012.

Researchers from Congo, Uganda, Belgium and other countries published findings ‌in the journal Nature Medicine on Monday, suggesting the outbreak began ‌with an animal-to-human transmission event and was then spread between people.

Given the severity of the outbreak, authorities are looking into the possibility that the pathogen may have mutated.

Jean Kaseya, the head of the Africa CDC, last week warned that fewer and fewer new cases could be traced back to contacts of existing confirmed patients, with researchers falling well below the WHO's targets of tracking 95% of potential contacts to contain the spread.

World.title: Ex-Marine released and returning to US from Russian prison
World.content:
A US citizen and former military serviceman has been released after four years in prison in Russia. President Trump said the release was not part of any exchange and expressed appreciation to Russia's Putin.

Russia on Tuesday released Robert Gilman, a former US Marine who had spent more than four years in prison on disputed charges, according to a group advocating for him and US officials.

US President Donald Trump and the State Department both said the release was on "humanitarian grounds" and that it was not part of an exchange or prisoner swap with Russia.

Who is Robert Gilman?

The 32-year-old former service member had been working as a teacher in Russia when he was first detained in 2022, accused of assaulting a police officer after being ejected from a train for causing a disturbance.

He was later accused of other violent offenses while incarcerated and was given a longer jail sentences, ultimately reaching a total of roughly 10 years.

Advocacy group Global Reach had warned of Gilman's deteriorating health condition in detention. His mother was in Russia trying to secure his release as the news developed.

What did Trump and the State Department say about the release?

Trump posted about the release on his Truth Social platform, also including what appeared to be a photo of a sedentary Gilman, his mother and others on a plane, holding an American flag.

"After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis," Trump wrote. "We appreciated the decision, and the fact that Russia asked for no one in return — No exchange took place."

He said that Gilman and others would land at Andrews Air Force Base in Washington later on Tuesday to be welcomed back to the US.

The State Department, meanwhile, issued a statement attributed to Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"We thank Russia for working with Special Envoy Steve Witkoff to release Mr. Gilman and allowing him to receive the necessary medical treatment here in the United States," Rubio said. "While we appreciate this positive step, we are still seeking the immediate return of all other unjustly detained Americans, including wrongful detainee Stephen Hubbard."

The statement lauded Trump's efforts to free US-Americans from foreign detention during his second term and concluded that Trump "will not stop until all unjustly detained Americans are home."

Gilman's sister credits Trump, Democrat senator with her brother's release

Gilman's sister Lexie Hudson said in a statement from advocacy group Global Reach that Trump hearing about the case and taking action was the "reason that Robert is alive today."

She also thanked Democrat Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey "for leading our advocacy efforts in Congress."

"The Russians treated my brother so badly," Hudson said. "They hurt him for no reason, other than that he was both an American and a Marine. What did they get out of this? Why did they do this to such a wonderful person?"

According to Global Reach's chief strategy officer Eric Lebson, Gilman had been in a "dissociative stupor" for 47 days, attributing this to abuse he suffered in prison.

He had been moved to a civilian hospital prior to his release, and would soon be medically and psychologically assessed and treated at a US military hospital, Lebson said.

Gilman's mother had traveled to Russia amid the reports of her son's deteriorating health to try to see him.

"It is a tragedy that it took Robert's near-death condition for his case to receive the attention that it required for his release to be negotiated," Massachusetts Senator Markey said in the statement from Global Reach. "Throughout his detention, Robert was subjected to physical torture, forced medication, and provocations by Russian authorities. There is no doubt that his treatment by Russian authorities is the reason Robert is in this precarious state today."

Gilman was arrested in January 2022, a few weeks before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. His prosecution proceeded as relations between Putin's Russia and NATO members deteriorated markedly.

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier
