World.title: Can the new PKK law bring peace to Turkey?
World.content:
Turkey’s parliament has passed a framework law for the peace process with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK). What does it stipulate, why is it controversial and what does it mean for the future of the peace process?

One year ago, the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) burned its weapons in a symbolic ceremony. The move was seen as a sign of its willingness to disband. Since then, the Kurdish side has been calling on the Turkish government to take political steps.

Now, parliament has passed a bill submitted by the conservative Islamic ruling party AKP and its ultranationalist ally. Officially called the "Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration," it is intended to provide the legal framework for the ongoing peace process.

According to official figures, 467 out of 592 MPs voted in favor of the bill. The ruling party and its ally see this as the beginning of a new era: Under certain conditions, the bill provides for a suspension of sentences for PKK members — but only after the PKK and its affiliated groups have been confirmed to have disbanded and disarmed, so that peace, brotherhood and solidarity can prevail throughout the entire country.

The pro-Kurdish DEM party also supports the bill, but it views it only as a first step that must be followed by further reforms.

The pro-Kurdish DEM party also voted in favor of the PKK law. At the same time, it is calling for swift political and legal reforms Image: Adem Altan/AFP

PKK law divides society and parliament

Fierce opposition came from the ultranationalist opposition party IYI. Even during consultations, its delegate Ayyuce Turkes, daughter of the founder of the ultranationalist and right-wing extremist Grey Wolves, accused the government of rushing a landmark bill through parliament.

She also criticized what she felt was an overly conciliatory stance toward PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan. She avoided using his name, calling him a "baby killer" instead, just as government agencies and media have done for decades. There was even a physical altercation.

The debate highlights just how deep the divides are within Turkish society. While the ultranationalist IYI party rejects the process, the MHP, from which the Grey Wolves emerged, is now among its most important supporters — even though it had, previously, vehemently opposed earlier peace initiatives.

Observers believe this shift in course and the progress in the peace process are also a result of the changed security situation in the region. Among other things, they mention the fall of the Assad regime in Syria, the war in Gaza and the conflict between Israel, the United States and Iran. Syria and Iran are also home to large Kurdish populations that are supported by various regional actors.

According to the prevailing view, a more stable relationship with the Kurds who live within Turkey's own borders could provide Ankara with more leeway in domestic and foreign policy.

The justice committee of the Turkish parliament convened to discuss the draft "Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration" Image: ANKA

What's in the law?

The law applies to convictions for PKK membership, propaganda, financing or intentional support of the organization and its structures. For prison sentences of up to 15 years, enforcement is to be suspended for five years; for longer or life sentences, the suspension is to last ten years. Ongoing investigations are to be put on hold. According to pro-government media, up to 3,600 prisoners could benefit from this.

The prerequisite is the complete disbanding of the PKK and the surrender of all its weapons and ammunition. Both of these conditions have to be verified by Turkish authorities and, subsequently, officially confirmed by the National Security Council, chaired by Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Excluded are PKK members who were convicted prior to June 1, 2005 — the date on which the current penal code came into force — as well as those convicted of homicide and whose convictions are final. That means the regulation does not apply to PKK founder Ocalan either. In February 2025, the 77-year-old had called on the PKK to disband, declared an end to the armed struggle and spoke out in favor of a political solution.

Turkey: An end to the Kurdish conflict? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

PKK views law as a mere first step

The PKK also calls the bill a first step; it criticizes, however, wording and content. Its key demand remained unfulfilled: As long as Ocalan cannot directly coordinate the peace process under conditions of freedom, the issue of disarmament could not be resolved either.

They said penal code regulations alone did not go far enough, more comprehensive democratization reforms were needed. The message was that as long as returning fighters or exiled politicians continued to be criminalized and were unable to engage in political activities legally, hardly any of them would leave the mountains where they've been staying.

PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan in February 2026. The law passed by Turkey's parliament does not provide for his release from prison Image: DEM

Even legal pro-Kurdish political activity has ben restricted in Turkey for decades: parties were banned, politicians were arrested or barred from political activity. To this day, elected mayors are being removed from office, and numerous politicians and activists are in prison. Among them are two former co-chairs of the Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP) that mainly represented Kurds, Selahattin Demirtas and Figen Yuksekdag.

Peace without democratization?

Political scientist Berk Esen criticizes the law for failing to offer concrete democratic solutions to the Kurdish issue. He also noted that, parallel to the peace process involving the PKK, the government had significantly increased the pressure on the largest opposition party CHP.

For about two years, the Turkish judiciary has increasingly been cracking down on leading CHP politicians. Critics view this as an attempt to weaken the government party's strongest political rival. Among the most high-profile cases is that of former mayor of Istanbul and CHP presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu. He and hundreds of other party members are in prison, on charges of fraud and corruption.

The entire CHP leadership under Ozgur Ozel was removed as well. He formed a new party several weeks ago.

Criticism of Erdogan's role

Esen primarily criticizes Erdogan's strong influence on the peace process. Although it is to be implemented by a committee chaired by the vice president and key ministers, who are also heads of the intelligence services and the National Security Council, Esen argues that it will ultimately be Erdogan as chairman of the National Security Council who decides when and which steps in the peace process will be implemented.

This assessment is also shared by Reha Ruhavioglu, director of the Kurdish Studies Center.

"Erdogan will clearly set the pace," Ruhavioglu said, attributing this to the asymmetric balance of power between the Turkish state and the PKK.

In addition, Erdogan had learned his lessons from the failure of the peace talks between 2013 and 2015 and would now certainly assemble more control in his own hands. At the same time, experts say, Erdogan has his sights set firmly on the 2028 presidential and parliamentary elections, and would want to limit any political risks associated with the process.

Ruhavioglu expects further controversy, especially if former PKK fighters return to Turkey and remain at large. The government is therefore likely to allow their return, suspended sentences and political activity only gradually, and largely in response to public reaction.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Hungary's parliament elects Orban critic as new president
World.content:
Hungary's parliament has overwhelmingly confirmed Andras Baka, formerly the head of the Supreme Court, to the largely ceremonial role of president. New Prime Minister Peter Magyar controversially removed his predecessor.

Hungary's parliament voted in Andras Baka, formerly the head of the Supreme Court, as the country's next president on Tuesday.

The symbolic step is part of new Prime Minister Peter Magyar's sweeping efforts to dismantle the legacy of former premier Viktor Orban after winning April's general elections.

Baka was a staunch critic of Orban who was removed from his Supreme Court role during the former PM's tenure.

Now, he will replace Tamas Sulyok, a president appointed by Orban, whose term in office was shortened via constitutional amendment in order to remove him from the largely ceremonial role.

What happened in Tuesday's parliamentary vote?

The vote in parliament to appoint Baka was always likely to be a formality, given the massive majority that Magyar's conservative, pro-European TISZA party holds in the chamber.

It went almost entirely along party lines, 140 lawmakers voted in favor and six voted against. TISZA holds 141 seats.

Orban's right-wing populist Fidesz party, which has 52 lawmakers, boycotted the vote in protest — but did so knowing it would be powerless to prevent Baka's appointment.

Baka took his oath of office and gave a short speech to the chamber after Tuesday's vote Image: Bernadett Szabo/REUTERS

Who is Andras Baka?

Baka, 73, is a jurist and politician who was briefly a member of parliament from 1990 to 1991.

He spent almost 20 years as a judge at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), before returning to Hungary in 2009 to become president of its Supreme Court.

In December 2011, not long after Orban returned to power as prime minister after a stint in opposition, he was removed from his role three years before his term was set to expire and sidelined from public life in Hungary.

Magyar said Baka's life served "as an example of commitment to the democratic rule of law and constitutional principles" as the central European country needs to be "guided back onto the path of the rule of law and constitutional governance."

Baka, 73, spent almost 20 years at the European Court of Human Rights earlier in his career as a jurist Image: Zoltan Balogh/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Why was Baka's appointment and his predecessor's removal contentious?

Baka's appointment prompted protests from Fidesz, but also some critical comments elsewhere in Hungary, with some rights watchdogs likening the removal of Tamas Sulyok to the "illiberal" practices of the Orban-era.

Sulyok, appointed in 2024, was deemed an Orban ally.

Magyar used his two-thirds majority in parliament — which he holds thanks to Hungary's winner-takes-all first-past-the-post electoral system, as Orban used to — to amend the constitution and bring his term to an early end.

Fidesz and their nationalist KDNP allies in parliament had called this "tyrannical" and "illegitimate," while Magyar argued it was necessary to pursue the "system change" he promised amid April's landslide election victory.

Magyar briefly tapped Hungarian national treasure and chess superstar Judit Polgar as a possible replacement president, but she quickly declined, saying she did not feel she had "the strength to take on the historic responsibility of uniting a divided nation," but pledging to do "everything in my power" to support a new, independent and respected president.

Magyar initially floated the notion of presidential star power, until chess phenom Judit Polgar said 'thanks, but no thanks' Image: Judit Polgar Foundation

What has Baka said about the process and his appointment?

Baka himself had not criticized Sulyok's removal, despite the echoes of the mechanisms used to oust him in 2011.

"In a country governed by the rule of law, such extraordinary measures cannot be used, but Hungary became a captured state under Orban," he told the AFP news agency last month. He said that state officials like Sulyok "were appointed not to restrain the government's power, but to ensure the political survival of the former system even after an electoral defeat."

However, speaking in parliament on Tuesday, Baka seemed to strike a conciliatory tone, even for supporters of the old regime.

"There is one thing we certainly cannot do: we cannot build the new Hungary on revenge," he told parliament, vowing to "encourage public and professional debate, uphold [parliament's] openness and impartiality, and consistently insist that constitution-making must never again become the exclusive project of a single political force."

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier

World.title: Se acabó la espera: España vivirá su primer eclipse de Sol total en más de un siglo
World.content:
Millones de españoles y turistas ultiman los preparativos para ver, sobre las 20.30, cómo la Luna cubre completamente el Sol. Estas son las claves de un fenómeno acompañado de un enorme desafío logístico

El ritual comenzará pasadas las 19.30 en los primeros puntos del noroeste peninsular. Millones de españoles y turistas levantarán la mirada hacia el horizonte para ver un evento astronómico ancestral y fascinante: comprobarán cómo se va haciendo de noche en pleno día, mientras la Luna cubre completamente el Sol en el primer eclipse total en cruzar la Península en 121 años, de Galicia a Baleares, que será visible en su totalidad en buena parte de la mitad norte peninsular.

El fenómeno astronómico, que se produce por la alineación de la Tierra con la Luna y el Sol, pasa de media una vez cada 18 meses en alguna parte del mundo. Lo extraordinario es que pase justo por encima de nuestras cabezas, sin tener que desplazarnos miles de kilómetros. Por eso, pocos quieren perdérselo y estos días las zonas más deshabitadas de la España interior, que ofrecen miradores privilegiados para el eclipse, están llenas de gente que busca el mejor punto para verlo. A los veraneantes habituales que llegan cada año de las ciudades y multiplican la población de pueblos y aldeas semivacías, se han sumado quienes eligieron estos municipios por sus cielos limpios, los miles que se desplazarán en estas últimas horas para no perderse el evento y los que cambien de ubicación en el último momento por temor a que las nubes les estropeen la fiesta.

Pero el fenómeno que desata la fascinación de la población es también un desafío logístico para las autoridades, que han anunciado un enorme despliegue para tratar que el eclipse se produzca sin incidentes. En primer lugar, está la recomendación para la salud de no mirar nunca a la luz del Sol —aunque esté parcialmente cubierto—, sin gafas especiales protectoras. A eso se le suma el plan de Tráfico para tratar de evitar atascos y accidentes en los hasta 1,5 millones de desplazamientos que se esperan y que se concentrarán en un puñado de carreteras y en pocas horas. Y también las recomendaciones para prevenir incendios en un mes en el que España está especialmente calurosa y seca, en riesgo extremo de incendios forestales. Porque, mientras miramos al Sol, no hay que olvidarse de cuidar la Tierra.

En EL PAÍS, les compartimos algunas claves del evento astronómico, que también se ha convertido en un movilizador social, económico y cultural para disfrutarlo con seguridad:

El enorme desafío logístico

En pleno 12 de agosto, los Gobiernos central, autonómicos y municipales deben hacer frente a las necesidades logísticas que generan millones de personas moviéndose a la vez y con un mismo objetivo. Será como una operación salida, pero en un solo día y con concentraciones en puntos inesperados.

El Gobierno prevé entre 400.000 y 1,5 millones de desplazamientos adicionales a los habituales desde zonas donde el fenómeno se observará parcialmente hacia el área de la totalidad, según ha señalado este martes el Ministerio de Ciencia y Universidades, citando una estimación de la Dirección General de Tráfico (DGT), que tendrá un dispositivo especial de vigilancia. En total, se desplegarán más de 24.000 guardias civiles y 9.400 agentes de la Policía Nacional para garantizar la seguridad.

La recomendación de las autoridades, para quienes tengan que desplazarse, es hacerlo “con mucha planificación”, hacer el regreso de manera escalonada, evitar paradas en arcenes que puedan interrumpir la actuación de los servicios de emergencias y llevar los suministros necesarios por si tuvieran que pasar más tiempo del esperado en la carretera. El riesgo es que se incrementen los atascos y accidentes como sucedió en otros países, como en los eclipses totales de Estados Unidos de 2017 y 2024.

También podrían caerse las comunicaciones por saturación. Y hay un temor especial por el riesgo de incendios. La ministra para la Transición Ecológica y el Reto Demográfico, Sara Aagesen, ha dado este martes “varias recomendaciones sencillas y esenciales” a los ciudadanos para cuidar el entorno natural mientras observan el eclipse: “Prohibido encender fuego, no aparcar sobre vegetación seca, mantener los accesos libres para emergencias y consultar diariamente el nivel de peligro de incendios. El día del eclipse solar total es un día para disfrutar, pero también una llamada a la prudencia y a la precaución”, ha dicho.

Impacto económico y turístico

La expectación en torno al eclipse se traduce en beneficios para las provincias agraciadas por la lotería astronómica. Un informe del Ministerio de Economía, Comercio y Empresa presentado a finales de julio estima que las zonas de la totalidad recibirán 446.700 visitantes adicionales esta semana por el eclipse, que aportarán a la economía 347,6 millones de euros. Cerca del 37% son extranjeros.

También se ha visto un incremento en las reservas de plazas hoteleras y de restaurantes en la zona de la totalidad, donde los precios se han disparado. Según un análisis de más de 5.500 anuncios en Booking publicado la semana pasada por EL PAÍS, en 90 días, los precios se multiplicaron por seis en Soria, donde una habitación estaba en torno a unos 900 euros, o por ocho en Zaragoza, donde costaba en torno a los 500.

Dónde verlo

Para disfrutar de una experiencia plena, los astrónomos recomiendan, en primer lugar, estar en una zona de la totalidad, es decir, que se vaya a oscurecer al 100%. Dicen que las sensaciones en una zona en la que el Sol se cubre por completo no tienen nada que ver con aquellas en las que se cubre al 99%, aunque en la fase previa pueden ser muy similares. Lo que observaremos en ese punto álgido del fenómeno es la oscuridad total que, si el cielo está despejado, nos permitirá ver la desconocida corona solar con nuestros propios ojos. Esos filamentos plateados que rodean al Sol son la parte externa de su atmósfera, pero generalmente están ocultos por el propio brillo de la estrella.

Para quienes prefieren verlo acompañados o no han tenido tiempo de elegir un mirador propio cerca de su casa o su lugar de vacaciones, las comunidades autónomas y los municipios han seleccionado cientos de puntos oficiales. Son ubicaciones desde donde el eclipse tendrá buena visibilidad y que contarán con su propio dispositivo de seguridad y emergencias. En algunas de ellas, además, distribuirán gafas de protección.

Mapa de miradores oficiales donde ver el eclipse total de Sol EL PAÍS completa un buscador con casi 500 miradores oficiales

A qué hora es exactamente

Aunque en los primeros lugares de la península el Sol comenzará a eclipsarse sobre las 19.30 y la experiencia completa durará cerca de dos horas, el punto cumbre, el de la totalidad, no durará más de 1 minuto y 50 segundos para los más afortunados; y serán solo unos pocos segundos para los que estén en las zonas más periféricas de la totalidad.

Los primeros lugares de España que se oscurecerán completamente por la sombra de la Luna sobre el Sol son Cabo de Peñas, en Asturias, y Estaca de Bares, en A Coruña, pasadas las 20.26 de la tarde, y el último será el Faro de la Mola, en Formentera, sobre las 20.33, antes de que el eclipse desaparezca con la puesta de Sol.

Para saber las horas exactas en las que pasará el fenómeno en un lugar concreto, pueden consultar en el buscador del Instituto Geográfico Nacional (IGN). La web oficial creada por el Ministerio de Ciencia, Tecnología y Universidades para el Trío de Eclipses ofrece también un visor que simula dónde estará el Sol en una localización determinada a la hora del eclipse.

El lío de las gafas: entonces, ¿cuándo y cómo usarlas?

Las gafas para ver eclipses como hoy las conocemos fueron desarrolladas por astrónomos y ópticos en la década de 1970 para que podamos mirar directamente al Sol en estos fenómenos sin poner en riesgo nuestra vista, así que esta será la primera vez en la historia de nuestro país en que podamos ver un eclipse de Sol total en España con este elemento de protección, que en los últimos días ha sido altamente cotizado en tiendas y farmacias.

La clave es llevarlas siempre que miremos directamente al Sol, es decir, durante la mayor parte del fenómeno. Con ellas, podremos ver cómo la Luna va cubriendo el Sol poco a poco y, después, cómo el Sol va saliendo nuevamente. Las gafas de protección ISO 12312-2 solo se las pueden retirar quienes están en la zona de la totalidad cuando el Sol está completamente cubierto, es decir, en la oscuridad total. Solo así podrán apreciar la corona solar.

Para usarlas de manera correcta y no dañarse la vista, es importante saber cuánto va a durar la totalidad en el lugar donde se va a ver el eclipse y volvérselas a poner antes de que la luz solar aparezca de nuevo por detrás de la Luna.

El regalo de las perseidas

Al contrario de los precios astronómicos de muchos de los hoteles de la zona de la totalidad, mirar al cielo todavía es gratis y este 12 de agosto, el universo tiene reservado un regalo doble para quien se quede observando las estrellas poco después del eclipse, cuando anochezca: será el pico de máxima actividad de las Perseidas o ‘Lágrimas de San Lorenzo’, la lluvia de estrellas más conocida del año. Que coincidan los dos fenómenos en un solo día es, como explica Daniel Medavilla en el video que acompaña este artículo, “una coincidencia cósmica que se da cada muchos milenios”. De hecho, los últimos humanos que vieron los dos fenómenos juntos fueron los neandertales.

Y si se van a perder este fenómeno porque están fuera de la banda de la totalidad, pronto habrá una nueva oportunidad, porque España ha sido agraciada con una particular lotería astronómica estos años en los que vivirá lo que se ha llamado un Trío de Eclipses. El próximo año, en 2027, el extremo sur de la Península, Ceuta y Melilla recibirán otro eclipse de Sol total. Y en 2028, será el turno de otro anular.

World.title: 16 pueblos españoles que piden manga larga cuando cae la tarde
World.content:
Vielha (Lleida). La gran baza de los pueblos seleccionados radica, sobre todo, en la posibilidad de tener que taparse para descansar, algo que se ha convertido en todo un lujo durante la canícula. Es un requisito que cumple Vielha, a la vera de los ríos Garona y Nere, con su casco histórico construido a la manera aranesa, a golpe de piedra, pizarra y madera. Sus mínimas descenderán hasta los 12ºC la noche del domingo; las máximas alcanzarán picos de 33ºC en las horas centrales del jueves y viernes, pero bajarán a los 24ºC (y con probabilidad de lluvias) el lunes, según la Aemet. La capital del Valle de Arán se presenta como un buen campamento base para conocer este territorio del Pirineo catalán, con sus 33 núcleos de población, sus algo más de 10.000 habitantes y sus iglesias románicas. Es recomendable acercarse a la cascada Saut deth Pish, probablemente la más bonita de la zona. Más información: visitvaldaran.com/descubre-la-val-daran/pueblos/vielha/.

Toni M (GETTY IMAGES)

World.title: Dos senderos idóneos para explorar el Valle de Arán en verano
World.content:
En la zona occidental de la comarca pirenaica esperan la Artiga de Lin y la Val de Toran. Cascadas, mariposas, pequeños pueblos y antiguos caminos para el contrabando que se disfrutan sin multitudes

Que levanten la mano quienes hayan estado en Baqueira, Salardú o Artíes. ¡Hala, cuánta gente! Ese es el Naut Aran (el Alto Arán, en aranés), al que más de un millón de personas acuden en invierno a esquiar. Que la levanten ahora quienes hayan estado en Es Bòrdes o en Canejan. Ni la décima parte. Esta zona occidental del Valle de Arán, por la que corren el río Garona y la carretera N230 poco antes de entrar en Francia, no es tan famosa como la oriental, pero por eso mismo está rodeada de montañas silenciosas, virginales, sin remontes ni aparcamientos para 1.600 vehículos.

Cuando la nieve se retira, aquí se ven flores, mariposas y cascadas. Hay dos senderos idóneos para explorarla: el que recorre el pasmoso valle de la Artiga de Lin, donde surgen a chorros las aguas del glaciar del Aneto después de circular casi cuatro kilómetros bajo tierra, y el camino del Contrabando, entre Canejan y Sant Joan de Toran, por el que los vecinos traficaban durante la posguerra con café y azúcar de la vecina Francia.

Los Ojos de Júpiter, del Diablo o del Judío

La Artiga de Lin es el paraje natural más espectacular de la comarca. En este valle glaciar hay dos lugares difíciles de creer: a 1.370 metros de altura, se encuentra la surgencia de los Uelhs deth Joèu (­los Ojos de Júpiter, del Diablo o del Judío, que de las tres formas lo traducen), donde brotan 1.580 litros de agua por segundo —y hasta 10.000 en pleno deshielo—. Cien metros más arriba, a 1.470, está el Plan dera Artiga, una gran pradera alpina rodeada de hayedos, abetales y escarpadas montañas calizas a casi 3.000 metros de altura donde lindan el Valle de Arán y el de Benasque, Lleida y Huesca, Cataluña y Aragón.

Surgencia de los Uhels deth Joèu, en la Artiga de Lin. Andrés Campos

A diferencia de lo que ocurre en la zona oriental del Valle de Arán, aquí no se puede aparcar a pie de pista porque no hay ninguna. Tampoco hay atascos porque los meses de mayor afluencia de visitantes en esta zona, los estivales, es obligatorio estacionar junto a la ermita dera Mair de Diu dera Artiga de Lin, tres kilómetros antes de llegar al final de la estrecha carretera que sube culebreando por el valle desde el pueblo de Es Bòrdes. Luego se puede continuar subiendo por el asfalto en un trenecito turístico o hacerlo a pie por el camino del Agua, que es una senda ribereña fácil y preciosa.

Siguiendo el camino, antes de una hora se verá la surgencia de los Uelhs deth Joèu. “¿De dónde sale tanta agua?“, se preguntan todos los que examinan por primera vez este nacedero torrencial, porque aunque su caudal medio se reduce en verano a 250 litros por segundo, sigue siendo mucha fuente. Pues resulta que sale del Aneto, el techo de los Pirineos, en la vecina Huesca. Y se sabe porque, en 1931, el espeleólogo francés Norbert Casteret vertió 60 kilos de colorante inocuo en el Forau d’Aigualluts —un sumidero kárstico del valle de Benasque donde las aguas recién fundidas del glaciar del Aneto desaparecen bajo tierra después de pegar un buen salto—, y comprobó que estas aparecían teñidas en los Uelhs. Así que estas aguas nacidas al sur de los Pirineos, en vez de ir al Ebro y al Mediterráneo, que sería lo lógico, corren cuatro kilómetros bajo las montañas para engrosar el río Garona y acabar en el Atlántico.

Indicador de rutas en la Artiga de Kin, en el Valle de Arán. Andrés Campos

Flores mil, más de 150 mariposas y dos guías excelentes

Al pie de la cascada tumultuosa, hay una pasarela metálica que permite cruzar el río Joèu para seguir subiendo por el abetal de la margen contraria y acabar saliendo, tras dos horas de paseo, al Plan dera Artiga de Lin. Es un rellano glaciar bellísimo, presidido por la mole rocosa del Malh dera Artiga (2.711 metros) y alfombrado de prados llenos de flores —gencianas, astrancias, violetas de los Pirineos, geranios silvestres, consueldas mayores, malvas moscadas…— y mariposas de montaña: la apolo, la mnemosine, la colias alpina, la erebia oeme, la común, la dentada…

Para distinguir las más de 150 especies que viven en este Shangri-La de las mariposas, es sumamente útil la guía ilustrada que ha publicado el Conselh Generau d’Aran. Otra guía excelente para explorar la Artiga de Lin es Sara Arjó, bióloga que dirige la empresa de ecoturismo y educación ambiental Verd e Blu y que es la autora de Parpalhòles dera Val d’Aran, un juego didáctico de papiroflexia con 14 recortables de mariposas de siete especies, las más llamativas del lugar.

Mariposa zygaena osterodensis en la Artiga de Lin. Andrés Campos

Todo es bonito en la Artiga de Lin, hasta el espléndido refugio donde Arjó se toma un refresco y algún tentempié con sus clientes, dejándolos disfrutar un rato largo de este paisaje embobador antes de acercarse al siguiente lugar destacado de la ruta: la cascada de Pomèro. En esta última, a solo 300 metros del refugio, les presenta la amapola amarilla (Papaver cambricum), una flor rara en España, pero muy abundante y estimada en las islas británicas, a tal punto que la usa como emblema Plaid Cymru, el partido nacionalista que ahora gobierna en Gales. Una microcentral eléctrica produce en este florido salto la energía de la que se abastece el refugio, que es grandecito, con habitaciones para 27 montañeros y un buen restaurante para cualquiera que pase.

Vista al Aneto desde el mirador de Vilamòs

Desde el refugio se baja cómodamente por la carretera asfaltada hasta la ermita donde se aparcó al principio. Como no se tarda mucho en completar la vuelta a pie (la ruta circular descrita, de algo menos de ocho kilómetros, lleva hacerla unas tres horas, cuatro con paradas contemplativas y de refresco), hay tiempo para acercarse en coche al mirador de Vilamòs, que está a solo siete kilómetros de la Artiga de Lin en línea recta, pero a 17 por una carretera loca (la LV5055) que sube desde El Pont d’Arròs trazando 16 revueltas. El mirador no está señalizado en la carretera, pero sí en Google Maps.

Vista del refugio de la Artiga de Lin, en el Valle de Arán. Andrés Campos

Desde aquí, con la ayuda del móvil y de la aplicación AR AlpineGuide (disponible en Google Play y en Apple Store), pueden identificarse las montañas que se alzan alrededor de la Artiga de Lin, arropando su formidable recuenco glaciar: la doble cima de la Forcanada, el Malh dera Artiga, la Tuca Blanca de Pomèro… Detrás de esta última cumbre asoman las nieves perpetuas y los riscos estratosféricos del macizo de la Maladeta, señoreados por el Aneto (3.404 metros).

Después de este atracón de montañas, apetece bajar a El Pont d’Arròs para darse otro de cocina aranesa en el restaurante del hotel Peña. Este es un cuatro estrellas cómodo y hogareño a más no poder, al que solo le falta aire acondicionado en las habitaciones para ser extraordinario. Pronto lo instalarán: el cambio climático obliga. Luego, un baño en la piscina climatizada y a la cama, que mañana hay que madrugar para explorar otra cara oculta de Arán, su rincón más desconocido y solitario: la Val de Toran.

Republicanos, judíos, maquis y contrabandistas

En Puntaut, poco antes de que el río Garona se cuele en Francia y de que la carretera N230 española se convierta en la N125 gala, se desvía a la derecha otra muy estrecha, sin eje central y sumamente virada que se adentra en la recóndita Val de Toran. Seis kilómetros y 38 curvas más arriba, se llega a Canejan, un pueblecito-balcón que domina desde su altura un inmenso panorama ­de las montañas donde España y Francia se besan.

Una cruz occitana en en suelo de la Plaça dera Castra, en Canejan. Andrés Campos

En la Plaça dera Castra, la mayor y más cuidada, la del Ayuntamiento, de pavimento decorado con una gran cruz occitana —la enseña aranesa—, dos paneles informativos recuerdan que por Canejan pasaban a Francia no pocos republicanos que huían de la represión franquista tras la Guerra Civil y judíos que escapaban en dirección contraria, de la Europa ocupada por los nazis, durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial. También recuerdan que esta fue la primera localidad atacada y tomada por los guerrilleros antifranquistas en octubre de 1944 durante la llamada Operación Reconquista de España, que pretendía deponer al dictador y restaurar la República. No dicen nada, en cambio, de los contrabandistas que trajinaban aquí en los años del hambre y del racionamiento, entre 1939 y 1952. Para decirlo, están los vecinos. No es que haya muchos en la Val de Toran (unos cien), pero casi todos están en Canejan. Una de ellas, Generosa Marqués, cuenta al que quiera oírla el caso de sus padres, Pedro y Palmira, que una vez al mes iban a la comuna gala de Fos y volvían cargados de café y azúcar, productos que escaseaban en el mercado regulado español y por los que sacaban un buen pico. Hasta que una noche los sorprendieron y pasaron las 15 siguientes entre rejas.

Difícil saber qué caminos usaban los contrabandistas para cruzar la raya. Como dice Generosa, “el tiempo, el del reloj y el atmosférico, los ha borrado”. Sin embargo, se conservan bien algunos de los que seguían para trapichear en este valle fronterizo, como el histórico que une Canejan, Porcingles y Sant Joan de Toran. Para andar por él solo hay que subir a lo más alto de Canejan y salir del pueblo siguiendo la calle Era Cau, que pronto se hace de tierra, asciende dejando a la derecha unas rústicas bordas y se vuelve prácticamente llana. Para más señas, hay indicadores de dirección y marcas de pintura blanca y roja a lo largo de todo el recorrido, pues coincide con el sendero GR-211. Y se puede consultar el mapa y descargar el track de la ruta en Wikiloc.

La soledad de Porcingles y Sant Joan de Toran

Tras una hora de paseo por este camino alto y horizontal, contemplando cómo desde una terraza el callejón sin salida montañoso de la Val de Toran, se entra en Porcingles, una aldea fantasma con solo dos casas temporalmente habitadas, calles impracticables y un lavadero cuyas aguas llevan tanto tiempo sin reflejar a un humano, que las mariposas (los sátiros del bosque y los ocelados, por citar dos especies que aquí se ven), se posan sobre las manos del recién llegado, sin saber qué es. Las ruinas de Porcingles son un recuerdo escalofriante de cuando a la Val de Toran llegó para quedarse una muchedumbre de 500 personas poseída por la fiebre del oro o, más bien, del zinc y del plomo, que eran lo que se sacaba de las minas de Liat, en la cabecera del valle, durante el siglo XIX y a principios del XX. Había incluso un teleférico de 13 kilómetros que transportaba todo lo extraído valle abajo, hasta el lavadero de mineral de Puntaut.

El camino, bastante llano hasta Porcingles, gana luego altura, cruza el barranco de Gotèrs y la pierde para llegar, al cumplirse dos horas de marcha, a Sant Joan de Toran. Tampoco es un lugar donde viva una multitud: solo tres personas. Pero junto a los prados que alguien se ha tomado la molestia de segar, hay una iglesia con macetas floridas a cada lado de la puerta y una docena larga de casas y bordas tradicionales de piedra en perfecto estado, en cuyos tejados de afilado caballete no falta una sola losa de pizarra: señal de que aquí viene a pasar cortas temporadas gente harta del mundanal ruido, que sabe lo que es bueno y que puede permitírselo. En este pueblo de postal se encuentra uno de los pocos negocios turísticos de la Val de Toran, el restaurante Estupendet, buen sitio para tomarse una ensaladilla rusa de verdad y una cerveza artesanal Refu. Este pulcro pueblecito rodeado de prados y montañas es lo más encantador del Valle de Arán, con permiso de la Artiga de Lin.

World.title: Amsterdam transport chief hid €850m bridge costs before election
World.content:
Amsterdam’s former transport chief, Melanie van der Horst, knew before March’s local elections that a planned cycle and pedestrian bridge over the IJ would cost up to €850 million – more than double the sum set aside – but did not tell the city council, documents released under a freedom of information request show.

Van der Horst, who is now the city’s head of economic affairs and was also lead candidate for the social-liberal party D66 at the elections, had been told by officials that the estimate for the Oostbrug had risen to between €650 million and €850 million, compared with the €325 million budgeted. The papers were obtained by Amsterdam broadcaster AT5.

Officials circulated the final estimate internally around December 2 and, according to AT5, explicitly gave Van der Horst the choice of making the figures public before or after the vote. At a meeting on February 12 it was decided to keep the older, lower amounts in the city’s official investment note.

Eight days before the elections Van der Horst was given a presentation setting out how the new range had been calculated. During the campaign she cited the IJ crossings as one of her administration’s achievements.

The new estimates only surfaced in early June, when the city published the documents handed to coalition negotiators.

The bridge, which at 1.2 kilometres would be one of the longest in the country, is being paid for jointly by the council and the regional transport authority Vervoerregio Amsterdam.

Emergency debate

Seven opposition parties – PvdD, Volt, JA21, Denk, BIJ1, CDA and SP – said in a joint statement they were shocked by the revelations but were not yet drawing conclusions, and an emergency debate has been requested. The coalition party PRO and D66’s own council group have also said they want answers.

Van der Horst declined to comment, referring questions to Elise Moeskops (D66), who took over the transport brief. Moeskops said the provisional estimates carry wide margins and could still change, that work on the design is continuing and that a final figure is not expected until early next year.

World.title: Dutch navy to take part in Nato exercise in Greenland next month
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Netherlands is to send dozens of navy personnel to Greenland as part of an international mission next month, defence minister Dilan Yesilgöz has confirmed.

Yesilgöz would not give an exact number when she revealed details of the plan on evening talk show Goedenavond Nederland, but said “a few vehicles” would also be sent on the mission.

She said the exercise was significant because of the “increasing activities of the Russians and the Chinese” in the Arctic Circle.

She insisted it had “nothing to do” with US president Donald Trump’s repeated declaration that he wants to buy the ice-clad, mineral-rich island.

“It’s a Nato exercise and the United States is also in Nato,” Yesilgöz said, even though no US military personnel are taking part.

Trump threatened sanctions against the Netherlands in January after Yesilgöz’s predecessor as defence minister, Ruben Brekelmans, said one naval officer was taking part in a Nato exercise in Greenland, but the US president later withdrew the threat.

World.title: Amsterdam’s robot bricklayers take on the Dutch housing shortage
World.content:
Monumental, an Amsterdam-based tech company that builds autonomous brick-laying robots, is working to help ease the country’s housing crisis by offsetting a critical shortage of construction industry workers.

Its machines use cranes and grippers, guided by sensors and computer vision, to build walls for new homes. Monumental raised $32 million in July in a round led by US firm Khosla Ventures, taking total investment past $60 million. CEO Salar al Khafaji has said in the future thousands of robots could be helping construct houses throughout Europe.

The Dutch housing crisis is compounded by an ageing workforce, which is not being replaced by new labourers fast enough. “The reality is that there simply aren’t enough skilled tradespeople available today,” Al Khafaji told DutchNews.

“Many projects are delayed because companies can’t find masons for the jobs. Our goal isn’t to replace people, but to give the industry the additional capacity it needs. By taking on repetitive bricklaying work, the robots allow skilled workers to focus on higher-value tasks.”

How it works

“The work starts well before we get to a site,” Al Khafaji explained. “Everything runs through our software, Atrium, which controls the whole operation from the robots themselves up to the screen an operator is looking at.”

“We take the architect’s drawings and work out in advance every brick and mortar joint based on the constraints of the project. Designs are broken down segment-by-segment and can automatically be translated into build-ready plans for our robots.”

Once on site, the company deploys a fleet of three robots named Pisa, Petra and Panama. Pisa places bricks and applies mortar. Petra supplies the bricks to Pisa and Panama supplies the mortar to Pisa. They are able to move around a building site autonomously alongside human workers.

Continuous learning

Al Khafaji said that for every project the company works on, its machines improve.

By acting as subcontractors rather than selling the machines, he said the company removes financial risks for construction companies. “If the wall is not right, that is on us and we’ll finish it manually if we have to. In exchange, we’re learning valuable information on every site that makes the next wall more predictable.”

“Every site we work on feeds back into Atrium, whether it’s difficult weather, an awkward corner, or a brick that behaves differently. That learning loop is why the system gets better, and it only works if we are the ones operating the fleet.”

Easing the housing burden

Monumental has built the walls for more than 100 homes so far, plus a school, a hotel, a community centre and hundreds of metres of Amsterdam canal wall. This is a tiny amount given the 69,000 homes built in 2025, and the national plan for 100,000 new homes per year.

“No single company will solve the housing shortage on its own,” Al Khafaji said. “The challenge is much bigger than bricklaying, and housing delivery depends on many other factors.”

“What we can do is ease one of the industry’s biggest bottlenecks by helping address the shortage of skilled bricklayers. Every additional robot allows more masonry work to happen in parallel without requiring more people in an already constrained labour market.”

“If you need to build twice as fast, we don’t need one robot to work twice as hard. We deploy twice as many. Robots parallelise in a way a scarce human workforce can’t.”

World.title: Two arrests for spraying graffiti in village hit by asylum riots
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Two people have been arrested for allegedly spraying graffiti on houses and cars during violent protests against plans to house asylum seekers in a Noord-Brabant village.

The 52-year-old man and 18-year-old woman were arrested at a house in Engelen, near ’s-Hertogenbosch, during a police raid on Saturday night.

Slogans such as “AZC nee” (no asylum seekers’ centre) and obscene insults were sprayed on the property of people accused of supporting plans by the local council to house 50 teenage refugees in the village’s former police station.

The site has been attack with an explosive device and been the focus of protests and stand-offs with police for several weeks. Anti-asylum protesters also blockaded the nearby A59 motorway.

The pair were arrested after 13 villagers filed official complaints and camera footage from the area was handed in. Police have not ruled out further arrests.

An area around the house in De Bloemendaal was cordoned off and police searched the premises using sniffer dogs, Omroep Brabant reported.

An investigation is also under way into the theft of a car from outside a house where a poster for the refugee agency Vluchtelingenwerk was displayed in the window. The vehicle was found dumped in a canal 500 metres away.

Local mayor Jack Mikkers said: “We cannot live in a country in which intimidation and violence are brought to bear on a decision. We expect further arrests to follow.”

World.title: “Taghi of Curaçao” goes on trial for numerous murders
World.content:
A gang leader dubbed the “Taghi of Curaçao” by prosecutors has gone on trial at the Netherlands’ high-security prison in Vught, where he is being held for his own safety.

Shurendy “Tyson” Q. is accused by public prosecutors of being one of the leaders of the No Limit Soldiers, a Curaçao gang, and of involvement in eight murders as well as several attempted killings.

Q. was extradited from Dubai in June and followed Monday’s opening hearing by video link from his cell. The prosecution is being made from Curaçao but being heard in the Netherlands, and is expected to run well into next year, with around 13 separate case files and large volumes of encrypted communication still to examine.

Much of the evidence consists of encrypted messages that prosecutors say were used to discuss targets, money and killings. Prosecutors told the court there was no doubt that Q. was the user of the accounts.

No Limit Soldiers gang members have been convicted of serious drug offences and murders in the Caribbean. Its members are also implicated in the 2013 murder of Curaçao politician Helmin Wiels.

In 2014, Q. was acquitted in the Netherlands after judges found prosecutors had not proved he was behind a set of intercepted messages. The next hearing is on 27 November.

World.title: US transgender woman returns home after failed Dutch asylum bid
World.content:
A transgender woman from the US who sought asylum in the Netherlands has returned home after her application bid failed and she suffered serious intimidation at the Ter Apel refugee centre.

Jane-Michelle Arc, from California, was one of approximately 76 Americans that sought asylum in the Netherlands last year. She flew to Schiphol airport and was instructed by customs officers to report to the immigration service IND at Ter Apel, which houses roughly 2,000 asylum seekers.

Her reason for leaving the US was the change in policy enacted by the Trump administration, which in an executive order denounced “ideologues who deny the biological reality of sex”, and ended the federal recognition of any gender identity besides male and female, rolling back anti-discrimination policies and protections on employment, housing and healthcare protections for trans people.

But the conditions at Ter Apel, which Arc described as “dire”, were life-threatening, she said, citing anti-trans hostility from other people at the camp.

Dangerous conditions

“This is the dumbest thing I’ve ever done”, Arc told the Guardian. “The situation I have in the US as a trans person, not good, right?. But here, I will be hurt or killed,” she separately told outlet Powned last month.

She said it was too dangerous to even walk to the supermarket, and spoke of the rising violence around the centre that has occurred this summer amid an overflow of refugees who were sleeping outside the facility gates in the heat.

After numerous fights, including two stabbings, aid organisations temporarily stopped working there for their own safety. Asylum minister Bart van den Brink subsequently enacted new measures including more security guards, CCTV cameras, and rooms for people without beds at the centre to stay indoors during the day.

US asylum claims

Arc estimated there are roughly 35-50 other trans people at the centre, housed in a special block away from other residents. It is unclear how many are seeking asylum on the grounds of gender discrimination, but Dutch group LGBT Asylum Support said in mid-2025 it was assisting around 20 US trans individuals with pending asylum claims.

“The IND generally states that discrimination by authorities and fellow citizens can be considered an act of persecution if it is so severe that victims can no longer function socially and societally,” the group said in a statement reported by Reuters.

“But the IND maintains that there are no grounds for exceptional treatment of transgender and queer refugees from the US.”

Another US asylum seeker, Lisa Gayle Carter-Stewart, who fled Montana with her 14-year old transgender daughter said their application was automatically rejected because America is considered a safe country, according to the Guardian.

The IND dismissed her daughter’s statement that they would commit suicide if forced to return to the US, Carter-Stewart said. Her daughter did not feel safe to ever leave her room at Ter Apel and attempted suicide three times while staying there, before they were moved to a more family-friendly camp near Leiden. Despite their experiences in the Dutch camps, they still feel unsafe returning to the US.

More than 500 reports of discrimination were received by a volunteer hotline during last week’s WorldPride event in Amsterdam.

The online portal RITA (Report It Always), set up for members of the LGBTQI+ community, said reports were still coming in following the two-week event, which included the city’s annual Pride canal parade on August 1.

Altogether 520 discriminatory incidents were reported, including 74 last weekend as the festivities drew to a close.

Co-founder Jerrald Justin told RTL Nieuws the figures were a “sad success” that reflected his organisation’s efforts to raise its profile during WorldPride.

This year RITA set up 35 ”safe spaces” around the city, including hotels, the Stedelijk Museum and the Nieuwe Kerk, where people could seek shelter from discrimination and report incidents in confidence.

The figures are hard to compare with previous years because WorldPride was a bigger event than the one-day canal parade, attracting more visitors, while RITA’s publicity campaign also led to more reports.

“Behind those 520 reports are 520 people who wanted to have a nice day but didn’t,” Justin said.

He told NOS the figures showed that much still needed to be done to highlight and combat homophobia. “It always starts with swearing and heckling and ends with violence,” he said. “We need to think of something together.”

World.title: Drought could force football clubs to delay start of season
World.content:
Amateur football clubs face having to cancel fixtures in the opening weeks of the season because the drought has made pitches unplayable.

The Delfland water authority has imposed a sprinkler ban across an area covering Delft and the Westland region, while the council has told them not to play on grass until the ban is lifted.

“We have 11 football pitches, but we can only use the three that have artificial surfaces,” Dick Hartman, secretary of FC ’s-Gravenzande told NOS.

“There is a chance that matches can’t go ahead,” he said. “We are doing a rain dance every day in the hope that it rains.”

The Dutch football association KNVB sent clubs a letter on Monday ahead of the start of the second and third division seasons, which kick off this weekend.

It urged clubs to “move matches to available artificial pitches if possible” and spread matches across the weekend to conserve grass surfaces. Otherwise clubs will have to apply to postpone matches using “the regular procedure”.

Jean Demollin, chair of southern Limburg club SNC ’14, said it was a struggle to keep the pitches in shape for training. “When the league matches start it will get worse,” he said. “We’ll have to move games or start with away fixtures. We haven’t got to that point yet, but I fear the worst.”

Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians. The figures also show that the overall number of registered foreign workers has risen more than 8% over the last year, a faster rate of growth than in recent years. However, the government official responsible for migration strategy says this is because stricter government measures have pushed some employers to register previously uninsured workers. The ZUS data, reported by Dziennik Gazeta Prawna (DGP), a leading daily, show that there were 1.34 million foreign workers registered in ZUS at the end of June, up from 1.24 million at the same point last year. That 8.2% increase is larger than the growth rate of around 6% seen in each of the previous two years, notes the newspaper. Maciej Duszczyk, the deputy interior minister responsible for migration, commented that the rise actually reflects the government’s tougher migration strategy, which he said “forces employers to report for insurance those who arrived earlier” but were working unregistered The official pointed to recent data showing that, in fact, in the first half of this year, Poland issued 50% fewer work permits to foreigners than in the same period of 2025. Dane ZUS pokazują dokładnie to co zakładaliśmy w Strategi Migracyjnej. Radykalny spadek liczby wydawanych, nowych zezwoleń na pracę (ponad 50% rok do roku) wymusza na pracodawcach zgłaszanie do ubezpieczenia, tych którzy przyjechali wcześniej. Tylko w pełni legalne zatrudnienie! — Maciek Duszczyk (@MaciekDuszczyk) August 11, 2026 Ukrainians remain by far the largest group of registered foreign workers, with 901,000 now in the system, a 10.1% rise from a year earlier. Belarusians (144,000, up 4.9%) remain in second. But two non-European migrant groups whose numbers have been growing rapidly in recent years now occupy third and fourth place: Indians (25,500, up 4.9%) and Colombians (23,000, up 31%, which was the fastest growth of any national group). Georgians, who had previously been the third-largest group, saw their number fall by 17% to 22,000, meaning they are now in fifth, ahead of Filipinos (15,400, down 2%), Moldovans (14,200, down 1%), Nepalis (13,400, up 8.3%), Vietnamese (12,200, up 6.1%), and Russians (11,800, down 2.5%). Latin American migration to Poland is booming, with 45,000 work permits issued last year, five times more than in 2022@Gosia_Tomczak looks at what is driving this trend and what challenges and opportunities it has created for both the migrants and Poland https://t.co/tl1wUTCaC0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2025 ZUS’s data also show that foreign workers are increasingly establishing their own businesses in Poland, which Dziennik Gazeta Prawna notes is a sign that they are establishing longer-term ties with the country but also a result of an easier online system for registering businesses. In 2021, only 22,700 foreigners had a registered business in Poland, a figure that now is now almost five times higher, at 102,000. The rise has been driven in particular by Ukrainians, many of whom are legally entitled to establish companies in Poland under the same terms as Polish citizens. As a result, 7.6% of foreign workers now run their own business, up from 6.7% a year ago and from 2.7% before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which led to a wave of Ukrainian refugees settling in Poland. Ukrainian refugees boosted Poland’s GDP by 2.7% last year while not raising unemployment or lowering wages, finds a report by the UN @Refugees agency and @Deloitte "Whoever thinks refugees are a burden on the economy should think again," says @UNHCRPoland https://t.co/rOvtOvBNwG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2025 Over the last decade, even before the war in Ukraine, Poland has experienced a wave of migration unprecedented in its history and among the largest anywhere in Europe. For six years running, between 2017 and 2022, it issued more first residence permits to immigrants from outside the European Union than did any other member state. Much of the surge in immigration came during the rule of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government from 2015 to 2023, despite its strong anti-migrant rhetoric. The current government, a more liberal coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, came to power pledging to reduce immigration, which it said had got out of control under PiS. Under Tusk’s government, in 2024, Poland issued the lowest number of residence permits to non-EU immigrants in a decade. In 2025, the government introduced tougher entry requirements for foreign workers and students. It has also stepped up deportations of foreigners who have broken the law. However, Duszczyk notes that the current government still sees “selective and responsible migration” as a way to “maintain the competitiveness of the economy without limiting wage growth”. ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Mother bear and cubs spotted on busy hiking trail in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. A female brown bear and her three cubs have been spotted in Poland’s Tatra mountains crossing a popular trail filled with hikers, with the animals coming unusually close to people. According to an official from Tatra National Park, where the incident took place, the behaviour could be a survival strategy by the mother to protect her young from male bears, which can kill cubs but tend to avoid humans. In a video posted on Sunday, the mother and three cubs were seen crossing the Chochołowska Valley trail in broad daylight, as crowds of people looked on Videos of the bear family have appeared increasingly often on social media, prompting questions about whether the animals are becoming less wary of people. But park officials say the female’s behaviour may have a biological explanation. “As we know, male brown bears are infanticidal. They kill not only other bears’ cubs, but their own as well. So the females, to avoid contact with the males, tend to stay closer to people,” Tomasz Zwijacz-Kozica, a park official, told local newspaper Gazeta Krakowska. “Females sense this instinctively and generally use the presence of people as a sort of shield to defend themselves against these males,” he added. The park staff hope to gather more detailed data on the female bear’s movements and behaviour in the future by possibly fitting her with a telemetry collar. They note that similar behaviour has been seen before. Around 20 years ago, a female bear drew attention when hundreds of tourists photographed her. They advise visitors to remain calm if they encounter a bear and to follow several basic rules, including staying calm and not running or making sudden movements, which may trigger a pursuit; not approaching the animals; and not attempting to take close-up photographs or use a flash. If a bear is encountered, visitors should slowly retreat in the direction from which they came while maintaining eye contact with the animal. Particular caution is required when cubs are present. Visitors should also avoid feeding bears or leaving rubbish behind. The smell of food can attract animals to trails and encourage behaviour that brings them into dangerous contact with people. A woman has died after being attacked by a bear in a forest in southeastern Poland. Such incidents are extremely rare, with the last fatal bear attack in the country reported in 2014 https://t.co/sAC2MPAvfh — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 23, 2026 Estimates of Poland’s brown bear population vary between 120 and 400, with most found in the southeastern Bieszczady mountains as well as the Tatras and Beskids further west. The population is thought to be growing, with a rise in reports of encounters with humans. In April this year, a woman was killed in a bear attack, Poland’s first such fatality since 2014. Another bear attack earlier in the year in the same region left a man with head and limb injuries. In March, the government launched a new 16 million zloty (€3.7 million) scheme aimed at both protecting bears and ensuring the safety of their human neighbours. It includes the creation of a special force to monitor and respond to bear sightings, including fitting the animals with tracking collars. In 2022, the town of Zakopane, located at the foot of the Tatra mountains, installed bear-proof rubbish bins to prevent animals from foraging in them – and thereby coming closer to areas of human population Poland has launched a new programme to protect brown bears and ensure the safety of their human neighbours, amid growing reports of encounters. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has called on opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections. His appeal comes as PiS, which for the last two decades has dominated the Polish right, is in crisis, amid falling polling numbers, a split by a breakaway faction, and a growing challenge from far-right parties that have long been critical of PiS. That has created a fragmented opposition, with parties competing against one another as much as or more than with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition. Some on the right hope that Nawrocki, who enjoys good relations with various parts of the opposition, could act as a unifying figurehead bridging those divides. 🔴 Jarosław Kaczyński ujawnił, o co osobiście poprosił Karola Nawrockiego. Podczas miesięcznicy smoleńskiej prezes PiS odniósł się do podziałów na prawicy i przyznał, że widzi dla prezydenta wyjątkowo ważną rolę: ma pomóc scalić zwaśnione środowiska. „Ja prezydenta swego czasu… pic.twitter.com/qwXhmccun2 — Super Express (@se_pl) August 10, 2026 Speaking on Sunday at a monthly commemoration of the 2010 Smolensk air disaster that killed his identical twin brother, then-President Lech Kaczyński, Jarosław was reported by a variety of Polish media outlets as saying that he had asked Nawrocki to act as a “patron” for a unified right. “I asked the president some time ago, and I hope he will do it,” said Kaczyński, quoted by newspaper Fakt. “It would be very good if the president took up this matter energetically.” “We could continue to develop – as we did during our years of government – not only in terms of achieving GDP growth, but also by undertaking major investments, by undertaking everything that would truly change Poland.” Kaczyński was referring to the period between 2015 and 2023 when a PiS-dominated coalition, known as the United Right (Zjednoczona Prawica), ruled Poland. In the latter year, it was ousted from power by a more liberal coalition led by Tusk, Kaczyński’s great rival. Since then, the landscape on the Polish right has changed dramatically. One of PiS’s partners in the United Right, the hard-right Sovereign Poland (Suwerenna Polska), merged with PiS in 2024. The other, the centre-right Agreement (Porozumienie), is now defunct. Meanwhile, support for PiS itself has collapsed. Having won 35% of the vote at the 2023 elections, it now averages only around 20% in polls – the party’s lowest figures for almost 20 years. To make matters worse, last month, around a fifth of the party’s MPs formed a breakaway group in parliament led by PiS deputy leader and former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki. They plan to soon form their own, separate party, Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), with a more moderate, centre-right agenda than PiS. At the same time, PiS has found itself challenged by a growing far right. Confederation (Konfederacja), which won 7% of the vote in 2023, is now polling around 12-13%. The even more radical Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), which broke away from Confederation last year, is at 9%. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 That has resulted in a much more fragmented right, with four separate entities not only opposed to Tusk’s government but also competing with one another for overlapping electorates. With parliamentary elections scheduled for autumn 2027, there have been questions over whether and to what extent the opposition should seek to cooperate with one another. One option would be an agreement not to stand candidates against one another for seats in the upper-house Senate, which are contested on a single-member-district system rather than through the proportional representation that decides the share of seats in the more powerful lower-house Sejm. Parties in Tusk’s current ruling coalition themselves formed such a “Senate pact” at the 2019 elections, helping them win control of the upper house, then repeated that in 2023, when they retained control. Although the Senate has a limited legislative role, it would be a significant prize for Nawrocki and the opposition, especially if Tusk’s coalition wins the Sejm, because the Senate has the power to approve or reject national referendums proposed by the president. An even more ambitious plan that has been rumoured is for some elements of the right-wing opposition to run joint electoral lists for the Sejm. That would require a far greater degree of programmatic consensus and longer negotiations over how to distribute places on lists. The government's majority in the Senate has, for the second time, rejected a proposal by opposition-aligned President Nawrocki to hold a referendum on whether Poland should continue implementing the EU's climate policies, which he argues are too costly https://t.co/Idm6dnzQEH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 6, 2026 Nawrocki is seen as key to any such plan coming to fruition. He was elected last year to the presidency as an independent, but with the formal backing of PiS. Ahead of the second-round run-off vote, he also received endorsements from defeated first-round rivals Sławomir Mentzen, one of the leaders of Confederation, and Grzegorz Braun, the leader of KKP. Since taking office, Nawrocki has continued to cultivate good relations with PiS and Confederation, as well as with Morawiecki’s new breakaway faction. However, he has kept his distance from Braun, whose anti-Americanism, antisemitism and sympathy towards Russia makes him something of a pariah. The European Parliament has again voted to strip Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face further charges for Holocaust denial as well as various antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT incidents during last year's presidential campaign https://t.co/4EHVEuSDnM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 26, 2026 Media reports have suggested that Nawrocki is planning to play a role in creating a “broad patriotic camp” among the opposition ahead of next year’s elections. Last week, during an event celebrating the first anniversary of his swearing in, the president also hinted at this role. He noted he will, in the coming months, be presenting “a presidential development strategy”, which “I believe will become a point of reference in the upcoming parliamentary elections for all those who aspire to govern Poland, a real plan for the future of the republic”. The strategy would be aimed in particular at “patriotic forces” who are “ready for dialogue between the offices of the president and future prime minister”. Given that Nawrocki and Tusk’s government are bitterly opposed to one another, that was a clear reference to opposition parties. A report on Sunday by Newsweek Polska, based on unnamed inside sources, claimed that Kaczyński is hoping to form a single electoral list for the Sejm elections compromising PiS, Development Plus and all or parts of Confederation, under the patronage of Nawrocki. 💥 Nowa obsesja Jarosława Kaczyńskiego, w jaki sposób odzyskać władzę. Prezes PiS naciska na Karola Nawrockiego, by prezydent stworzył "listę Nawrockiego" prawicy do Sejmu. To najbardziej ryzykowna, ale też o ogromnej stawce, decyzja prezydenta.https://t.co/sqRPFUuiZ7 — Jacek Gądek (@JacekGadek) August 9, 2026 Other leaders on the right have expressed varying degrees of willingness to work with one another. Speaking to broadcaster TVN on Saturday, Krzystof Bosak, another of Confederation’s leaders, expressed support for the idea of a Senate pact. On Friday, Morawiecki said that he can “fully imagine working with Sławomir Mentzen”, who “I believe is absolutely part of the patriotic camp”. However, Mentzen himself quickly ruled out the idea, tweeting that he’d rather “quit politics than join this gang leading Poland to disaster”, adding that Tusk, Kaczyński and Morawiecki are “one and the same”. Whereas Bosak represents a nationalist faction of Confederation seen as more compatible with PiS, Mentzen represent’s a libertarian wing that is bitterly opposed to the former PiS’ government’s high social spending, support for Ukraine, and the restrictions it introduced during the COVID-19 pandemic. Tusk, Kaczyński, Morawiecki, Czarzasty, jeden pies. Demonstrations took place in around 25 Polish cities on Sunday against a “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. The protests came after police data showed a significant increase in reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland so far this year, including a number of high-profile incidents of verbal and physical aggression. Sunday’s demonstrations, which took place under the slogan “Do Not Be Indifferent”, were organised by the Committee for the Defence of Democracy (KOD), an NGO, with support from other groups, including Amnesty International. “[This is] a nationwide campaign aimed at expressing opposition to the growing wave of hate, xenophobia, nationalism and violence directed against Ukrainians and members of other minorities,” wrote KOD ahead of the events. On Sunday, hundreds gathered on Warsaw’s Castle Square carrying Ukrainian and Polish flags and many waving signs saying “With U”, with the letter “U” coloured in Ukrainian national colours. #Siódemka Plac Zamkowy w Warszawie, protest w ramach: 🛑 NIE BĄDŹMY OBOJĘTNI! WSPÓLNIE PRZECIWKO NIENAWIŚCI! W wielu miastach Polski wyszliśmy na ulice, żeby jasno powiedzieć: nie ma zgody na hejt, przemoc i agresję wobec Ukraińców. W ostatnim czasie coraz częściej słyszymy… pic.twitter.com/kOfq4zBuGT — Piotr #FBPE Fijałkowski (@piotr4913) August 9, 2026 In Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, local media reported that around 150 people attended a demonstration, carrying placards saying “Let’s defend our neighbours from the aggression and stupidity of others” and “Putin is the enemy, Ukraine is our neighbour”. In Gdańsk, on Poland’s northern coast, around 300 people gathered, according to local media. However, they were also met with a small counter-demonstration of around a dozen people, led by the New Hope party that is part of Poland’s far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) opposition group. The counter-protesters held a banner declaring “Solidarity with victims of mass immigration” and “Down with Bandera”, a reference to historical Ukrainian nationalist leader Stepan Bandera, who in Poland is associated with the massacres of around 100,000 Poles by Ukrainians during World War Two. Separately, on Friday, a group of NGOs organised a demonstration against anti-Ukrainian violence outside the prime minister’s chancellery, during which they delivered a petition, signed by over 11,000 people, calling for the government to take “decisive action against xenophobic attacks”. Police data published last month showed that the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025. Among those incidents have been a number of high-profile cases, including two 11-year-old Ukrainian girls being verbally abused by a man on a bus in the city of Bielsko-Biała and a violent attack on young Ukrainians by a group of Polish teenagers in Warsaw. Ukrainians are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group, with around 1.6 million living in the country. While Poland welcomed Ukrainian refugees in 2022, there has been growing negative sentiment towards them recently, indicated in polls and through anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from prominent politicians. Tenions have been stoked further by a diplomatic crisis that began in May, when President Volodymyr Zelensky named a Ukrainian military unit after a group responsible for massacring Poles during World War Two. That prompted Polish President Karol Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 In particular, two far-right opposition parties, Confederation and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have used anti-Ukrainian rhetoric, while the largest opposition group, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has recently taken a tougher line towards Ukraine. Last week, PiS announced that, if it returns to power, one of its first actions would be to deport Ukrainian conscription-age men who are not in legal employment. At one of Sunday’s protests, in Kraków, a demonstrator responded with a placard declaring “Deport xenophobia”. Poland’s more liberal ruling coalition has condemned anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from the right-wing opposition. Last month, Prime Minister Donald Tusk called for a “war against this violence”, saying that “thugs and hooligans have gained courage, audacity and political patronage” from the opposition. Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative PiS, has called for Ukrainian men of conscription age who are not legally working to be deported to Ukraine.
