If none of this happens, or only some of it is achieved, the assessment could be different.

But once again, the stability that came to the region as a result of the Washington summit is extremely important for Armenia. From 2020 to 2025, security threats dominated our lives. Progress on security, without a doubt, also gives us an opportunity to focus on other issues.”

Washington peace summit: one year on

World.title: Eight Turkish parliamentary parties call for ending Abkhazia’s isolation
World.content:
Eight parliamentary parties in Turkey have called for an end to Abkhazia‘s isolation. The initiative primarily calls for Turkey to recognise the Abkhaz passport as a valid document for crossing the Turkish border, as well as for direct sea and air links between Turkey and Abkhazia to open.

Representatives of opposition factions announced the initiative at a joint press conference in the Turkish parliament. The initiative forms part of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” public campaign, which the local diaspora launched in early July 2026. The diaspora organised the campaign.

“Just imagine: hundreds of thousands of people of Abkhaz origin and their relatives live in Turkey, yet the Abkhaz passport is not valid here. Abkhaz people cannot travel to Turkey to attend the funerals of their relatives, while young people cannot enrol in universities.

These are the realities of international relations. Sometimes states are prepared to turn a blind eye to tragedies and anti-democratic practices that affect their own citizens’ relatives.

We are saying openly: Abkhaz passports must be recognised as valid documents at our border crossings. This disgrace must come to an end,” said Tuncer Bakırhan, an MP from the Democratic Party.

The eight parliamentary parties calling for an end to Abkhazia’s isolation represent a broad range of political forces, from the far right to the far left. What unites them is that they are all in opposition. The largest of them is the Yeni Parti (“New Party”), which has 91 MPs in the current parliament. Together, the eight parties hold 166 of the 600 seats in parliament.

The support from the opposition parties was not welcomed by the leadership of the Federation of Abkhaz Cultural Centres in the Republic of Turkey. More precisely, the Federation’s leadership appears to have objected not to the MPs themselves, but to the organisers of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” campaign.

The Federation does not dispute the campaign’s demands: recognition of Abkhaz passports and the opening of transport links between Abkhazia and Turkey. Its objections concern the “right to represent” and the “right to initiate” such efforts.

In Abkhazia, the Federation’s reaction was met with strong criticism from both politicians and civil society representatives.

“If any Abkhaz person in Turkey or elsewhere makes progress on our common cause, we should all support them and, if possible, join them, rather than argue over who is authorised to do what.

If our representatives in Turkey focus solely on preserving the language and culture, they should not interfere with those working to advance the political cause. If they consider such advocacy part of their remit, they should join them. That is how it looks from Abkhazia,” said Duat Khutaba, head of the Abkhaz parliament’s Committee on Legislation.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Campaign to end Abkhazia’s isolation

World.title: WA town sliding into ocean gets funding for temporary sea wall
World.content:
A small coastal town fighting to stop its pub and caravan park from sliding into the sea has been given a $1.1 million lifeline from the WA government.

Residents of Lancelin, about 125 kilometres north of Perth, have been trying to save their town from worsening erosion for more than a year, with pub owner Glen Trebilcock telling the ABC he had seen about 50 metres of the northern part of the beach disappear in 15 months.

A storm surge in June 2026 saw increased rates of coastal erosion in Lancelin. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Today the state government announced it would give $1.1 million towards the construction of a 110m-long rock wall, touted as an interim solution to the town's vanishing shorelines.

The Shire of Gingin will also kick in $150,000 towards the project, which is expected to provide protection from erosion for about five years.

Lancelin Sands Hotel owner Glen Trebilcock said he had spent about $10,000 on sand alone to protect his business, and the planned new wall would "mitigate any further potential damage and ensure the longevity of our town".

Glen Trebilcock has spent about $10,000 on sand alone to protect his business. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

But critics say it is not enough.

Save Lancelin Community Coalition member Kirsty Harding described it as "woefully inadequate" and said the wall would only protect the pub and the adjacent Lancelin North End Caravan Park.

"It protects two properties only, which is great for these properties that are at the most imminent risk, but it doesn't protect the Lancelin community," she said.

"There's a longer length of dune that's really rapidly eroding too, and that now sits at the edge of where this structure is proposed to go.

" We're really happy something is being done but what about the rest of the town? "

Linda Balcombe says the funding would help the town 'move forward' with their efforts against coastal erosion. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Shire of Gingin president Linda Balcombe welcomed the plan and said it would allow the town time to work out what was causing the erosion.

"Until we know the answers, we don't know what the permanent solution is," she said.

"This [funding] will allow us the time to collect the data."

Ms Balcombe said designs for the temporary wall would go before the local council next week.

Tenders for construction of the wall are expected in September.

World.title: Western Power staff stood down over character references for rapist manager
World.content:
Three Western Power employees who gave favourable character references to a senior manager who raped a female colleague on a work trip have been stood down, with the energy minister ordering an investigation into the government-owned utility.

Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing, including descriptions of sexual assault.

Jeffrey David Spinner, 59, was sentenced to five years in jail in June after he took the victim to his hotel room while she was heavily intoxicated in 2024.

The court heard the woman had vomited earlier in the night and required assistance to walk, which Spinner witnessed.

After she went back to Spinner's hotel room thinking it was hers, she sat in the shower fully clothed with the water running.

Spinner helped her out of the shower and the woman got into his bed with a towel on. She woke up to him raping her, the court heard.

Jeffrey David Spinner was sentenced in June to five years in jail for raping a colleague in Bunbury in 2024. (Facebook: Jeff Spinner)

In sentencing remarks, District Court Judge Gary William Massey referred to character references provided by colleagues, finding the offending was "out of character".

"I'll give you the benefit of being a person of prior good character," he said while considering an appropriate sentence.

He referred to references from a colleague who had worked with Spinner closely for a long period of time, and who described the senior manager as "a highly respected work colleague known for [his] professionalism, integrity and strong work ethic".

Spinner (right) was described by a relative as someone who has always shown respect for women. (Facebook: Jeff Spinner)

Despite that, the judge said the case was serious, featured aggravating circumstances and left the victim feeling "scared, vulnerable and uncertain about her future", to the point that a security guard was placed outside her home.

'Completely unacceptable': minister

WA Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson lashed out at the Western Power employees who provided the character references.

"This case is shocking and disturbing, and completely unacceptable," she said.

She ordered Western Power to conduct an immediate investigation, and said the power provider had stood down the employees who provided the character references.

Ms Sanderson (right) says employees who gave character references lacked judgement. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"Firstly I want to offer my full support to the woman involved at the centre of this case," Ms Sanderson said.

"She has shown incredible strength and resilience in coming forward in reporting these charges, in pursuing the charges, and enduring a court case.

"In my view these actions do not meet the standard required of Western Power employees, and they demonstrate an appalling lack of judgement.

Ms Sanderson would not rule out a third-party review into the handling of the case, but said she would first allow the internal review to complete its course.

"The review is intended to take around two weeks, and the outcomes of that review will be made public," she said.

Jeffrey David Spinner spoke to ABC News about a Western Power story in 2016. (ABC News)

Ms Sanderson said the state government had previously committed to removing character references as a mitigating factor in the sentencing of child sexual abuse offences, and would now consider removing them from other offences, including sexual assault.

The minister said she had also ordered Western Power to review how it communicated with government and escalated serious issues.

"It is disappointing that there was no formal briefing to me or my office around the full extent of this case," she said.

CEO learned of character references this week

Western Power chief executive officer Gair Landsborough, who was appointed to the role at the end of last month, said the utility investigated the incident in 2024.

"This resulted in the immediate [standing] down of the accused employee, and following an investigation, the termination of employment," he said.

Gair Landsborough says he only learned of the characters references when contacted by a journalist. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Despite Spinner being sentenced in June, Mr Landsborough said Western Power was only "made aware" on Monday evening that three of its employees had provided character references to Spinner, before a story was published in local media.

"As soon as we were made aware of this, again an investigation into that … has been initiated," he said.

Mr Landsborough said it was "absolutely not good enough" his organisation was not aware.

"That's part of the review … that we had our own staff providing character witnesses in a sentencing and we were not aware of it," he said.

Western Power provides energy to most of the state's population. (ABC News: Kenith Png)

He said management did not attend the sentencing as planned because they were not told of a change of date.

"But we should've been there and we've got to learn from this and make sure that it doesn't happen again," he said.

Mr Landsborough said his immediate concern was for the wellbeing of the victim.

"Very concerned about her welfare, I gave her a call yesterday just to check how she's going, and more importantly let her know any support that she needs, Western Power is here for her," he said.

"We've instigated a review of our safety and culture program, that means everything from reviewing our code of conduct, the leadership training we provide our senior people, the mandatory training we do provide already for sexual harassment and misconduct and the like."

World.title: Legendary boot-studder hangs up his own after 58 years with Port Adelaide
World.content:
He's outlasted big names and seen many more games without the limelight but after nearly six decades looking after boots for Port Adelaide Football Club, Alfie Trebilcock is hanging up his own.

A young butcher from Broken Hill who came to the club during 1968, the boot-studder enjoyed 11 SANFL premierships, one AFL premiership, and watched footwear evolve from ankle-high boots with wooden knock-in sprigs, to light-weight multi-coloured fashion statements.

"I came down here [to Adelaide] in 1961. My grandparents followed Port Adelaide so I started following them and used to go to their games and all that type of thing," Trebilcock told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"I got friendly with the runner, Harry Vincent, got talking one day and said I'd like to get into the club and he said, 'I'll keep an eye out for you'."

A position opened up in the boot department and Trebilcock was told to have a "talk to the sprigger" who was also a bootmaker.

"He said, 'Are you prepared to learn?', and I said, 'Oh yeah', so I did a seven-year apprenticeship with him," Trebilcock said.

"After those seven years he got leukaemia and said, 'You're going to have to take over', and I said, 'Gee whiz, I'm a butcher'.

" But I was pretty lucky because moulded soles were coming in then and so I took it on and I've been there ever since and enjoyed every single minute of it. "

But from the day Trebilcock started looking after the players' footwear in 1968 and up to 1976, the Port Adelaide Magpies played without winning a SANFL premiership.

"I was beginning to think I was jinx," Trebilcock said.

But the club won a flag in 1977 and another 10 during Trebilcock's time, as well as a 2004 AFL premiership with its AFL side, The Power.

"The 2004 AFL premiership was mighty.

"I always pictured standing on the MCG on Grand Final day, celebrating a flag. That dream came true in 2004. I'll never, ever forget that day."

Bobby to say farewell as well

Also retiring is fellow volunteer Bob "Bobby" O'Malley after 18 years at the club mixing water barrels and player rehydration bottles, and helping set up for training sessions.

Former Port Adelaide Power player and captain Travis Boak with Bob O'Malley during a game against Carlton. (Supplied: Port Adelaide Football Club)

"I just loved being involved in this football club," he said.

"Port Adelaide was always a family club, and all my family barracked for Port Adelaide."

He will have his final home game with Port Adelaide against Melbourne on Saturday night.

Trebilcock will be saying goodbye after 58 years with the club.

He said he became "real friends" during this time with the late and great Russel Ebert OAM, who started with the Magpies the same year as him.

An Australian Football Hall of Fame member since 1996, Ebert played 392 games for the Magpies and remains the only SANFL player to win four Magarey Medals.

"He was a people's person," Trebilcock said.

"He was a player that never played a game of football in moulded sole boots. To the day he retired he still had knock-in sprigs.

"Every now and then you'd have to re-sprig his boots.

"As he got older his sprigging would change … then he got his Achilles problems and we made a [raised] heel for him."

The late Russell Ebert shares a laugh with Alfie Trebilcock at Port Adelaide Football Club. (Supplied: Port Adelaide Football Club)

Ebert once said of Trebilcock that he loved the players and the club, and the players loved him.

"He can talk to any player at any time and would have the complete respect of the entire playing and coaching group … we couldn't have had the success we had without him," Ebert said.

The AFL awarded Trebilcock the Jack Titus Award for conspicuous service to the game in 2013.

He was awarded Life Membership at PAFC in 2013 and was inducted into its Hall of Fame in 2025.

PAFC chairman David Koch said the club was what it was today because of people like O'Malley and Trebilcock.

"Nearly 60 years of turning up, asking for nothing and giving everything to the club he loves," he said.

"On behalf of every player, coach and supporter we say thank you, Alfie, and thank you, Bobby. We are the club we are today because of people like you."

World.title: Musician identified as man killed in tree-car crush on Mount Buller
World.content:
A man killed when a tree fell on a car at Mount Buller has been identified as musician Talae Rodden.

Mr Rodden died at the scene on Monday. He was a passenger in a car driven by his mother on Mount Buller Road when a tree fell on the vehicle.

His mother was taken to hospital with serious upper body injuries.

Mr Rodden is being remembered as a talented musician and part of a family that is "deeply ingrained in life at Mount Buller", according to an online fundraiser.

He was a budding musician with a solo musical project called RiceWine.

Talae Rodden was a regional musician based in Victoria's High Country. (Supplied: Go Fund Me)

He is survived by his mother, Sally, father Cha and brother Jared.

The family managed lodges on the mountain and ran retail shops in Mansfield and nearby Merrijig where they live.

"At this incredibly difficult time, we want Sally, Cha and Jared to know that they are not alone," the fundraising page reads.

Mansfield Shire Council Mayor Steve Rabie said Mr Rodden's death would be felt across the shire for some time.

Talae Rodden was a regional musician. (Supplied: Go Fund Me)

"Mansfield is a small and very close-knit community," Cr Rabie said.

"When something like this happens, the impact reaches well beyond those immediately involved and I know many people across our community have been deeply affected by this news.

"Our thoughts are with the family and as a community, we stand with them."

Police said the investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death remained ongoing.

A report will be prepared for the coroner.

World.title: It should have been this girl's 18th birthday. Instead, it was her vigil
World.content:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name and photo of an Aboriginal person who has died, used with the permission of their family.

Instead of celebrating a "kind and loving" local girl's 18th birthday, last night more than 200 people on Elcho Island in the remote Northern Territory gathered for a vigil to remember her following her alleged murder last month.

The mourners marched through the community of Galiwin'ku to the girl's parents' home where 'happy birthday' banners hung on the patio and candles were lit in honour of her short life.

A vigil was held on what would have been the girl's 18th birthday. (Supplied )

The girl, referred to as T. Bukulatjpi, had been in her final year of high school and had a leadership role with her local girls' empowerment program.

She was found dead in an Elcho Island home on July 6 from what police have alleged were blunt force injuries.

A 34-year-old man, who police allege she was in a domestic relationship with, has been charged with her murder.

Before her alleged murder, T. Bukulatjpi had been in her final year of high school and held a leadership role within the local empowerment group for girls. (Supplied)

Her uncle Marcus Lacey said "in Yolŋu terms, she was one of my daughters", and that she was the next in line to be taught her grandmother's cultural knowledge.

"Describing our daughter, she was very loving, kind, gentle, cheeky," he said.

"Coming from a Yolŋu all male [family], this has really hurt my mum, her grandmother, because she never had daughters.

"She was a really beautiful, kind woman."

Marcus Lacey (left) says she was a kind, loving and cheeky girl. (Supplied)

Pillar of girl empowerment group

Before her tragic death, T. Bukulatjpi was part of a local group called 'Girl Power', which was led by her second cousin and chairperson of Yalu Aboriginal Corporation, Jasmine Yunupiŋu.

The group provides young women a safe space to feel heard in yarning circles and works to empower them through programs like bush camps and self defence classes.

Jasmine Yunupiŋu says the girl encouraged many others to attend the girls' empowerment group. (Supplied)

Ms Yunupiŋu described the 17-year-old as a "young, precious girl" and a leader of the group, which was created to help young women have a voice.

"She was so kind, she was loving … I can still see her smile," she said.

"She was very humble … she was one of the girls that had to pass out the message to other girls that [were] missing out on the program.

"We ended up with 50 girls coming to the program."

People gathered at a vigil to remember a 17-year-old girl in Galiwin'ku after she was allegedly murdered. (Supplied)

Participants from the Girl Power program attended the vigil to remember their friend, but Ms Yunupiŋu said it was also an opportunity to stand against violence in the community.

"We all know that violence affects all of us, our children, our families, our whole community — we must continue to speak up and teach our young people that violence is never the answer," she said.

"The chain starts with all of us.

"We must stand strong together and say no more violence for our children, our families."

A time to speak up

Yalu Aboriginal Corporation chief executive Anahita Tonkin said in addition to the candles, community members brought ribbons to the vigil: white for domestic violence, and grey and black, which were T. Bukulatjpi's favourite colours.

After the mourners visited the girl's parents' home, Mr Lacey decided the community needed to face the place where she was found dead.

"Marcus led us to the house where she [allegedly] took her last breath," Ms Tonkin said.

"We stood there and it was organised by Marcus to have people speak up."

People marched through Galiwin'ku in the girl's memory.

Mr Lacey said being at the site of the alleged murder and speaking about what had occurred there was important to him.

"We need to break that chain, that curse and speak openly about it," he said.

"Because if we don't speak openly about it in that area where she was taken, then it's not valued.

"We need to value life and value the situation."

The family of the victim and the alleged perpetrator were both present at the vigil, with speeches given by a local women's shelter, police and community members.

World.title: Melbourne Royal Show cancels poultry exhibits due to H5 bird flu spread
World.content:
The Melbourne Royal Show has cancelled poultry competitions and exhibitions for 2026 in the wake of surging H5 bird flu cases around the country.

The decision was made earlier today, and follows a state government announcement that Phillip Island's wild population of little penguins would be vaccinated against the disease.

Event organisers say they hope to welcome poultry back to the show in 2027. (Melbourne Royal Show)

Melbourne Royal Show executive general manager Hannah von Bibra said the committee had been in consultation with Agriculture Victoria and the state's chief veterinary officer, with the health and wellbeing of all animals at the show being the number one priority.

"Melbourne Royal is taking this precautionary step to protect the health and wellbeing of the Victorian poultry community," she said.

"Whilst there are currently no detections of H5N1 in Australian poultry, the situation is not predictable and, as such, we want to give our community as much certainty as possible."

The poultry exhibits and competitions were previously cancelled in 2024 due to the H7 bird flu outbreak. (Melbourne Royal Show)

Ms von Bibra said the show committee was appreciative of the time and effort exhibitors put into preparing for the show, and hoped to welcome poultry back in 2027.

She told Statewide Drive while there are no recorded H5 cases in poultry yet, the decision was made as a precaution.

"The show has been going for over 178 years and the poultry part of that for 150," she said.

"It's absolutely a wonderful addition to our show. What it means is we've made this announcement to give real certainty of what is happening during this time."

Concerns for the show were raised at the weekend, with a number of other poultry shows taking place across regional Victoria.

The Royal Adelaide Show has also cancelled bird competitions ahead of next month's event due to bird flu concerns.

World.title: Bali ferry catches fire in rough seas off Lombok
World.content:
Emergency crews are working to rescue passengers from a Bali ferry that caught fire this morning.

Rescuers and passing vessels had managed to save 106 people and were battling rough seas to get the remaining 25 off the burning ship, authorities said.

"Our top priority is the safety of all passengers and crew members," said Muhammad Hariyadi, who heads the Mataram Search and Rescue Office.

He said rough seas with waves reported as high as 4 metres complicated rescue efforts.

The fire started about 4:15am while the Putri Yasmin ferry was en route from Padang Bai port in Bali to Lembar port on the neighbouring island of Lombok, according to the search office in Mataram, the provincial capital.

The agency received an emergency report almost half an hour later and immediately deployed personnel and rescue vessels.

Mr Hariyadi said the rescue effort was supported by Indonesian navy ships, patrol boats, rescue vessels and a helicopter to make an aerial survey.

The ferry was carrying 114 passengers and 17 crew members, Mr Hariyadi said, citing passenger manifest data released by the Padang Bai's port authority.

The ferry was also with loaded 44 vehicles and 53 motorcycles.

It is unclear if any Australians were on board. The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has been contacted for comment.

Indonesia is an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands where ferries are a common method of travel.

Disasters occur regularly, with weak safety enforcement often blamed.

Earlier this month, an Indonesian ferry carrying 271 passengers caught fire while travelling between East Java and South Sulawesi, killing five people.

AP/ABC

World.title: NSW Liberal faction's 'filthy schools money' text a 'stupid joke', ICAC hears
World.content:
A former NSW Liberal Party operative has told the state's corruption watchdog a text he sent referring to handing over "filthy schools money" was a "stupid joke".

The NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) is examining allegations that prohibited political donations were funnelled through third parties to support the Liberal-aligned, right-wing faction NSW Reformers and advance the interests of fugitive property developer Jean Nassif.

The inquiry has heard that members of the Reformers used companies, sham invoices, and consulting agreements to disguise political donations, including payments allegedly channelled through Catholic Schools NSW (CSNSW).

It is also examining allegations involving lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood's former company, Beckington, which is alleged to have been used to disguise political donations as payments for lobbying and government relations work.

Mr Perrottet was involved in a text message exchange with Mr Greenwood. (AAP: George Chan)

At the inquiry's first hearing last month, a text exchange was shown in which Mr Greenwood told Jean-Claude Perrottet: "Hey, so you know I'm good to you and help you and give you your filthy schools money and put up with you f***ing whinging."

Mr Perrottet replied: "Don't put that in writing."

Mr Greenwood then responded: "It deletes."

Jean-Claude Perrottet is the brother of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet and a was a member of the Reformers faction.

Counsel assisting the commissioner, Peggy Dwyer SC, alleged the money referred to payments from CSNSW intended to fund Liberal Party recruitment work.

Mr Greenwood says the message is a "joke". (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

Dr Dwyer had previously said the exchange would form part of the evidence the commission would rely on to argue main Reformers players knew "sham arrangements" were used.

On his third day of evidence, Mr Greenwood said it was a "stupid joke" with a friend about something that would "make him nervous to hear".

Dr Dwyer said: "You knew it was, in your words, filthy schools money, because that was a dodgy arrangement where you were passing on money from Catholic Schools that was intended to fund his recruitment work for the Liberal Party, correct?" Mr Greenwood replied: "No … Look, it's a stupid joke. I rile him up all the time … I regret it, because it's become prominent here, but it's just our relationship."

The commission also heard that Mr Perrottet deleted the message from his phone.

In Dr Dwyer's opening statement, it was revealed Mr Perrottet travelled to Fiji to avoid giving evidence in a 2023 parliamentary inquiry, with "financial assistance from others named" in the allegations.

Mr Greenwood told the ICAC on Wednesday he paid for the trip to help him to avoid being summonsed.

The commission also heard a security guard organised by former Labor councillor Sharangan Maheswaran — and likely paid by Mr Nassif's company — was stationed outside his home to also help him avoid being contacted by process servers.

World.title: ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Greenwood told NSW Catholic Schools boss to avoid inquiry, wanted Nassif to pay for Jean-Claude Perrottet’s Fiji trip to avoid commission
World.content:
Jeremy Greenwood met with Jean-Claude Perrottet at the Oaks, a pub in Double Bay, after Greenwood gave evidence to the ICAC and placed their phones at a different table to avoid being surveilled, the commission has heard.

Greenwood gave private evidence to the ICAC in June 2025 and was told by the commissioner then that he should not discuss his evidence with anyone, which he told the ICAC on Wednesday that he took very seriously.

Jeremy Greenwood arrives at ICAC on Tuesday. Peter Rae

It is a criminal offence to disclose evidence given to the ICAC once the commissioner has ordered it remain a secret.

He couldn’t recall going to the pub afterwards or arranging to meet up with anyone, but said he wouldn’t be shocked if he wanted a drink afterwards. When counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer, SC, told him he met with Jean-Claude Perrottet at the Oaks he said he wouldn’t be surprised since they go there often.

World.title: ‘Assert yourself’: Refreshed skipper Cummins has clear message for Cam Green
World.content:
Breaking SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘Assert yourself’: Refreshed skipper Cummins has clear message for Cam Green Daniel Brettig Updated August 12, 2026 — 3:44pm ,first published 2:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Darwin: Australia’s captain Pat Cummins believes that playing just one Test in 12 months can extend his Test career, and has urged all-rounder Cameron Green to learn the lessons of the past six years and impose himself on Bangladesh. A back stress injury kept Cummins to a sole Ashes Test last summer, but the side effect of his absence is that numerous other trouble spots – notably his hamstrings – are fresher and stronger for what could amount to 21 Test matches in the space of 12 months. Australian captain Pat Cummins and his Bangladesh counterpart Najm ul Shanto promote the Test that starts in Darwin on Thursday. Getty Images “I missed a few Test matches but it feels like I’ve had a proper 12-month block of gym work, running and things I don’t ever think I would have done,” Cummins said on Wednesday. “Something like my hamstrings I’ve probably managed the last five or six years. “I’m sure they’ll flare up gain, but they feel 100 per cent right now. I only have to look at someone like Starcy [teammate Mitchell Starc] to see someone going well late into his 30s. I think this block has set me up pretty well.”



Josh Hazlewood tipped out Scott Boland, while Green kept his place alongside fellow all-rounder Beau Webster in Australia’s team to face Bangladesh in the first Test on Thursday. Hazlewood will play his first Test since the Caribbean tour a little over a year ago, after missing the Ashes with hamstring and Achilles injuries. Josh Hazlewood has got the nod for the first test against Bangladesh. Getty Images Nathan Lyon has also been recalled to the team following surgery on a serious hamstring tendon injury he suffered during the third Ashes Test in Adelaide in December. Teammates have been taken by Lyon’s level of dedication, eschewing alcohol and working assiduously in the gym to get the most out of his 38-year-old frame.



“I was looking at some footage the other day of that Adelaide Test, and I think that’s the best he’s bowled in years,” Cummins said. “So it was really bad timing, but it’s been pretty public how hard he’s worked over the last six months or so. “He looks in incredible shape, he’s been bowling beautifully, and as captain and teammate it’s going to be awesome to have him back out there.” Loading Boland was a most unfortunate omission from the team given his superb displays in the Ashes and a hat-trick in the West Indies, but he and Hazlewood can be expected to share a place in the team over the next 12 months provided both stay fit. “They’re both pretty class aren’t they,” Cummins said of the pair. “We were pretty certain we wanted ‘Lyono’ in the side so it’s then working out what the makeup of the quicks were.



“It’s always a pretty tight call, and there’s not much you can say to Scotty other than there’s a lot of cricket coming up. He knows his worth and how good he is, and I’m sure he’ll be back at some point pretty soon.” Related Article Australian cricket Australia confront Cameron Green question ahead of Darwin Test Green had a long state-of-the-union style chat with Cummins and head coach Andrew McDonald at training on Tuesday, and he will have a great opportunity to impose himself on a modest Bangladesh team in Darwin. “He’s had a bit of time to think about his own game, and the good thing is he’s played quite a lot,” Cummins said of Green. “In his Test career he’s had moments where it’s worked and moments where it hasn’t. “I think it’s that journey of most cricketers, particularly all-rounders where it’s a really tough job being the finished product when you’re young. Now the job for someone like Cam, who’s 27, is to learn the lessons from his career so far and work out how he plays when he’s at his best.



Cameron Green training for the first test against Bangladesh. Getty Images “We like when he’s nice and busy and putting pressure back on the bowlers, he’s really intimidating. Same when he’s bowling, having that presence. He’s quite an intimidating sight when he gets going, so just taking a lot of confidence and asserting himself on the game.” Cummins argued that Green’s gentle and introverted countenance should be no barrier to him finding a way to turn into the Incredible Hulk in the middle. “You meet all kinds of personalities, even really gentle, but when they get into the competition they turn into different people,” Cummins said. “You see him in some T20 games, he’s banging the ball around. “He’s almost got too many skills, so it’s like, just get out there, assert yourself, strip it away, there’s no pressure from us, you’ve got freedom, get out of your own way and just go play.”



Bangladesh will wait until the toss to confirm the team for their first Test in Australia for 23 years. “Bowling I’m pretty confident we will adjust to these conditions and give them a challenge,” said skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto. Related Article Test cricket Snap judgment: What Ricky really thinks about ‘Clicky Ponting’ Much will depend on senior fast bowler Taskin Ahmed, following the enforced absence of spearhead Nahid Rana, to ask questions of Green, Marnus Labuschagne and Darwin native Jake Weatherald. Australia team: Pat Cummins (capt), Travis Head, Jake Weatherald, Marnus Labuschagne, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Alex Carey, Beau Webster, Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood. World.title: Suaalii scratched for Wallabies as Gordon returns to No.10 hot seat
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Suaalii scratched for Wallabies as Gordon returns to No.10 hot seat Iain Payten Updated August 12, 2026 — 3:43pm ,first published August 12, 2026 — 8:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Wallabies backline is set for a shake-up for the rematch against Japan in Townsville, with Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii ruled out with another hamstring injury and Carter Gordon poised to return at five-eighth. The backline shuffle comes as the likelihood of the Wallabies naming the 1000th player also firms, with young Queensland prop Massimo De Lutiis set to win a spot against the Brave Blossoms. Loading Suaalii was scratched from the clash at Queensland Country Bank Stadium after picking up a “minor” hamstring injury in the Wallabies’ three-point win in Osaka at the weekend. His injury was revealed in a release by the Wallabies on Tuesday night and is the latest in a series of hamstring injuries for the big-money recruit. Suaalii played six games for the Waratahs this year due to hamstring complaints.



Josh Flook has joined the squad as cover and will come into contention to play a role in the Test in Townsville. With Len Ikitau (ankle) also injured, Hunter Paisami wore the No.12 in Japan and Isaac Henry debuted off the bench at outside centre, pushing Suaalii to the wing. Gordon is set for a recall to the starting No.10 jersey, replacing Declan Meredith, who had an unhappy night in Osaka. Gordon started against Ireland in July before picking up a calf injury and missing the Tests against France and Italy. When Ben Donaldson was also ruled out for the France Test, Meredith was given a debut and he held the spot through to the Japan Test, but his form waned in Osaka. Wallabies coach Les Kiss flagged changes for the second Test after the win, saying he expected some players to be impacted by the sapping 30 degree heat.



Carter Gordon will come into the No.10 jersey. Getty Images It is in this context that De Lutiis is set to make his Test debut and become Wallaby No.1000, with tighthead prop Allan Alaalatoa expected to be rested ahead of the upcoming Argentina tour. Taniela Tupou, who has been coming off the bench, is set to start at tighthead. De Lutiis would also come off the bench. Rugby Australia and Queensland successfully fended off the attention of Ireland earlier this year to re-sign De Lutiis, who is a hulking tighthead prop. Speaking on Wednesday, Wallabies prop Angus Bell was coy on whether De Lutiis was going to be Wallaby No.1000 this weekend, but said the approaching milestone offered great perspective for the squad. “It’d be very special,” Bell said. “Zacky (Henry) was 999, wasn’t he? And then, obviously, the next Wallaby up is 1000, which is pretty cool, puts everything into perspective for you.



Prop Massimo De Lutiis is in line to become the 1000th Wallaby on Saturday. Getty Images “I think Slips (James Slipper) is Wallaby 100. It just shows how little people over the whole history of the Wallabies have played, and how special it is to be one of the 1000 Wallabies. It’s a pretty prestigious group. It’s a pretty cool time, and whoever gets that opportunity - obviously Mass (De Lutiis) is in the squad, he’s been training really well. For a young bloke, he’s super strong and he’s a big boy, so it’ll be awesome, whoever gets that 1000th cap.” Bell, who is a close friend of Suaalii, said the centre’s injury was “really minor” and said his run of injuries over the past two seasons of rugby had not affected him psychologically. “There’s one thing that I’ve never questioned Sue on, it’s his preparation, he’s probably one of the most professional blokes I’ve ever met, and I know that he’ll get his injury right,” Bell said. “It’s honestly just probably a bit of maturing in the body, I went through the exact same thing, I went through, you know, two and a half, three years where I wasn’t playing any rugby for the Waratahs, which was tough.



Related Article Vale Former Wallaby and Tiger Brian Smith dies, age 59 “It’s only a really minor injury, and we’ll look forward to getting Sue back. But we have a next up mentality, and we’re going to go into the game with the same plan.” Paisami said the Wallabies had good options to replace Suaalii. “We’ve tried a lot of combinations this week, obviously, with ‘Flooky’, Filippo (Daugunu), Isaac (Henry) there as well,” he said. Paisami welcomed the prospect of Gordon returning, saying his Reds teammate was a “natural 10”.



RA PAY FEE TO SCOTLAND TO SECURE NEW WALLAROOS COACH The Wallaroos have a new head coach after Rugby Australia announced the appointment of Sione Fukofuka through to the end of the home Rugby World Cup in 2029. But Fukofuka won’t be starting until the beginning of 2027, as part of a messy contract wrangle with the Scottish Rugby Union. Sione Fukofuka seen while working as head coach of the USA Paul Harding The 47-year-old is an experienced coach who served as Wallaroos assistant coach for three years from 2021, and then served as head coach of the USA Women’s side in 2024-25.



Fukofuka subsequently moved to Scotland as their women’s head coach, but last week it was announced he would be returning to Australia on compassionate grounds, due to family reasons. It was a stroke of fortune for Rugby Australia, who have been without a Wallaroos head coach since Jo Yapp departed last year and had recently had their drawn-out recruitment process extended even further when a priority target, Canadian coach Kevin Roeut, backed out of a potential deal. Fukofuka became the new target of RA and a deal was quickly agreed, but given Fukufoka had agreed to non-compete clauses with the SRU as a condition of his exit, a deal between RA and the SRU was also necessary. Former Wallabies coach Dave Rennie and captain Michael Hooper pose in 2022 with then-Wallaroos assistant coach Sione Fukofuka and Shannon Parry. Getty RA agreed to pay the SRU a fee, and for Fukofuka to not begin his role until the start of 2027. The Wallaroos play against Scotland in three of their remaining six Test matches this year.



The timing of Fukofuka’s new job has been viewed suspiciously in Scotland, with sections of the media questioning whether he had been poached by Rugby Australia before requesting an exit from his contract. “This is an unusual situation in so far as we released Sione on compassionate grounds a week ago,” said Scottish Rugby via a statement. “Whilst we always expected Sione to work again and would never wish to hold anyone back, we were surprised to learn of this news so quickly. “We have a release agreement in place with Sione, which will allow him to take up his post at the start of 2027, and an agreement in place with Rugby Australia who will pay Scottish Rugby an agreed fee.” An interim coaching team of Waratahs head coach Mike Ruthven, Duncan Chubb, Ben Mowen, Reg Tayler and Rugby Australia’s director of women’s high performance Tim Walsh is set to coach the team for the seven Tests remaining this year. Wallaroos squad Jemma Bemrose, Lily Bone, Emily Chancellor, Piper Duck, Waiaria Ellis, Martha Fua, Caitlyn Halse, Tia Hinds, Brianna Hoy, Eva Karpani, Kaitlan Leaney, Alysia Lefau-Fakaosilea, Michaela Leonard, Maddison Levi, Hera-Barb Malcolm Heke, Brittany Merlo, Desiree Miller, Faitala Moleka, Tania Naden, Leilani Nathan, Bridie O’Gorman, Siokapesi Palu Sekona, Allana Sikimeti, Piper Simons, Cecilia Smith, Maya Stewart, Pia Tapsell, Bienne Terita, Amelia Whitaker, Samantha Wood



“I would like to express my gratitude to Scottish Rugby for their understanding of my family situation and desire to return home to Australia,” Fukofuka said in a statement. “Although a difficult decision to leave the Scottish role, this opportunity allows me to be in Sydney closer to my family. I wish the players and staff all the best for the future. Australia Sevens star Maddison Levi is in line for a possible Wallaroos debut after being included in the Test squad for the upcoming 100th international against New Zealand in Auckland on August 22. Levi is one of four uncapped players named in a new-look squad that also features NSW Waratahs player of the year Amelia Whitaker, Queensland Reds captain Jemma Bemrose and Western Force forward Pia Tapsell.

World.title: Is it time to buy a house? Here is what the CBA chief would tell his kids
World.content:
BusinessThe economyBig four Opinion Is it time to buy a house? Here is what the CBA chief would tell his kids Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Updated August 12, 2026 — 3:39pm , first published 3:14pm

Updated August 12, 2026 — 3:39pm ,first published 3:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

House prices are falling, interest rates are probably peaking, the economy is slowing and consumers are nervous. Not so Commonwealth Bank boss Matt Comyn, who says he would advise his own child to be looking to buy their first house soon. Given Comyn’s children are still teenagers, this was his reply to a theoretical question, but it reflects the top banker’s views on the dynamics of the housing market. To be fair, his precise answer was that he would tell his child to get into the market over the coming 12 months. CBA chief executive Matt Comyn suggests it may be a good time to get into the housing market. Louie Douvis The price of housing has already fallen over the past quarter in Sydney and Melbourne, by 4 per cent and 3.4 per cent, respectively, and most experts see this continuing for the remainder of the year and into 2027. But Comyn, who understands the market and the psychology of borrowers better than most, subscribes to the CBA house view that we have already hit the top of interest rates in this cycle and the next move will be down – albeit not until next year.



Thus, borrowers/first-time buyers are approaching a sweet spot, where prices are falling, rates are no longer rising, and a new batch of spring real estate listings is about to hit the market. And if CBA’s 15 per cent fall in home-loan applications (and 28 per cent fall in investor home-loan applications) since May is any guide, buyers looking to bid won’t be elbowed out by competition crowding the front lawns on auction day. That certainly represents the glass half-full view. And if CBA’s fall in home-loan applications is any guide, buyers looking to bid won’t be elbowed out by competition crowding the front lawns on auction day. But what advice would Comyn give to CBA’s 800,000 shareholders, given the bank’s bread-and-butter home-lending business has developed a fissure created by higher rates and exacerbated by the government’s new tax policy on capital gains and negative gearing?



Jarden analyst Matthew Wilson threw diplomacy to the wind when he laid out his thoughts to investors: “Home-loan application trends are clearly persistently negative. Loans create deposits. This scenario has materially negative consequences for bank revenue growth. “Less loans, less deposits and more competition doesn’t bode well for [the bank’s] net interest margins ... shift happens,” he warned. Comyn concedes that additional competition for home loans is becoming evident with the emergence of some improved “deals” on interest rates – which is great for borrowers, but not for the bank’s profit margins. While Comyn can’t argue with the numbers that suggest home-loan applications have hit an air pocket, he says demand began to stabilise this month. Given loan applications only hit the slide in May, the full-year result that CBA reported on Wednesday mostly covered a period (from July last year to the end of June this year) when credit growth for homes was booming. And while the bank is heavily skewed towards retail banking, it hasn’t felt the challenges in its business banking arm, which is still humming along nicely.



Related Article Updated

Earnings season When CBA chief expects first-home buyers to return Thus, the result reflected 12 months of strong performances from most of its divisions and 10 months from retail lending, leading to a cash earnings improvement of an impressive 7 per cent and a larger than expected dividend. It was another example of the well-pitched results we have come to expect from CBA. But the spectre of the rocky road ahead in mortgage growth will reignite the debate about the bank’s premium share price. Jarden, for example, has a 12-month share price target of $90 for CBA – a long way short of the stock’s current trading price of about $172. Citi’s target price is a relatively generous $135, in line with UBS, while Barrenjoey sits in the middle of the pack with a price target of $120, but below Goldman Sachs, which has set a 12-month expectation of $129.



For years, shareholders – dominated by mum and dad investors – have been ignoring the brokers’ analysis and sell recommendations. As CBA’s stock bounced between gains and losses on Wednesday, there was no evidence that shareholders were particularly spooked. Alert, maybe, but not alarmed. World.title: Moonlight pushes QLD gold system length past 1km
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Moonlight pushes QLD gold system length past 1km Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 12, 2026 — 3:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The latest round of drilling by Moonlight Resources at its flagship Clermont gold project in Queensland has resulted in a significant expansion in the mineralised footprint to more than one kilometre of strike with the third batch of assays from 37 holes for 6126 metres completed delivering broad and consistent mineralisation. Notable results from the Phase 2 Reverse Circulation, or RC program include a 24-metre intersection grading 1.22 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 87m, which held a higher-grade 9 metre core at 1.28g/t gold and a solid 2 metre slice at 4.47g/t gold. Moonlight Resources’ RC drill rig in action at its Clermont gold project in The Drummond Basin, Queensland. Other significant hits were 19 metres at 1.95g/t gold from 99m, including a solid 6 metre section going 2.29g/t gold, and another 19 metre strike at 1.36g/t gold from 142m that contained a sharp one metre intercept at a high-grade 8.39g/t gold. Moonlight says the results have confirmed the continuation of the mineralised Leo Grande shear zone to the north and south of the central area, providing a major boost to the scale of the system ahead of a planned maiden mineral resource estimate.Phase 1 drilling at Leo Grande Central earlier this year confirmed the project’s potential with a stellar 40m hit at 1.3g/t gold from surface ending in mineralisation along with 34m running 1.37g/t from a shallow 6m.



‘The mineralised structure extends well beyond the area where most of our drilling has been concentrated to date.’ Moonlight Resources managing director Greg Starr Moonlight Resources managing director Greg Starr said:“The Phase 2 RC programme has materially advanced our understanding of Leo Grande. What began as a programme to validate historical drilling has now successfully demonstrated a coherent gold-bearing shear system that extends unconstrained over more than 1km of strike, with Leo Grande Central continuing to deliver broad and locally higher-grade mineralisation. At the same time drilling is underway at Goldfinger and Peak Downs, proving an active pipeline of additional discovery opportunities across Clermont while we continue to advance Leo Grande.” The company, which only listed on the ASX in December last year after a $10 million IPO, has been quick to build momentum across its broader Clermont project in central Queensland’s prolific Drummond Basin. Drummond is credited with a historical production and endowment of more than 6.5 million ounces of gold. Moonlight’s project area covers 268 square kilometres and hosts a pipeline of prospects including Leo Grande, Goldfinger, Petersens and Peak Downs. While Leo Grande is the company’s main event, Moonlight is also running a maiden RC drilling campaign at its Goldfinger prospect, a compelling high-grade gold target just south of Leo Grande. The company has also kicked off its first drill program at the Peak Downs prospect adding a copper string to its bow. Moonlight also holds a district scale position at the MacDonnell Ranges REE- Uranium project in the Northern Territory and the Drysdale Project Application in Western Australia also targeting uranium.



The Phase 2 RC program at Leo Grande Central, South and North is now complete and Moonlight is next planning a short diamond drilling campaign to nail down the structural controls of the mineralisation ahead of delivering its maiden mineral resource estimate. With the final assays from Leo Grande still to come, a diamond rig about to spin the rods to lock in the geology, and drill bits already kissing the dirt at its Goldfinger gold and Peak Downs copper prospects, Moonlight looks to be moving on multiple fronts. As the company marches towards a maiden resource at its flagship discovery and the parallel exploration push across its broader Clermont portfolio it appears the news might be about to potentially hot up and just be getting started. World.title: Yes, it has White Lotus holiday-from-hell vibes, but this Brit drama has much to say about female rage
World.content:
★★★★ CultureTV & radioReview Yes, it has White Lotus holiday-from-hell vibes, but this Brit drama has much to say about female rage Jared Richards August 12, 2026 — 3:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two Weeks in August ★★★★ Don’t let Two Weeks in August’s generic, placeholder-that-stuck title turn you off, nor its familiar premise – the resentments of the London vacationing class sizzle under the relentless late-summer heat of a gorgeous, unnamed Greek island. From left: Leila Farzad as Nat, Hugh Skinner as Jacob, Dylan Brady as Will, Jessica Raine as Zoe, Nicholas Pinnock as Solomon, Antonia Thomas as Jess and Maria Almeida as Avery in Two Weeks in August. Yes, this British drama is yet another post-White Lotus entry into the “luxurious holiday from hell” subgenre. Between the infidelity, co-dependent friendships, terrible French nanny and an ominous flash-forward to a wildfire ravaging through the island, Two Weeks in August offers plenty of schadenfreude for those left at home shivering in Australia watching a never-ending social media parade of Euro summers. But this eight-part BBC series, created by Catherine Shepherd, uses TV’s trending tropes for its much more startling centre: a deeply embodied reawakening within Zoe (Jessica Raine, The Devil’s Hour; Call the Midwife), a middle-aged teacher, mother and people-pleaser who has sanded down her personality into an unremarkable, forgettable politeness.



Editor's pick Logies ‘I think you can do it all’: Can Robert Irwin make the Logies relevant again? It doesn’t make up for the title, but it’s easy to imagine “two weeks in August” as Zoe’s mantra of sorts in the months leading up to this holiday. If her sunny disposition can’t brighten up her unemployed husband Dan (Damien Molony), maybe soaking in the Mediterranean rays with their old university friends (and kids) can? Maybe not. On day one, Dan could be mistaken for her sullen teen son, sticking to a black hoodie while complaining of the heat and rejecting suggestions for a swim. But the show refuses to villainise Dan or valorise Zoe, whose self-sacrifices to avoid upsetting others (taking the worst room; lying to her friends about Dan’s depression) carry an air of pride and resentment. Zoe’s deep unhappiness is instantly clear to everyone but herself, held brilliantly in Raine’s quivering smiles, erratic laughs and frantic, panicked eyes. Jessica Raine and Damien Molony as husband and wife Zoe and Dan, who are caught in a crisis while on holiday in Greece. When a drunken transgression occurs on night one, Zoe’s anger emerges – not just as a gale force, but a reassessment of her compulsion towards peace-keeping. She’s not the only one on the trip who realises that a holiday can’t reset relationships, including self-centred actor Solomon (Nicholas Pinnock) and his younger wife (Antonia Thomas), as well as best friends Nat (Leila Farzad) and Jacob (Hugh Skinner, Twenty Twenty Six), who struggle to tap into their usual role as the fun, child-free friends.



Related Article Review What to stream this week: Netflix’s new take on an Australian classic, plus five more picks One potentially alienating element is the show’s supernatural bent. Throughout, Zoe is haunted by foreboding, alluring apparitions from Greek mythology only she can see, including scorpions and three women embodying the Fates. A sprinkling of divine intervention within a grounded character-driven drama is jarring, but so is Zoe’s new self – anything but generic. Two Weeks in August is streaming on Binge. Want more TV? We’ve got you.

World.title: What Hemingway got wrong about the world’s most captivating continent
World.content:
InspirationAfrica Opinion What Hemingway got wrong about the world’s most captivating continent Catherine Marshall Travel writer August 12, 2026 — 3:34pm

August 12, 2026 — 3:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“All I wanted to do was get back to Africa. We had not left it, yet, but when I would wake in the night I would lie, listening, homesick for it already.” I could have written these words, but Ernest Hemingway beat me to it. Nevertheless, they prove a theory I’ve long advanced: since Africa is the cradle of humankind, most visitors feel at home as soon as they put sole to soil. For those of us with roots stretching down through more recent generations, the sense of belonging is still more profound. Africa smells like petrichor without the rain, a melancholic scent of sun blasting the ancestral bedrock. It’s a sign I’m home: the plane door opens, and I breathe in the motherland I left nearly 25 years ago, when my youngest child was a toddler. Photo: Illustration: Jamie Brown Though mostly raised in Australia, she and my two older children possess a distinctly African sensibility – hard to avoid when growing up with parents tethered by an umbilical cord to a far-distant country.



When Hemingway spoke of his homesickness for Africa, he was really referring to the part sequestered from its human population – the bushveld where he liked to go on safari and hunt big game. 



Consider Africa’s size: the US, China and India would fit comfortably into its landmass, with room to spare for assorted European nations. An unfathomable number of ethnic groups, languages, beliefs and traditions spill across Africa’s arbitrarily drawn borders. But a modern continent birthed from centuries of struggle ends up acquiring common characteristics, notably resilience and ingenuity. Related Article South Africa I thought I knew South Africa, until I did it in a new way Stop at a “robot” (traffic light) in South Africa and you might see a homeless person directing traffic in the hope of scoring a tip, or a hawker selling takeaway coffee from his thermos. Drive from Kigali into Rwanda’s Virunga Mountains, and you’ll see men on bicycles hitching a lift from passing trucks by holding onto their trays. Visit the meat market in Arusha, Tanzania, and you’ll spy not a scrap of offal going to waste. Some people imagine Africa as a rambunctious, disorderly place, but the so-called “developed” world can feel rather sterile by comparison. Disarray breeds flexibility, street smarts and a remarkable problem-solving capacity.



Returning home, I’m buoyed, too, by the population’s multilingual agility, and by the prevailing spirit of “ubuntu”, which roughly translates to, “I am, because we are”. Such interconnectedness is more easily forged when life is tough and neighbours tightly packed. But this human connection transcends community boundaries. Upon hearing my accent, young men often address me as “Mama”, and women call me “Sister”. That’s not to say peace reigns. Conflict is rife and xenophobia grows. But harmless verbal skirmishes often bring a wry smile to my face. They affirm the rich humour and indomitable spirit inherent in my kinfolk. And so, like Hemingway, I longingly await each return trip. But our Africas sound unalike; I’m homesick, it seems, for an altogether different place.

World.title: Defibrillators in our ambulances randomly shut down, TGA admits
World.content:
The medical watchdog has broken its silence over its move to suspend troubled ambulance defibrillators – revealing unexpected shutdowns were behind the decision. After repeated criticism from political leaders over a lack of transparency about the suspension, the Therapeutic Goods Administration on Wednesday said on its website that the issue centred on the devices randomly shutting down and rebooting. The corpuls3T modular defibrillator. The agency issued safety alerts in 2024 and 2025 – including one where a “reasonable possibility of serious injury or death was flagged” – about the corpuls shutting down during patient care, leaving them without defibrillation for up to 60 seconds. The 2025 issue was meant to be “closed out” by July this year.



“These products were suspended whilst investigations continue into reports of unexpected device shut down and rebooting during use,” the TGA said on Wednesday. “Actions to reduce the risks associated with these issues have been communicated to users by the sponsor, and are published on the TGA website. “The TGA has requested documentary evidence to further demonstrate the effectiveness of those actions, including software-related reboot issues, as well as the adequacy of the systems and processes it uses to identify, investigate and respond to future device-related issues and non-conformances in a timely manner. “A suspension does not represent a finding that the devices are unsafe. “Defibrillators in Australian ambulances and healthcare facilities continue to be safe to use. The TGA has not issued a recall of these devices.” Brett Simpson, NSW President of the Australian Paramedics Association said the software issue was one of many facing paramedics using the device. “Sure they shut down mid-resuscitation, but it’s one of 10 or 12 issues,” he said.



The TGA also said it would be launching a consultation process on increasing transparency around medical device suspension. That comes after the NSW government demanded an explanation from the health watchdog over its suspension on the sale of the defibrillators used in the state’s ambulances. NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said he will ask the TGA for clarification. Louise Kennerley “I’ll be writing to the TGA to see if they could give us a little bit more information,” Health Minister Ryan Park said. “They’ve made a decision not to disclose the details … that can be a little bit frustrating.” The corpuls defibrillator has been the subject of 16 market actions by the TGA since 2012.



The government and NSW Ambulance continue to assert that the devices are safe for patient use, despite widespread complaints from paramedics, including reports of the device failing to discharge a shock. On Tuesday this masthead revealed that a senior NSW Ambulance figure told staff that the corplus 3 and corplus 3T defibrillators recorded 1229 failures in 2025 alone. Park said that “not all of those have been serious failures. It could be a lead not working. It could be a range of different areas”. “I’m still confident, based on the advice of the NSW Ambulance ... as well as the TGA, that this should remain in our ambulances and form a part of the life-saving equipment that we have for people,” he said. NSW opposition health spokesperson Sarah Mitchell said it was “pretty concerning that the health minister hasn’t been made aware already by the TGA what the major concerns are”.



Related Article Exclusive

Ambulance ‘I am not happy’: Top paramedic dumps on disappointing defibrillator Marty Nichols, Ambulance NSW’s associate director of clinical practice, sympathised with paramedics who had raised concerns about the devices on an internal forum of more than 4000 members, where he said they had a “right to be disappointed”. Nichols, responding to one of the hundreds of comments from paramedics about the $30,000 defibrillators, said in his post that while paramedics at large stations might hear of failure “almost every day”, that should be weighed against the 1.5 million callouts every year. Alan Morrison, NSW Ambulance’s executive director of clinical capability, said these complaints did not represent failures, but a “range of technical issues in a complex piece of machinery”. “We’re not talking about a large number of defibrillation failures … we have not identified any safety issues impacting on patients,” he said. “However, our staff, as they should as clinicians, raise these technical issues as they arise. They are a thing we need to look into and address.”



He said there were various issues reported, including those related to the defibrillator’s connection to its leads. This masthead has also obtained a series of posts from paramedics complaining about problems with the device. The South Australian ambulance union has also raised concerns. Related Article Exclusive

Medical Malfunctions Confusion and concern: NSW ambulance defibrillators removed from sale, still on the road NSW Greens health spokesperson Dr Amanda Cohn said defibrillators were the “single most time sensitive piece of equipment in an ambulance.



“If a defibrillator fails, waiting for a back-up from another ambulance could cost a life,” she said, and called for NSW Ambulance to move to a different device and bring their tender process forward, rather than waiting for the devices’ contract to expire in six years’ time. World.title: ‘Assert yourself’: Refreshed skipper Cummins has clear message for Cam Green
World.content:
Breaking SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘Assert yourself’: Refreshed skipper Cummins has clear message for Cam Green Daniel Brettig Updated August 12, 2026 — 3:44pm ,first published 2:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Darwin: Australia’s captain Pat Cummins believes that playing just one Test in 12 months can extend his Test career, and has urged all-rounder Cameron Green to learn the lessons of the past six years and impose himself on Bangladesh. A back stress injury kept Cummins to a sole Ashes Test last summer, but the side effect of his absence is that numerous other trouble spots – notably his hamstrings – are fresher and stronger for what could amount to 21 Test matches in the space of 12 months. Australian captain Pat Cummins and his Bangladesh counterpart Najm ul Shanto promote the Test that starts in Darwin on Thursday. Getty Images “I missed a few Test matches but it feels like I’ve had a proper 12-month block of gym work, running and things I don’t ever think I would have done,” Cummins said on Wednesday. “Something like my hamstrings I’ve probably managed the last five or six years. “I’m sure they’ll flare up gain, but they feel 100 per cent right now. I only have to look at someone like Starcy [teammate Mitchell Starc] to see someone going well late into his 30s. I think this block has set me up pretty well.”



Josh Hazlewood tipped out Scott Boland, while Green kept his place alongside fellow all-rounder Beau Webster in Australia’s team to face Bangladesh in the first Test on Thursday. Hazlewood will play his first Test since the Caribbean tour a little over a year ago, after missing the Ashes with hamstring and Achilles injuries. Josh Hazlewood has got the nod for the first test against Bangladesh. Getty Images Nathan Lyon has also been recalled to the team following surgery on a serious hamstring tendon injury he suffered during the third Ashes Test in Adelaide in December. Teammates have been taken by Lyon’s level of dedication, eschewing alcohol and working assiduously in the gym to get the most out of his 38-year-old frame.



“I was looking at some footage the other day of that Adelaide Test, and I think that’s the best he’s bowled in years,” Cummins said. “So it was really bad timing, but it’s been pretty public how hard he’s worked over the last six months or so. “He looks in incredible shape, he’s been bowling beautifully, and as captain and teammate it’s going to be awesome to have him back out there.” Loading Boland was a most unfortunate omission from the team given his superb displays in the Ashes and a hat-trick in the West Indies, but he and Hazlewood can be expected to share a place in the team over the next 12 months provided both stay fit. “They’re both pretty class aren’t they,” Cummins said of the pair. “We were pretty certain we wanted ‘Lyono’ in the side so it’s then working out what the makeup of the quicks were.



“It’s always a pretty tight call, and there’s not much you can say to Scotty other than there’s a lot of cricket coming up. He knows his worth and how good he is, and I’m sure he’ll be back at some point pretty soon.” Related Article Australian cricket Australia confront Cameron Green question ahead of Darwin Test Green had a long state-of-the-union style chat with Cummins and head coach Andrew McDonald at training on Tuesday, and he will have a great opportunity to impose himself on a modest Bangladesh team in Darwin. “He’s had a bit of time to think about his own game, and the good thing is he’s played quite a lot,” Cummins said of Green. “In his Test career he’s had moments where it’s worked and moments where it hasn’t. “I think it’s that journey of most cricketers, particularly all-rounders where it’s a really tough job being the finished product when you’re young. Now the job for someone like Cam, who’s 27, is to learn the lessons from his career so far and work out how he plays when he’s at his best.



Cameron Green training for the first test against Bangladesh. Getty Images “We like when he’s nice and busy and putting pressure back on the bowlers, he’s really intimidating. Same when he’s bowling, having that presence. He’s quite an intimidating sight when he gets going, so just taking a lot of confidence and asserting himself on the game.” Cummins argued that Green’s gentle and introverted countenance should be no barrier to him finding a way to turn into the Incredible Hulk in the middle. “You meet all kinds of personalities, even really gentle, but when they get into the competition they turn into different people,” Cummins said. “You see him in some T20 games, he’s banging the ball around. “He’s almost got too many skills, so it’s like, just get out there, assert yourself, strip it away, there’s no pressure from us, you’ve got freedom, get out of your own way and just go play.”



Bangladesh will wait until the toss to confirm the team for their first Test in Australia for 23 years. “Bowling I’m pretty confident we will adjust to these conditions and give them a challenge,” said skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto. Related Article Test cricket Snap judgment: What Ricky really thinks about ‘Clicky Ponting’ Much will depend on senior fast bowler Taskin Ahmed, following the enforced absence of spearhead Nahid Rana, to ask questions of Green, Marnus Labuschagne and Darwin native Jake Weatherald. Australia team: Pat Cummins (capt), Travis Head, Jake Weatherald, Marnus Labuschagne, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Alex Carey, Beau Webster, Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood.
