World.title: Suaalii scratched for Wallabies as Gordon returns to No.10 hot seat
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Suaalii scratched for Wallabies as Gordon returns to No.10 hot seat Iain Payten Updated August 12, 2026 — 3:43pm ,first published August 12, 2026 — 8:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Wallabies backline is set for a shake-up for the rematch against Japan in Townsville, with Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii ruled out with another hamstring injury and Carter Gordon poised to return at five-eighth. The backline shuffle comes as the likelihood of the Wallabies naming the 1000th player also firms, with young Queensland prop Massimo De Lutiis set to win a spot against the Brave Blossoms. Loading Suaalii was scratched from the clash at Queensland Country Bank Stadium after picking up a “minor” hamstring injury in the Wallabies’ three-point win in Osaka at the weekend. His injury was revealed in a release by the Wallabies on Tuesday night and is the latest in a series of hamstring injuries for the big-money recruit. Suaalii played six games for the Waratahs this year due to hamstring complaints.



Josh Flook has joined the squad as cover and will come into contention to play a role in the Test in Townsville. With Len Ikitau (ankle) also injured, Hunter Paisami wore the No.12 in Japan and Isaac Henry debuted off the bench at outside centre, pushing Suaalii to the wing. Gordon is set for a recall to the starting No.10 jersey, replacing Declan Meredith, who had an unhappy night in Osaka. Gordon started against Ireland in July before picking up a calf injury and missing the Tests against France and Italy. When Ben Donaldson was also ruled out for the France Test, Meredith was given a debut and he held the spot through to the Japan Test, but his form waned in Osaka. Wallabies coach Les Kiss flagged changes for the second Test after the win, saying he expected some players to be impacted by the sapping 30 degree heat.



Carter Gordon will come into the No.10 jersey. Getty Images It is in this context that De Lutiis is set to make his Test debut and become Wallaby No.1000, with tighthead prop Allan Alaalatoa expected to be rested ahead of the upcoming Argentina tour. Taniela Tupou, who has been coming off the bench, is set to start at tighthead. De Lutiis would also come off the bench. Rugby Australia and Queensland successfully fended off the attention of Ireland earlier this year to re-sign De Lutiis, who is a hulking tighthead prop. Speaking on Wednesday, Wallabies prop Angus Bell was coy on whether De Lutiis was going to be Wallaby No.1000 this weekend, but said the approaching milestone offered great perspective for the squad. “It’d be very special,” Bell said. “Zacky (Henry) was 999, wasn’t he? And then, obviously, the next Wallaby up is 1000, which is pretty cool, puts everything into perspective for you.



Prop Massimo De Lutiis is in line to become the 1000th Wallaby on Saturday. Getty Images “I think Slips (James Slipper) is Wallaby 100. It just shows how little people over the whole history of the Wallabies have played, and how special it is to be one of the 1000 Wallabies. It’s a pretty prestigious group. It’s a pretty cool time, and whoever gets that opportunity - obviously Mass (De Lutiis) is in the squad, he’s been training really well. For a young bloke, he’s super strong and he’s a big boy, so it’ll be awesome, whoever gets that 1000th cap.” Bell, who is a close friend of Suaalii, said the centre’s injury was “really minor” and said his run of injuries over the past two seasons of rugby had not affected him psychologically. “There’s one thing that I’ve never questioned Sue on, it’s his preparation, he’s probably one of the most professional blokes I’ve ever met, and I know that he’ll get his injury right,” Bell said. “It’s honestly just probably a bit of maturing in the body, I went through the exact same thing, I went through, you know, two and a half, three years where I wasn’t playing any rugby for the Waratahs, which was tough.



Related Article Vale Former Wallaby and Tiger Brian Smith dies, age 59 “It’s only a really minor injury, and we’ll look forward to getting Sue back. But we have a next up mentality, and we’re going to go into the game with the same plan.” Paisami said the Wallabies had good options to replace Suaalii. “We’ve tried a lot of combinations this week, obviously, with ‘Flooky’, Filippo (Daugunu), Isaac (Henry) there as well,” he said. Paisami welcomed the prospect of Gordon returning, saying his Reds teammate was a “natural 10”.



RA PAY FEE TO SCOTLAND TO SECURE NEW WALLAROOS COACH The Wallaroos have a new head coach after Rugby Australia announced the appointment of Sione Fukofuka through to the end of the home Rugby World Cup in 2029. But Fukofuka won’t be starting until the beginning of 2027, as part of a messy contract wrangle with the Scottish Rugby Union. Sione Fukofuka seen while working as head coach of the USA Paul Harding The 47-year-old is an experienced coach who served as Wallaroos assistant coach for three years from 2021, and then served as head coach of the USA Women’s side in 2024-25.



Fukofuka subsequently moved to Scotland as their women’s head coach, but last week it was announced he would be returning to Australia on compassionate grounds, due to family reasons. It was a stroke of fortune for Rugby Australia, who have been without a Wallaroos head coach since Jo Yapp departed last year and had recently had their drawn-out recruitment process extended even further when a priority target, Canadian coach Kevin Roeut, backed out of a potential deal. Fukofuka became the new target of RA and a deal was quickly agreed, but given Fukufoka had agreed to non-compete clauses with the SRU as a condition of his exit, a deal between RA and the SRU was also necessary. Former Wallabies coach Dave Rennie and captain Michael Hooper pose in 2022 with then-Wallaroos assistant coach Sione Fukofuka and Shannon Parry. Getty RA agreed to pay the SRU a fee, and for Fukofuka to not begin his role until the start of 2027. The Wallaroos play against Scotland in three of their remaining six Test matches this year.



The timing of Fukofuka’s new job has been viewed suspiciously in Scotland, with sections of the media questioning whether he had been poached by Rugby Australia before requesting an exit from his contract. “This is an unusual situation in so far as we released Sione on compassionate grounds a week ago,” said Scottish Rugby via a statement. “Whilst we always expected Sione to work again and would never wish to hold anyone back, we were surprised to learn of this news so quickly. “We have a release agreement in place with Sione, which will allow him to take up his post at the start of 2027, and an agreement in place with Rugby Australia who will pay Scottish Rugby an agreed fee.” An interim coaching team of Waratahs head coach Mike Ruthven, Duncan Chubb, Ben Mowen, Reg Tayler and Rugby Australia’s director of women’s high performance Tim Walsh is set to coach the team for the seven Tests remaining this year. Wallaroos squad Jemma Bemrose, Lily Bone, Emily Chancellor, Piper Duck, Waiaria Ellis, Martha Fua, Caitlyn Halse, Tia Hinds, Brianna Hoy, Eva Karpani, Kaitlan Leaney, Alysia Lefau-Fakaosilea, Michaela Leonard, Maddison Levi, Hera-Barb Malcolm Heke, Brittany Merlo, Desiree Miller, Faitala Moleka, Tania Naden, Leilani Nathan, Bridie O’Gorman, Siokapesi Palu Sekona, Allana Sikimeti, Piper Simons, Cecilia Smith, Maya Stewart, Pia Tapsell, Bienne Terita, Amelia Whitaker, Samantha Wood



“I would like to express my gratitude to Scottish Rugby for their understanding of my family situation and desire to return home to Australia,” Fukofuka said in a statement. “Although a difficult decision to leave the Scottish role, this opportunity allows me to be in Sydney closer to my family. I wish the players and staff all the best for the future. Australia Sevens star Maddison Levi is in line for a possible Wallaroos debut after being included in the Test squad for the upcoming 100th international against New Zealand in Auckland on August 22. Levi is one of four uncapped players named in a new-look squad that also features NSW Waratahs player of the year Amelia Whitaker, Queensland Reds captain Jemma Bemrose and Western Force forward Pia Tapsell.

World.title: Is it time to buy a house? Here is what the CBA chief would tell his kids
World.content:
BusinessThe economyBig four Opinion Is it time to buy a house? Here is what the CBA chief would tell his kids Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Updated August 12, 2026 — 3:39pm , first published 3:14pm

Updated August 12, 2026 — 3:39pm ,first published 3:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

House prices are falling, interest rates are probably peaking, the economy is slowing and consumers are nervous. Not so Commonwealth Bank boss Matt Comyn, who says he would advise his own child to be looking to buy their first house soon. Given Comyn’s children are still teenagers, this was his reply to a theoretical question, but it reflects the top banker’s views on the dynamics of the housing market. To be fair, his precise answer was that he would tell his child to get into the market over the coming 12 months. CBA chief executive Matt Comyn suggests it may be a good time to get into the housing market. Louie Douvis The price of housing has already fallen over the past quarter in Sydney and Melbourne, by 4 per cent and 3.4 per cent, respectively, and most experts see this continuing for the remainder of the year and into 2027. But Comyn, who understands the market and the psychology of borrowers better than most, subscribes to the CBA house view that we have already hit the top of interest rates in this cycle and the next move will be down – albeit not until next year.



Thus, borrowers/first-time buyers are approaching a sweet spot, where prices are falling, rates are no longer rising, and a new batch of spring real estate listings is about to hit the market. And if CBA’s 15 per cent fall in home-loan applications (and 28 per cent fall in investor home-loan applications) since May is any guide, buyers looking to bid won’t be elbowed out by competition crowding the front lawns on auction day. That certainly represents the glass half-full view. And if CBA’s fall in home-loan applications is any guide, buyers looking to bid won’t be elbowed out by competition crowding the front lawns on auction day. But what advice would Comyn give to CBA’s 800,000 shareholders, given the bank’s bread-and-butter home-lending business has developed a fissure created by higher rates and exacerbated by the government’s new tax policy on capital gains and negative gearing?



Jarden analyst Matthew Wilson threw diplomacy to the wind when he laid out his thoughts to investors: “Home-loan application trends are clearly persistently negative. Loans create deposits. This scenario has materially negative consequences for bank revenue growth. “Less loans, less deposits and more competition doesn’t bode well for [the bank’s] net interest margins ... shift happens,” he warned. Comyn concedes that additional competition for home loans is becoming evident with the emergence of some improved “deals” on interest rates – which is great for borrowers, but not for the bank’s profit margins. While Comyn can’t argue with the numbers that suggest home-loan applications have hit an air pocket, he says demand began to stabilise this month. Given loan applications only hit the slide in May, the full-year result that CBA reported on Wednesday mostly covered a period (from July last year to the end of June this year) when credit growth for homes was booming. And while the bank is heavily skewed towards retail banking, it hasn’t felt the challenges in its business banking arm, which is still humming along nicely.



Related Article Updated

Earnings season When CBA chief expects first-home buyers to return Thus, the result reflected 12 months of strong performances from most of its divisions and 10 months from retail lending, leading to a cash earnings improvement of an impressive 7 per cent and a larger than expected dividend. It was another example of the well-pitched results we have come to expect from CBA. But the spectre of the rocky road ahead in mortgage growth will reignite the debate about the bank’s premium share price. Jarden, for example, has a 12-month share price target of $90 for CBA – a long way short of the stock’s current trading price of about $172. Citi’s target price is a relatively generous $135, in line with UBS, while Barrenjoey sits in the middle of the pack with a price target of $120, but below Goldman Sachs, which has set a 12-month expectation of $129.



For years, shareholders – dominated by mum and dad investors – have been ignoring the brokers’ analysis and sell recommendations. As CBA’s stock bounced between gains and losses on Wednesday, there was no evidence that shareholders were particularly spooked. Alert, maybe, but not alarmed. World.title: Moonlight pushes QLD gold system length past 1km
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Moonlight pushes QLD gold system length past 1km Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 12, 2026 — 3:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The latest round of drilling by Moonlight Resources at its flagship Clermont gold project in Queensland has resulted in a significant expansion in the mineralised footprint to more than one kilometre of strike with the third batch of assays from 37 holes for 6126 metres completed delivering broad and consistent mineralisation. Notable results from the Phase 2 Reverse Circulation, or RC program include a 24-metre intersection grading 1.22 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 87m, which held a higher-grade 9 metre core at 1.28g/t gold and a solid 2 metre slice at 4.47g/t gold. Moonlight Resources’ RC drill rig in action at its Clermont gold project in The Drummond Basin, Queensland. Other significant hits were 19 metres at 1.95g/t gold from 99m, including a solid 6 metre section going 2.29g/t gold, and another 19 metre strike at 1.36g/t gold from 142m that contained a sharp one metre intercept at a high-grade 8.39g/t gold. Moonlight says the results have confirmed the continuation of the mineralised Leo Grande shear zone to the north and south of the central area, providing a major boost to the scale of the system ahead of a planned maiden mineral resource estimate.Phase 1 drilling at Leo Grande Central earlier this year confirmed the project’s potential with a stellar 40m hit at 1.3g/t gold from surface ending in mineralisation along with 34m running 1.37g/t from a shallow 6m.



‘The mineralised structure extends well beyond the area where most of our drilling has been concentrated to date.’ Moonlight Resources managing director Greg Starr Moonlight Resources managing director Greg Starr said:“The Phase 2 RC programme has materially advanced our understanding of Leo Grande. What began as a programme to validate historical drilling has now successfully demonstrated a coherent gold-bearing shear system that extends unconstrained over more than 1km of strike, with Leo Grande Central continuing to deliver broad and locally higher-grade mineralisation. At the same time drilling is underway at Goldfinger and Peak Downs, proving an active pipeline of additional discovery opportunities across Clermont while we continue to advance Leo Grande.” The company, which only listed on the ASX in December last year after a $10 million IPO, has been quick to build momentum across its broader Clermont project in central Queensland’s prolific Drummond Basin. Drummond is credited with a historical production and endowment of more than 6.5 million ounces of gold. Moonlight’s project area covers 268 square kilometres and hosts a pipeline of prospects including Leo Grande, Goldfinger, Petersens and Peak Downs. While Leo Grande is the company’s main event, Moonlight is also running a maiden RC drilling campaign at its Goldfinger prospect, a compelling high-grade gold target just south of Leo Grande. The company has also kicked off its first drill program at the Peak Downs prospect adding a copper string to its bow. Moonlight also holds a district scale position at the MacDonnell Ranges REE- Uranium project in the Northern Territory and the Drysdale Project Application in Western Australia also targeting uranium.



The Phase 2 RC program at Leo Grande Central, South and North is now complete and Moonlight is next planning a short diamond drilling campaign to nail down the structural controls of the mineralisation ahead of delivering its maiden mineral resource estimate. With the final assays from Leo Grande still to come, a diamond rig about to spin the rods to lock in the geology, and drill bits already kissing the dirt at its Goldfinger gold and Peak Downs copper prospects, Moonlight looks to be moving on multiple fronts. As the company marches towards a maiden resource at its flagship discovery and the parallel exploration push across its broader Clermont portfolio it appears the news might be about to potentially hot up and just be getting started. World.title: Yes, it has White Lotus holiday-from-hell vibes, but this Brit drama has much to say about female rage
World.content:
★★★★ CultureTV & radioReview Yes, it has White Lotus holiday-from-hell vibes, but this Brit drama has much to say about female rage Jared Richards August 12, 2026 — 3:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two Weeks in August ★★★★ Don’t let Two Weeks in August’s generic, placeholder-that-stuck title turn you off, nor its familiar premise – the resentments of the London vacationing class sizzle under the relentless late-summer heat of a gorgeous, unnamed Greek island. From left: Leila Farzad as Nat, Hugh Skinner as Jacob, Dylan Brady as Will, Jessica Raine as Zoe, Nicholas Pinnock as Solomon, Antonia Thomas as Jess and Maria Almeida as Avery in Two Weeks in August. Yes, this British drama is yet another post-White Lotus entry into the “luxurious holiday from hell” subgenre. Between the infidelity, co-dependent friendships, terrible French nanny and an ominous flash-forward to a wildfire ravaging through the island, Two Weeks in August offers plenty of schadenfreude for those left at home shivering in Australia watching a never-ending social media parade of Euro summers. But this eight-part BBC series, created by Catherine Shepherd, uses TV’s trending tropes for its much more startling centre: a deeply embodied reawakening within Zoe (Jessica Raine, The Devil’s Hour; Call the Midwife), a middle-aged teacher, mother and people-pleaser who has sanded down her personality into an unremarkable, forgettable politeness.



Editor's pick Logies ‘I think you can do it all’: Can Robert Irwin make the Logies relevant again? It doesn’t make up for the title, but it’s easy to imagine “two weeks in August” as Zoe’s mantra of sorts in the months leading up to this holiday. If her sunny disposition can’t brighten up her unemployed husband Dan (Damien Molony), maybe soaking in the Mediterranean rays with their old university friends (and kids) can? Maybe not. On day one, Dan could be mistaken for her sullen teen son, sticking to a black hoodie while complaining of the heat and rejecting suggestions for a swim. But the show refuses to villainise Dan or valorise Zoe, whose self-sacrifices to avoid upsetting others (taking the worst room; lying to her friends about Dan’s depression) carry an air of pride and resentment. Zoe’s deep unhappiness is instantly clear to everyone but herself, held brilliantly in Raine’s quivering smiles, erratic laughs and frantic, panicked eyes. Jessica Raine and Damien Molony as husband and wife Zoe and Dan, who are caught in a crisis while on holiday in Greece. When a drunken transgression occurs on night one, Zoe’s anger emerges – not just as a gale force, but a reassessment of her compulsion towards peace-keeping. She’s not the only one on the trip who realises that a holiday can’t reset relationships, including self-centred actor Solomon (Nicholas Pinnock) and his younger wife (Antonia Thomas), as well as best friends Nat (Leila Farzad) and Jacob (Hugh Skinner, Twenty Twenty Six), who struggle to tap into their usual role as the fun, child-free friends.



Related Article Review What to stream this week: Netflix’s new take on an Australian classic, plus five more picks One potentially alienating element is the show’s supernatural bent. Throughout, Zoe is haunted by foreboding, alluring apparitions from Greek mythology only she can see, including scorpions and three women embodying the Fates. A sprinkling of divine intervention within a grounded character-driven drama is jarring, but so is Zoe’s new self – anything but generic. Two Weeks in August is streaming on Binge. Want more TV? World.title: What Hemingway got wrong about the world’s most captivating continent
World.content:
InspirationAfrica Opinion What Hemingway got wrong about the world’s most captivating continent Catherine Marshall Travel writer August 12, 2026 — 3:34pm

August 12, 2026 — 3:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“All I wanted to do was get back to Africa. We had not left it, yet, but when I would wake in the night I would lie, listening, homesick for it already.” I could have written these words, but Ernest Hemingway beat me to it. Nevertheless, they prove a theory I’ve long advanced: since Africa is the cradle of humankind, most visitors feel at home as soon as they put sole to soil. For those of us with roots stretching down through more recent generations, the sense of belonging is still more profound. Africa smells like petrichor without the rain, a melancholic scent of sun blasting the ancestral bedrock. It’s a sign I’m home: the plane door opens, and I breathe in the motherland I left nearly 25 years ago, when my youngest child was a toddler. Photo: Illustration: Jamie Brown Though mostly raised in Australia, she and my two older children possess a distinctly African sensibility – hard to avoid when growing up with parents tethered by an umbilical cord to a far-distant country.



When Hemingway spoke of his homesickness for Africa, he was really referring to the part sequestered from its human population – the bushveld where he liked to go on safari and hunt big game. 



Consider Africa’s size: the US, China and India would fit comfortably into its landmass, with room to spare for assorted European nations. An unfathomable number of ethnic groups, languages, beliefs and traditions spill across Africa’s arbitrarily drawn borders. But a modern continent birthed from centuries of struggle ends up acquiring common characteristics, notably resilience and ingenuity. Related Article South Africa I thought I knew South Africa, until I did it in a new way Stop at a “robot” (traffic light) in South Africa and you might see a homeless person directing traffic in the hope of scoring a tip, or a hawker selling takeaway coffee from his thermos. Drive from Kigali into Rwanda’s Virunga Mountains, and you’ll see men on bicycles hitching a lift from passing trucks by holding onto their trays. Visit the meat market in Arusha, Tanzania, and you’ll spy not a scrap of offal going to waste. Some people imagine Africa as a rambunctious, disorderly place, but the so-called “developed” world can feel rather sterile by comparison. Disarray breeds flexibility, street smarts and a remarkable problem-solving capacity.



Returning home, I’m buoyed, too, by the population’s multilingual agility, and by the prevailing spirit of “ubuntu”, which roughly translates to, “I am, because we are”. Such interconnectedness is more easily forged when life is tough and neighbours tightly packed. But this human connection transcends community boundaries. Upon hearing my accent, young men often address me as “Mama”, and women call me “Sister”. That’s not to say peace reigns. Conflict is rife and xenophobia grows. But harmless verbal skirmishes often bring a wry smile to my face. They affirm the rich humour and indomitable spirit inherent in my kinfolk. And so, like Hemingway, I longingly await each return trip. But our Africas sound unalike; I’m homesick, it seems, for an altogether different place.

World.title: Defibrillators in our ambulances randomly shut down, TGA admits
World.content:
The medical watchdog has broken its silence over its move to suspend troubled ambulance defibrillators – revealing unexpected shutdowns were behind the decision. After repeated criticism from political leaders over a lack of transparency about the suspension, the Therapeutic Goods Administration on Wednesday said on its website that the issue centred on the devices randomly shutting down and rebooting. The corpuls3T modular defibrillator. The agency issued safety alerts in 2024 and 2025 – including one where a “reasonable possibility of serious injury or death was flagged” – about the corpuls shutting down during patient care, leaving them without defibrillation for up to 60 seconds. The 2025 issue was meant to be “closed out” by July this year.



“These products were suspended whilst investigations continue into reports of unexpected device shut down and rebooting during use,” the TGA said on Wednesday. “Actions to reduce the risks associated with these issues have been communicated to users by the sponsor, and are published on the TGA website. “The TGA has requested documentary evidence to further demonstrate the effectiveness of those actions, including software-related reboot issues, as well as the adequacy of the systems and processes it uses to identify, investigate and respond to future device-related issues and non-conformances in a timely manner. “A suspension does not represent a finding that the devices are unsafe. “Defibrillators in Australian ambulances and healthcare facilities continue to be safe to use. The TGA has not issued a recall of these devices.” Brett Simpson, NSW President of the Australian Paramedics Association said the software issue was one of many facing paramedics using the device. “Sure they shut down mid-resuscitation, but it’s one of 10 or 12 issues,” he said.



The TGA also said it would be launching a consultation process on increasing transparency around medical device suspension. That comes after the NSW government demanded an explanation from the health watchdog over its suspension on the sale of the defibrillators used in the state’s ambulances. NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said he will ask the TGA for clarification. Louise Kennerley “I’ll be writing to the TGA to see if they could give us a little bit more information,” Health Minister Ryan Park said. “They’ve made a decision not to disclose the details … that can be a little bit frustrating.” The corpuls defibrillator has been the subject of 16 market actions by the TGA since 2012.



The government and NSW Ambulance continue to assert that the devices are safe for patient use, despite widespread complaints from paramedics, including reports of the device failing to discharge a shock. On Tuesday this masthead revealed that a senior NSW Ambulance figure told staff that the corplus 3 and corplus 3T defibrillators recorded 1229 failures in 2025 alone. Park said that “not all of those have been serious failures. It could be a lead not working. It could be a range of different areas”. “I’m still confident, based on the advice of the NSW Ambulance ... as well as the TGA, that this should remain in our ambulances and form a part of the life-saving equipment that we have for people,” he said. NSW opposition health spokesperson Sarah Mitchell said it was “pretty concerning that the health minister hasn’t been made aware already by the TGA what the major concerns are”.



Related Article Exclusive

Ambulance ‘I am not happy’: Top paramedic dumps on disappointing defibrillator Marty Nichols, Ambulance NSW’s associate director of clinical practice, sympathised with paramedics who had raised concerns about the devices on an internal forum of more than 4000 members, where he said they had a “right to be disappointed”. Nichols, responding to one of the hundreds of comments from paramedics about the $30,000 defibrillators, said in his post that while paramedics at large stations might hear of failure “almost every day”, that should be weighed against the 1.5 million callouts every year. Alan Morrison, NSW Ambulance’s executive director of clinical capability, said these complaints did not represent failures, but a “range of technical issues in a complex piece of machinery”. “We’re not talking about a large number of defibrillation failures … we have not identified any safety issues impacting on patients,” he said. “However, our staff, as they should as clinicians, raise these technical issues as they arise. They are a thing we need to look into and address.”



He said there were various issues reported, including those related to the defibrillator’s connection to its leads. This masthead has also obtained a series of posts from paramedics complaining about problems with the device. The South Australian ambulance union has also raised concerns. Related Article Exclusive

Medical Malfunctions Confusion and concern: NSW ambulance defibrillators removed from sale, still on the road NSW Greens health spokesperson Dr Amanda Cohn said defibrillators were the “single most time sensitive piece of equipment in an ambulance.



“If a defibrillator fails, waiting for a back-up from another ambulance could cost a life,” she said, and called for NSW Ambulance to move to a different device and bring their tender process forward, rather than waiting for the devices’ contract to expire in six years’ time. World.title: Chris Penk loses ministerial portfolios after Luxon leadership challenge
World.content:
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has removed Chris Penk's ministerial portfolios.

"Chris Penk launched a leadership challenge this week, which resulted in today's confidence vote. This makes his role untenable and as such I have removed his portfolios," Luxon said.

Paul Goldsmith will pick up the Defence, Veterans, Space, GCSB, and NZSIS portfolios.

Simon Watts will become Minister for Building and Construction.

Earlier on Wednesday afternoon, Luxon held a press conference where he announced he had survived the second attempt to oust him this year.

In an abrupt statement to media, he said he had the full confidence of the National Party caucus before leaving without answering questions.

"Our caucus is united, and it is determined to win this election," he said.

"Our focus is on National's positive plan to fix the basics and to build the future, so that we realise the incredible potential that sits in this country, and that we set it up for our kids and our grandkids."

He was flanked by senior MPs, including Nicola Willis, Mark Mitchell and Chris Bishop.

Standing just behind them was Erica Stanford, who was rumoured to be gunning for the top job.

Chris Penk at Parliament on Wednesday. RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

Penk, who was ranked 14th on National's list published at the weekend, had earlier denied any involvement in a leadership challenge, after Politik and the New Zealand Herald reported he was doing the numbers for an Erica Stanford bid.

Upon arriving in Wellington on Tuesday night, Penk said he had confidence in Luxon, and would support him in any vote.

"I've always expressed confidence in the leader. Now is no different."

He would not say if anyone had called him about the leadership, saying he would not disclose private conversations, but said reports of his involvement as an instigator were "wrong".

He stuck to that position on Wednesday morning, again saying he had confidence in Luxon, and suggested people might be making up stories about him making calls for Stanford.

"I think everyone else needs to get their story straight because I'm hearing multiple different versions. None of them are true, and as I said, I'm not prepared to disclose private conversations, except only to say I have confidence in Christopher Luxon."

Penk had only been promoted to the Cabinet in April, following the retirement of Judith Collins.

World.title: 'Spree burglar' who targeted gliding club jailed for almost four years
World.content:
A "spree burglar" who brought a volunteer-run gliding club to its knees and raided farms around his home to fund a drug habit has been sentenced to almost four years in prison.

David Neho, of Awarua, in Northland, was sentenced in the Kaikohe District Court on 23 charges including burglary, receiving, theft, unlawfully taking motor vehicles, and possession of drug utensils.

But the crimes that drew nationwide attention were a series of break-ins at Kaikohe Gliding Club, leaving five gliders badly damaged and club members facing a repair bill of more than $250,000.

Members earlier told RNZ they took pride in running one of the most affordable and accessible gliding clubs in the country, and supported youth by hosting cadets from around the Far North.

However, in an effort to keep costs low, the club was uninsured, leaving members to carry the cost of the damage.

Judge Gordon Matenga told the court Neho, who was 28, broke into the club hangar at Kaikohe Aerodrome on three occasions between 22 and 27 March this year.

He took two Toyota RAV4s, which were used for towing the gliders, and a tractor, used for mowing the grass air strip.

In the process he caused major damage to all five gliders stored in the hangar.

He then tried to sell the RAV4s to a car parts company.

Five gliders were badly damaged when David Neho broke into a club hangar south of Kaikohe, stealing a tractor and two vehicles. Supplied

Neho was also sentenced for petrol drive-offs in Whangārei and Moerewa, receiving a stolen Volvo he said he had bought for $50, stealing quad bikes, diesel and farm equipment from properties around Awarua, and using a ute to rip a forest gate off its hinges so he could go hunting.

He also stole a truck loaded with specialist drilling equipment imported from the US at a cost of $40,000.

The drilling equipment was recovered by Kaikohe police, as were the gliding club's vehicles and tractor.

Judge Matenga described Neho as a "spree burglar", who had committed a large number of offences in the first few months of this year, but had few previous convictions and none for drugs or burglary.

"By way of explanation, you told police you were doing all of this because you were feeding a habit and you sold most of the stuff you stole or swapped it for other things."

Neho's lawyer said he had started taking methamphetamine at work after two close relatives died on one day.

That caused him to lose his job, so he took more meth and then lost his partner.

Judge Matenga discounted Neho's sentence for his very early guilty plea - in his view "the best evidence of remorse" - and for helping police find some of the stolen property.

That led to a sentence of three years and 11 months.

"Your offending has significantly affected everyone. I think you understand that now, now that you are clean and clear of drugs and can look back at what you have done," Judge Matenga said.

The victims sought reparations of just under $245,000, which Neho said he was willing to pay, but the judge said there was no way he could afford it.

Once he was out of jail and had a job he could make voluntary payments, or he could be pursued through the civil court.

World.title: Kiwi ICE detainee Everlee Wihongi on 'dehumanising conditions' in custody
World.content:
Listen on Checkpoint: Everlee Wihongi on her detention by ICE at 5.20pm

RNZ national

What gives you hope when you're being held in a US immigration detention facility?

For New Zealand citizen Everlee Wihongi, it was the support of her family and loved ones, but she says hope can be a bad thing in a place like that.

"Lots of times it was bad to have hope that things would go well," she said.

"It was like I can't look too far into the future because I don't know how long I'll be here."

Wihongi, who has lived in the US for decades and holds a green card, was detained by ICE in early April after coming back from New Zealand.

She was held for more than 70 days because of a 2016 cannabis conviction that was later thrown out by the courts.

Now, she's back home in Wisconsin with her family.

Speaking to RNZ, Wihongi said her time in detainment was one of the most miserable experiences of her entire existence.

Officials at the facility would refer to her as a bunk-bed number, rather than by her name, she said.

She wasn't Everlee Wihongi, she was 'Six Up'.

"It was dehumanising conditions," Wihongi said.

"Whenever you'd have an appointment or you had to go see a lawyer, anything, they would just go 'Six Up, you have an appointment'."

Wihongi said meal times at the facilities she was held in were another challenge.

"The first spot I was in, we had to get up at 6am to eat, and if you didn't get up for breakfast and you didn't eat," she said.

"When I was in Arizona, you had to get up at 3.45am to get breakfast, and if you didn't go, then you just didn't eat till lunchtime, which is around 1pm."

Wihongi was first held in an ICE facility in California, before being moved to Arizona and spending a night on the floor in a Texan holding facility along the way.

In transit, Wihongi described seeing other detainees being removed from a plane before they could board.

She and others had been woken at 1.30 that morning, shackled, and moved out, but weren't on the plane until later that evening.

"We could see the people coming off the plane, but they couldn't see into the van," she said.

"There were children in shackles, a pregnant lady, old people, everybody just being marched around like herded animals really, getting off the plane, getting into these other buses."

The conviction that saw Wihongi detained by ICE in the first place was thrown out by a court in June.

She described the moment as unbelievable.

"I didn't want to be too excited or get too ahead of myself," she said.

"I thought for sure it'd be a few more months they would try and hold me in there, I didn't think that they were going to let me out right away."

Wihongi said having hope in detention meant you'd be devastated at one point or another.

Everlee Wihongi and whanau Supplied / Courtney Wihongi

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade had been providing consular assistance during Wihongi's detainment. She said staff from New Zealand's Los Angeles consulate were helpful, even bringing her Kiwi chocolate on one visit.

Staff helped her recover documents like her passport, Green Card, and drivers license - something she didn't have when she was released.

Foreign Affairs Minister Winston Peters had said Wihongi was detained for not declaring her historic cannabis possession conviction, but that was completely false, she said.

"In all my time coming back and forth, I've never been given one of those forms."

"Even when the consulate asked, 'did you get one of those papers to mark your conviction?' I was never given one of those," Wihongi said.

She was shocked by the public response to her time in ICE custody.

"It was something else to come out of something like that to so much love and support from not only my family, but strangers and people I didn't know."

She hoped those still detained by ICE had the same love and support she experienced.

"There are just more people in there that have nothing, they don't have the family support like I did, they don't have their country supporting them like I did, I just wish more people could experience that," Wihongi said.

World.title: National leadership meeting sets back Queenstown regional growth deal
World.content:
The National Party's crisis talks on Wednesday morning scuppered a planned regional deal announcement in Queenstown at the last minute.

MPs and local leaders were due to unveil a 10-year plan for managing the region's growth after months of negotiations between government officials and representatives from Queenstown Lakes District Council, Central Otago District Council and Otago Regional Council.

But the plan was cancelled after the National Party caucus was called to the capital.

Walking into Parliament for the leadership vote, Southland MP Joseph Mooney told media he would rather be in Queenstown marking the deal.

A new announcement date is yet to be confirmed.

RMA Reform Under-Secretary Simon Court of the ACT Party organised a round-table infrastructure discussion in Queenstown in place of the planned announcement.

He said he was disappointed by the delay, but expected the deal to go ahead within weeks.

"The ACT Party can't control what National is doing right now. I'm sure that they will come to a resolution and we'll get back around the table with the mayors and other representatives from Queenstown and Central Otago and we'll sign the deal," Court said.

Queenstown mayor John Glover said he was also disappointed, but understood why the signing had to be rescheduled.

"It was a signing ceremony which had two ministers of the Crown - because it is a legal contract between the council and the Crown. So it was an in-person signing ceremony and circumstances changed," he said.

"For me, the sooner we get this signed the better - because if this deal had been in place five or ten years ago, I think we'd have had a more coordinated approach across all of government to provide a response to the needs that we're having as we grow."

The deal comes amid mounting infrastructure challenges for the region, in particular Queenstown which has recorded explosive growth in visitors and population.

Last month Glover announced he was setting up a mayoral taskforce to tackle severe peak-time traffic congestion, while the head of the regional tourism organisation warned the district was not equipped to handle further growth.

This week Glover and Auckland mayor Wayne Brown wrote to Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop with concerns about "out-of-sequence, out-of-zone" greenfield housing developments being fast-tracked.

The letter was a request to meet and discuss the impacts, Glover said.

Glover also attended a community meeting earlier this month about Ridgeburn, a planned 1210-home development near Arrowtown.

The development sits outside the council's planned growth zones and some residents fear it will exacerbate traffic congestion and harm tourism.

"Locally we know that our existing infrastructure really hasn't kept place with the growth. We have a long chat this morning about building more houses, and we're doing a lot of that. But the schools, the health services, the state highways, the public transport - they're all way, way behind where they should be," Glover said.

"The concern is that there will be consented quite significant housing developments without the tools to develop the infrastructure."

It was not just Wayne Brown who shared those concerns, he said.

"If you look at the Pegasus development [near Christchurch] with a 16,000 person petition against it - there's some huge concerns around the country."

World.title: Ex-cops not guilty of obstructing justice relating to Alan Hall case
World.content:
Two former police officers accused of obstructing justice in an investigation which led to the wrongful conviction of Alan Hall in the 1980s have been found not guilty.

The men, whose names are suppressed, have been on trial in the High Court at Auckland charged with wilfully attempting to obstruct, prevent, pervert or defeat the course of justice.

A third former defendant has since died.

Justice Ian Gault delivered the decision on Wednesday morning. The men's interim name suppression is extended while the court considers an application for permanent name suppression.

Arthur Easton. Supplied / Police

Hall spent 17 years in prison after being convicted of murdering Arthur Easton, who was killed during a home invasion by a man wielding a bayonet.

The decision was quashed by the Supreme Court in 2022 after it found a substantial miscarriage of justice had occurred.

As the decision was delivered, Hall sat at the back of the courtoom with his brothers. Outside the court, his brothers spoke on behalf of the family.

Geoff Hall said justice has run its course.

"Our road came to an end at the Supreme Court, that was our journey. This is a side road that the justice system had been abused, we were here in support of that and Alan as a victim in the family," he said.

"To an extent everybody is a victim of what happened in Alan's trial."

Alan Hall's brother Geoff (left) and Greg outside the Auckland High Court. RNZ

Geoff Hall said everyone deserved the right to a fair trial.

"What's happened here today, this trial, has put anybody on notice. If they want to go through and have their version of what the truth is or be tempted in any way, it's on notice that they can end up in court as well."

Greg Hall delivered a statement, saying they respected the court's decision even though it was difficult to accept.

"While a verdict did not result in a criminal conviction, some of the facts presented during the trial raised important questions about transparency and fairness," he said.

"Every person deserves a right to a fair trial. The right relies on the absolute assurance that all witness evidence presented in court is strictly maintained in its original, unedited state, fully consistent with the established evidentiary standards."

Private investigator Tim McKinnel helped prove Hall's innocence and was at court for today's decision.

He says the process was about accountability, but Arthur Easton's murder was still unresolved.

"It's one of those questions that's yet to be answered, who is responsible for what happened to Mr Easten and his sons and so it's a big deal," McKinnel said.

"It's one of the real tragedies of this case is that it's taken so long to begin to ask the right questions."

Assistant Police Commissioner Corrie Parnell acknoweldged the two families who have been seeking justice for decades - the Hall family and the Easton family.

"This decision brings an end to criminal proceedings and Police stand by our decision to put this case before the courts," Parnell said.

He said since the Supreme Court acquitted Hall in 2022, the onus has been on the entire justice system to find out how the substantial miscarriage of justice happened.

"It is our view after a thorough investigation decades later that there was an end-to-end Justice system failure, but we also recognised that individuals responsible for key steps in the case played a critical role and that needed to be answered in the courts," Parnell said.

He said police accepted that they had a part to play in the failure.

"While legislation, systems and processes in the Justice sector have advanced in the decades since this case was first prosecuted, we acknowledge the Hall family have been left waiting for answers for a long time," Parnell said.

Family 'profoundly relieved'

The family of one of the men found not guilty said the verdict brought much-needed closure but the trial caused stress and uncertainty as he defended the serious allegations about decisions made 40 years ago.

"Our family is profoundly relieved that our father has been found not guilty," they said.

"After four years living under serious allegations that questioned his character, integrity, and decades of service to the New Zealand public, this verdict brings much-needed closure."

They said their father's physical and mental wellbeing had been significantly affected.

"What should have been peaceful retirement years were instead consumed by fear, stress, and uncertainty, as he defended himself against charges concerning investigative decisions made approximately forty years ago."

They said they respected the court process and were grateful the evidence was thoroughly tested.

But they were concerned "the process appeared more focused on assigning blame than fairly assessing decisions made in a very different era, under the procedures and legal advice then available".

"We urge police leadership to reflect on how such matters are managed, particularly regarding the support and treatment of retired officers facing charges over historic duties," they said.

"Officers who act in good faith, following the procedures and legal advice available at the time, must be able to trust that their organisation will treat them fairly and provide appropriate support when allegations arise."

World.title: People 'unravelling': Fears a 'bad batch' of synthetic cannabis has hit Wellington's Newtown
World.content:
Paul Fletcher finds himself on a Monday, in the middle of the road, trying to stop traffic, as a man tries to attack another with a crutch.

It is a chaotic scene that for Fletcher - an Anglican priest working and living in the heart of Newtown - has become "sadly normal".

"Visible drug use on the streets, through the day; aggressive behaviour at least weekly that just plays out; and moments of psychosis often through a week, that is in our main drag."

Synthetic cannabis may be to blame for behaviour in Newtown Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Fletcher said the man he tried to stop attacking others had been threatening to stab customers and staff at the New World on Riddiford Street two weeks before.

"Cops pick him up, but the cops who are caring… he's not made for prison, that guy. He needs help and support, and rightly so, but he's back here two hours later."

Anglican priest Paul Fletcher. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Fletcher has a front-row seat to life in the suburb, and says services for mental health, addiction, trauma and housing are exhausted beyond limits. Government inaction was to blame, he said.

"People are unwell, and they're unravelling."

He's heard families are contemplating leaving, and doesn't want the vibrant, welcoming village he loves to lose some of its gold.

Fletcher is among community leaders and businesses in the suburb highlighting a spike in aggressive behaviour, and calling for more support, including more health services and extra police on the weekend.

Some are also asking whether harmful synthetic cannabis is to blame.

RNZ reported on concerns with anti-social behaviour last year, and while some say initial improvements were made, others are urging the city council to permanently extend an inner-city safety programme out to the suburb.

New World's owner has taken to playing classical music on weekends to calm the environment outside the store. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

The Salvation Army's Andrew Wilson and New World Newtown owner Dave Wickham said more police on the weekends are essential.

Wickham had taken to playing classical music in a speaker out the front of the store to calm the environment outside, he said. At times he fears for his customers and his staff.

"Yelling, screaming, blocking the entrance way has happened, we've got regular feedback on Facebook around people not wanting to come to the shop now, not wanting to come down Riddiford Street because they're just feeling unsafe.

"We've had instances of people being followed down the street, one of my staff got followed and ran back to the shop - just from somebody who is unfortunately on drugs."

When RNZ visited the suburb earlier this month, another business owner, who did not want to be named, said he called police regularly.

Fletcher outside St Tom's Anglican Church. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

With a person yelling at bystanders on the footpath, the business owner asked RNZ to phone the police because he had already done so multiple times.

Wellington Mayor Andrew Little said police have told him synthetic cannabis is fueling the spike in aggressive behaviour.

"I shared with them some video footage that a business owner had sent to me, they said, 'Yep that's the clear result of a bad batch of synthetic cannabis that had been circulating in Wellington.' It's caused a lot of concern for the police and health authorities."

Melanie Paddon. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Acting sergeant for the area Melanie Paddon would not talk specifically about synthetic cannabis, but said the quality and quantities of drugs fluctuated constantly.

"We rely on the community to let us know about this behaviour, so that we can manage it and address it on those instances.

"Police have done a number of search warrants at different addresses along those lines which has been the result of the community engaging with us."

Paddon said police had had an increase in reports of crime - such as shop-lifting - in the suburb, and staff had boosted presence there, though did not specify if there would now be a permanent presence on the weekend.

She said police were dealing with complex issues, involving vulnerable people, which couldn't fit into a "one-time response". She urged the community to keep calling the police.

Wilson said a number of troubled people were consistently "falling through the cracks" of a range of services.

Mental Health Minister Matt Doocey said the government had put mental health peer support workers in the emergency department in the suburb, so if they presented in a crisis, someone could help.

He said support had been boosted through the Wellington City Mission Crisis Recovery Cafe - somewhere people struggling with addiction and mental health could go.

Health New Zealand's Paul Oxnam said there was a range of mental health services in the suburb, including early intervention, community mental health and specialist teams for young people and mothers, addiction and treatment services including those who have opioid addiction, acute inpatient services and a crisis resolution service.

Renewed calls for Māori wardens, extension of Wellington's inner-city safety programme

Wilson said he wanted the council's City Safety Team, which operates only in the CBD, installed permanently in Newtown.

That involved community patrols from Māori wardens, urban liaison officers and work with homeless agencies.

Creeps Record Parlour owner Apa said he wanted to see Māori wardens in the suburb.

"It's quite worrying to see all these people, I get real hoha with it… but also you have to emphasise the whole situation."

He said being Māori, he could see the effects of colonisation play out in these situations.

Creeps Record Parlour owner Apa. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"Imagine having Māori wardens here in Newtown being able to walk the streets - Māori wardens are quite different from police and… they have a caring edge."

Following reporting from RNZ last year, a council team worked on a range of activities including boosting some lighting and CCTV cameras - but that ended when the council budget dried up.

Little said he wanted the City Safety Team in Newtown, but that would be part of long-term budget discussions

"I do have a commitment that we do make a permanent commitment, when we can and when that starts, I can't give a clear steer on that at this point - but that'll be another few months away before I can do that."

Police said they had had an increase in reports of crime - such as shop-lifting - in the suburb RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Fletcher said he did not want Newtown to lose its heart.

World.title: Homeless beg council to reconsider eviction from red zone
World.content:
A homeless man living in Christchurch's earthquake-damaged red zone has called on the local council to back down from its plan to evict the community.

Christchurch City Council has ordered dozens of homeless people living in the red zone near the Avon River to leave their makeshift camp by the end of February.

Leaflets were handed to the community of about 60, giving them the deadline for early next year.

Moko Reuben addressed councillors during a public deputation at Wednesday's meeting.

The red zone had gradually become a last-ditch haven for people without housing since the earthquakes, Reuben said.

"Those also excluded from the rental market are living in vehicles, caravans and we're living in makeshift shelters and unable to access state or community housing," he said.

"This is not a choice of convenience - it's a response to the systemic lack of options. The coming move-on order removes even the precarious foothold with no confirmed alternative housing or support plan in place."

The red zone camp - land cleared of homes due to earthquake damage - stood near the edge of the Avon River in Wetlands Grove in Bexley, a street abandoned after the 2011 earthquake and now lined with cars, caravans, buses, tents and a few ramshackle structures used as homes for a growing community.

Ngawai Timu RNZ / Nate McKinnon

The council had provided some support to those living there, including portaloos and rubbish skips.

But the council has said it ultimately planned to flood the area to turn it into wetlands.

"On the 28th of February, authorities will enforce a formal move-on order requiring all people and informal structures to leave the red zone," Reuben said. "To date there's been no public-funded or scalable housing response tied to this deadline."

No alternative housing options had been offered and moving them on would cause a bigger health crisis, he said.

"The impacts and risks of enforcing this order without prior preparation will lead to severe, predictable harm, escalated homelessness and displacement," Reuben told councillors.

"It's going to be a big shift. We want to pause... because we need to find that suitable place that we can go."

Fellow community member Ngawai Timu, who sat beside Reuben during the presentation, said the loneliness some felt in transitional housing was a possible reason why the red zone community was so big.

The caravan park land. RNZ / Rachel Graham

Plans for a caravan park in the red zone had also been given the green light by the Ōtākaro Avon River Corridor Regeneration Committee, a newly formed co-governance committee with representatives from council and mana whenua, following an application from the Motor Caravan Association.

World.title: Confidence only gets you so far: Undefeated, PM Christopher Luxon is still on the ropes
World.content:
Analysis: Christopher Luxon has survived another test of his leadership - but the job ahead has become even harder.

With just over 12 weeks until the election, this is the third credible public challenge to his leadership since last November, and the second confidence vote he has publicly faced down.

In a brief two-minute press conference at the Beehive Banquet Hall after the first vote in April, he revealed he'd called the vote on himself then lambasted the media for reporting on discontent in National's ranks.

Within hours, NZ First leader Winston Peters was criticising it as a bad move that only invited further confrontations from a dissatisfied caucus.

Luxon's repeat performance after Wednesday's vote was even shorter and more guarded: again answering no questions, but this time leaving unsaid who had asked for the vote and focusing squarely on the election rather than taking potshots at reporters.

His hollow victory follows a series of missteps over the past fortnight, including deciding on live radio - without consulting his party and MPs - to campaign on a referendum on the MMP electoral system.

They later backed the idea but his MPs would have been frustrated by the impromptu handling, and a costly referendum hardly fits the party's stated strategy of focusing squarely on cost of living.

On its own, this would not have been enough to prompt an upset, but it follows worsening polling and repeated gaffes. Examples from the past fortnight underline exactly some of the personal traits that have proven both a help and a hindrance in his political career so far.

Communication has never been Luxon's strength, with consistent criticism of his wordcloud-style CEO buzzwords like "gripped up" and filler phrases like "what I would say to you" peppering his speech, as well as unforced errors in media.

That happened as recently as Monday, when he found himself talking about new taxes the party might bring in rather than the budget responsibility rules he'd announced just a day before.

A week earlier he had to apologise for comments he made to the Rotorua Business Chamber, where he said small businesses had a "parent-child" mentality with the government.

As a former chief executive, Luxon's competent businessman image has also been undermined by a recurrent blind spot over how the less-well-off perceive his privileged position.

A week ago he had to justify using a Defence Force plane to get home from a National Party fundraising dinner on the same day unemployment hit a record 11-year high.

That just adds to earlier comments about being "wealthy and ... sorted" or being "entitled" to the $52,000 PM's accommodation allowance.

Luxon Leadership Challenge: What happens next? Afternoons Download MP3 11m

Where he has been praised is in his ability to manage holding together a three-party coalition - despite some scepticism - but those very partners have often undermined the prime minister's authority and have largely gone unpunished beyond some verbal criticism, at least in the public eye.

After Peters launched a tirade at an opposition MP in Parliament less than two weeks ago, Luxon labelled the comments "racist" and spoke to the foreign minister in private - but took no further action, despite former political leaders warning a sacking may be warranted even if it meant the end of the coalition and a snap election.

While those corporate-style, managerial, and somewhat disconnected from the common man traits have caused problems for Luxon in his time in the top job, they've also driven him and National back into government, and secured some valuable gains for the country.

The most visible of these is the India Free Trade agreement he and Trade Minister Todd McClay unveiled late last year, which is bound to significantly boost some exports and help diversify New Zealand's trading options - despite Peters' ongoing opposition to it.

The visit from Indian counterpart Narendra Modi is just one example of where Luxon has been able to connect with foreign leaders on a personal level, a role he has clearly relished.

That personable attitude when cameras aren't rolling was also an advantage in the strong campaign that led to Luxon's 2023 election win, built on a strategy that made a clear virtue of his business credentials and economic nous.

Opposition MPs have criticised National for political infighting. Zach Cornelisen / RNZ

Public opinion did turn against Labour's Covid-era governing and economic approach, but that was partly a result of Luxon's consistent economic messaging.

Boosting National from the dismal 25.6 percent result in the 2020 election that gave Labour a sole majority to the 38.0 percent the party staked out just three years later is an undoubted achievement.

His people management skills also helped revitalise National when he replaced Judith Collins in 2021 to become the party's fourth leader in five years.

He will need to work very hard indeed convincing his MPs, coalition partners and the voting public those skills are what New Zealand needs.

World.title: 'Nowhere to hide' for Australia's under-fire batters against Bangladesh
World.content:
Former Australian Test opener Ed Cowan says some of Australia's batters are under pressure to make significant scores as the summer of cricket begins against Bangladesh in the Top End this week.

"If you're in the Australian Test team, and not performing regularly, there is just nowhere to hide," Cowan said on the ABC Cricket Podcast.

"And unfortunately, sometimes you get these weaker teams, and the expectation actually goes up. Cricket is hard enough, let alone with the weight of the world on your shoulders."

The Australian team is about to enter a 12-month period with potentially 21 Tests scheduled, including key away fixtures in India, South Africa and England.

Between June 2025 and the start of this cycle tomorrow, they played eight Tests, five of which were in Australia.

Australia played five of their eight Tests over the last 12 months at home, including the Ashes against England. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

"That's two careers, 21 Test matches. You could have two careers in that time. That's a lot of Test cricket," Cowan said.

That cycle begins in Darwin when they take on Bangladesh, a nation ranked ninth in the ICC Test rankings.

At the conclusion of the recent successful Ashes series against England, the average age of the Australian team was just under 34. This is a team that has played together and had great success for a long time.

The Test between Australia and Bangladesh starts on Thursday August 13 in Darwin, and you can hear every ball live on ABC Listen.

Cowan does not believe that playing lower-ranked opposition necessarily provides younger players with a chance to gain experience.

"I think you are trying to pick your best available team and there's always an opportunity to work through your portfolio of players, and they've done this in recent years, usually away from home and it's less opposition dependent and more condition dependent," he said.

The bowling attack has been well established for some time with the likes of Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon proving a recipe for success.

Where the questions creep in is around the batting line-up.

Jake Weatherald was given an opportunity to open the batting in the recent Ashes series but is yet to score an international century, with a top score of 72.

Jake Weatherald will be looking to impress in front of his home crowd in Darwin against Bangladesh (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Cowan expects the Northern Territory product to open in the first game, but says he remains under pressure.

"If Jake Weatherald doesn't get 100 in the next five Test matches, more than likely we'll find someone who will get an opportunity to open the batting. And so there's going to be some natural attrition over the coming months," he said.

He is not the only player who will be searching for form in this two-match series against Bangladesh. Marnus Labuschagne has averaged 26.61 with the bat in his last 20 tests and has taken time away from playing to focus on a training block in Queensland.

"After eight weeks of being able to just go back to my fundamentals and working on my game, spending hours and hours on the simple things, just my shots, working on my shapes and my technique as a whole, is something that I definitely needed," Labuschagne told reporters in Brisbane last week.

Loading Instagram content

It has been over 1,100 days since he last reached triple figures in a Test match back in 2023. Cowan believes these Tests could be a step in the right direction for Labuschagne.

"The greatest thing that you can have as a Test batsman is confidence. And confidence is only bred through performance," he said.

The youngest member of Australia's most recent Test team is Cameron Green. When the West Australian debuted in 2020, aged 21, he was touted as one of the best young talents in the country, but his recent form has some questioning his future in the side.

The now 27-year-old has played 37 Tests and has a batting average of 32.75 and a bowling average of 38.94, but Australian coach Andrew McDonald is resolute that Green remains a vital member of his side.

"We believe Cam Green is a very, very skilled player, and we believe, sometimes, his performances have been taken a little bit out of context," McDonald told SEN Radio.

"He's been contributing to this team, as have a lot of that top seven, in conditions that haven't been favourable to batters."

Cowan believes these two Tests present an opportunity for those out of form to find some form at a time when there is less pressure coming from other domestic players.

The last time Australia played a Test against Bangladesh was 2017, where Australia won the series 2-1. (Getty Images: /SOPA Images/LightRocket/Md Manik)

"They get first crack at it. And when there's no other cricket going on, there was a CA XI game that we'll come to, but there's no Shield cricket, there's no Aussie A tours, no-one's putting pressure on anyone," he said.

"It's a bit of a free swing. And in many respects, that should free the batters up to just go and play."

World.title: High school American footballer rattled by snake in helmet
World.content:
A high school American football player in the United States had every right to be rattled after finding a venomous snake inside his helmet during practice.

A team was going through its paces at Maumelle High school in Central Arkansas when a student felt unusual movement inside his headgear following warm-ups and brought his helmet to an assistant coach for inspection.

A slithering 2-foot (61cm) cottonmouth was discovered behind some padding.

The pit viper was so reluctant to exit the helmet that police officers had to pour water into it to force the snake out and into a bag.

Animal services technicians arrived a few minutes later, identified the snake as a deadly cottonmouth and took it to a wooded area far from the school.

Cottonmouths are the second-most-venomous snakes found in Arkansas.

Snake caught in bike chain bites woman The woman, in her 60s, was riding on a northern NSW rail trail when she ran over a two-metre snake that became trapped then bit her.

Animal services director Chris Davis said the player wore the helmet for nearly an hour and was fortunate he was not bitten.

"It was unreal," Davis said. "You had to kind of be there and take pictures to say this was real."

The player grabbed a different helmet and continued practice.

But the situation caused the head coach to reiterate to his team that players should examine their equipment carefully before using it, to check for insects or anything larger and more dangerous.

AP

World.title: 'Right to privacy': Scott speaks as Geelong concussion saga continues
World.content:
Geelong coach Chris Scott insists there has been no negativity around the playing group since Jake Kolodjashnij identified himself as the player at the centre of the Cats' concussion crisis.

Kolodjashnij, who is out of contract at season's end, faces an uncertain future after being ruled out of playing at any level this weekend.

The 31-year-old has played 11 AFL games this season, but was managed out of the team in round 19 and has since made one appearance in the VFL.

Geelong sits atop the VFL ladder and should make a deep run in the finals, potentially giving Kolodjashnij more opportunities to press his case for an unlikely new contract.

Chris Scott would not be drawn on the details of what's going on behind closed doors at Kardinia Park. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

The mental toll of the saga is unknown, with Scott simply saying Kolodjashnij had been supported by teammates and the club.

The dual premiership coach also refused to go into the exact reasons why Kolodjashnij had been ruled out for the club's matches against North Melbourne this weekend.

Kolodjashnij decided to name himself last Friday, a day after news broke of Geelong's controversial waiver for a previously unidentified player.

"I think any player deserves the right to privacy," Scott said.

"I understand that we are in a public game, and there's a quite savage desire to know certain things.

"I suspect the players are saying, 'Hey mate, if there is anything we can do …'

"In terms of the impact on our broader group, I haven't seen any negativity at all.

Jake Kolodjashnij (right) with brother Kade. Kade was forced into early retirement due to concussion issues. (Getty Images: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

"I thought our players, as they have done for a long period of time, they just get on with the job.

"Difficult to compartmentalise sometimes, maybe this is a little more challenging than other times, but I'm still pretty confident we can do it.

"Because the situation is the status quo, I haven't felt the need to get an update [on Kolodjashnij].''

Geelong are facing a nervous wait after being issued with a belated "please explain'' for their handling of the secret concussion deal with Kolodjashnij.

The AFL has hired independent legal counsel to help decide on the case.

It was expected the league would wrap up its investigation yesterday, but the findings will likely not be released until early next week.

Kolodjashnij unavailable amid concussion saga Geelong confirms Jake Kolodjashnij will not be available for selection at VFL or AFL level this weekend as the spotlight continues to shine on the club over the controversial secret concussion waiver in his contract.

Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking and former Cats president (now AFL Commission boss) Craig Drummond have been under fire since news broke of the controversial waiver.

"There's a part of me that would like to give an impassioned defence of certain people within our club, but I just don't think it would help at the moment," Scott said.

"Even if it is to our detriment, our responsibility, and especially my responsibility, is to respect his [Kolodjashnij's] privacy."

Kolodjashnij dealt with concussions in the 2024 season, but ultimately signed a two-year deal until the end of 2026.

Instead of receiving a definitive answer when forced to face the AFL concussion panel in 2024, Kolodjashnij was left in limbo about playing on or retiring.

His twin brother Kade, who played for the Gold Coast and Melbourne, prematurely retired in 2020 due to concussion.

Multiple AFL players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern, and former number-one pick Paddy McCartin, have also been forced into retirement because of repeated concussions.
